#6780. My Most-Worn Winter Jacket Is $250

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Filson’s Insulated Canvas Outfitter is everything your vintage workwear isn’t.

Welcome to the Esquire Endorsement. Heavily researched. Thoroughly vetted. These picks are the best way to spend your hard-earned cash.

I was sitting at a dive bar in Brooklyn, looking past my wife and a friend during a lull in conversation at the two pool tables with two games going on. One guy—next team up, when I see him—was wearing the uniform: mesh-backed trucker hat, work pants with carabiner keys, and a vintage work jacket (you know the brand). But vintage gives that layer too much credit. It looked like its former owner was shot and left in a ditch—and our hero, like a member of the Joad family, needed a jacket, found the deceased, peeled this jacket off him, put it on, and kept on rolling toward the big city.

I focus back on the table. “Do y’all think we’ve run out of vintage?” I blurt out. “What?” My wife, with good reason, is confused; my buddy, silent, is equally so. “Like, vintage work jackets,” I say, pointing to this guy. “You know, America has been deindustrializing for half a century, and the whole 2020 resale boom has peaked. Maybe this guy is wearing that jacket because all the good vintage workwear is gone?” Neither of them cared enough to entertain me.

But I care to talk about it. The vintage-workwear ship has sailed, the bubble has popped—whatever. You do not need to pay $500 for some old guy’s work jacket in the name of “sustainability.” If you’re doing that at this point, you’re a victim. You’d be better off talking that $500 and splitting it in two. With the first $250, take someone out on a date. With the second $250, buy this Filson jacket—the unequivocally best barn coat, work jacket, or whatever you want to classify it as on the market. This is the only winter jacket a man needs.

The three-season version of this jacket, the regular Canvas Outfitter, is a perennial top seller for Filson. It is obviously a good barn jacket, classic in its hunting-inspired styling: flannel lining, corduroy collar, hand warmers, and big shell pockets. But if I were to get that style of old-school hunting jacket—and sorry to blaspheme against my beloved Filson—I would go to a few other brands.

Where Filson runs away with the barn-coat crown is in adding insulation; no one does it better. The original, though flannel lined, feels just a little too flimsy for me, and if it’s going to hit lower than my waist, I’d rather have full butt coverage. But with the insulation and the internal structure it provides, the jacket sits ever so slightly higher on the body. It’s not cropped, but the fit becomes more trucker or work jacket, less barn coat—hence my comparison to a Carhartt Detroit. Personally, it’s exactly what I want. Looks good no matter how you wear it; flatters any body type you can imagine.

That said, the actual benefit of that insulation is not aesthetic. It’s practical. This is one of the warmest jackets in my rotation, and it’s easily the most durable. The ten-and-a-half-ounce duck canvas never gets a nick—not on a hike, not on a day doing yard work. And while this is not at all a rain jacket, the polyester lining means it can put up with moisture infinitely better than something filled with down. If you get caught in a fall rainstorm, no worries. If you have a snow day, this is the ultimate outer layer. For that reason, it often ends up as one of my most-worn garments over the colder months.

To come back to my original point: Aren’t we all tired of the absurdity of vintage? I don’t mean to be anti-sustainability or anti–old clothes. But aren’t we tired of hype cycles around buying someone else’s clothing? Workwear is supposed to be bought cheap and worn hard. This jacket is the answer in my mind. It’s not trendy, nor is it especially expensive. You can buy one brand-new—novel, no?—for $250 (a steal these days) and know that every crease, every fade, every repaired armpit hole is yours and yours alone. Wear it for a few decades, then it’ll be your vintage. When you’re dead, some kid will sell it to a yuppie for a 200 percent markup. That’s the goal.

#6779. 40 Years On, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs’ Fashion Collection Remains Ahead of Its Time

An anniversary exhibition revisits key moments from MAD’s history

On my first trip to France in the mid-2000s, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs (MAD) became my go-to destination in Paris for a fashion-museum fix. With each subsequent visit, the intellectualized fashion scene became more saturated, as maisons increasingly invested in their heritage with public-facing venues (Fondation Azzedine Alaïa, Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris, and Galerie Dior), plus the opening of Palais Galliera’s permanent galleries. As far as I’m concerned, when it comes to fashion exhibitions, the more the merrier. But I remain loyal to my first love. For art and design lovers like myself, it’s hard to top MAD’s interdisciplinary approach—and, of course, that prime Rue de Rivoli address.

This fall, the museum’s self-contained fashion collection—the Musée de la Mode et du Textile (originally Musée des Arts de la Mode)—celebrates its 40th anniversary with an exhibition titled “Look: 40 Years of Fashion at the Museum,” open through April 4, 2027. While the museum’s central hall, the Nef (“nave”), pays homage to 40 of its 70-plus shows by spotlighting a look to represent each, the surrounding galleries invite visitors behind the scenes of an atelier and the museum itself.

“As the custodian of France’s National Fashion Collection, it was really important for us to show people their heritage, as well as the diversity of the collection,” Sophie Lemahieu, the museum’s curator of fashion and textile collections after 1947, told Harper’s Bazaar. Co-curating the exhibition with MAD director Bénédicte Gady, Lemahieu sought to convey the skills of the many professionals who made each garment a reality, as well as the museum workers who care for and prepare them for display.

The multilayered approach represents a consecration of fashion as art—a concept MAD’s Musée de la Mode et du Textile has been instrumental in transmitting since its inception, when such a notion was far from the prevailing opinion. “40 years ago, it was not obvious to have fashion in the museum, even in Paris. There were many curators and art historians who were extremely mad because all these floors could have been used to show Islamic art or other decorative art collections,” said Lemahieu. “It took time to legitimize fashion history as an art history field, but now every museum wants to have fashion exhibitions because they’ve seen how meaningful they can be. People identify with fashion because it’s part of our lives. We all wear clothes.”

For context, MAD was founded in 1864 and contained textiles and fashion prior to the official establishment of the Musée des Arts de la Mode. The decision to formalize its fashion collection was twofold: first, it marked the union of two monumental collections, the Union Centrale des Arts Décoratifs and the Union Française des Arts de la Costume. More broadly, during the 1980s, under President François Mitterrand, the French government began advocating for fashion as national cultural prestige, rather than a purely commercial entity (though it was undeniably one of the country’s leading exports). In 1982, the Louvre’s Cour Carrée courtyard became a designated venue for French ready-to-wear shows, making a powerful global statement. To quote Lemahieu, “Fashion became political.”

For the Musée des Arts de la Mode’s inaugural exhibition, “Moments de Mode” (1986)—which in “Look” is illustrated by a pristine 1760 robe à la française, the oldest garment in the show—MAD pulled out all the scenography stops. Working with theater professionals, curators presented an immersive history of fashion, including a mannequin, clad in a 19th-century cycling suit, in continuous movement on a mechanical bicycle. While today, such a display would never happen due to conservation requirements, it set the tone for MAD’s myriad innovations showcasing garments at their finest.

Another fascinating example from Moments de Mode is MAD’s usage of invisible mounts, which make garments appear as if they are floating. Visitors to Fondation Azzedine Alaïa may recall that these spectral mannequins have become somewhat of a signature for the institution. Lemahieu said this is not a coincidence: “Mr. Alaïa actually came to the exhibition in 1986 and thought this was an absolutely wonderful way to show a dress, so he asked the same person to do the mannequins for his foundation.”

Elsewhere are odes to MAD’s many monographic shows, from its first, Yves Saint Laurent in 1986, to its traveling blockbuster “Christian Dior, Couturier of Dreams” in 2017. Dior is one of the few designers to have multiple MAD exhibitions—another is Schiaparelli, who was the subject of shows in 2004 and 2022. Similarly, MAD staged two exhibitions about the 1980s—in 1989 and 2022. Lemahieu noted in all cases, however, MAD never repeats its approach to the same subject.

She also pointed to several exhibitions conceived by her colleague, Denis Bruna, curator in chief of the Fashion and Textile Department, who favors a more sociological approach. “The Mechanics of Undergarments: An Indiscreet History of the Silhouette” (2013), for example, explored techniques used by women and men to shape their bodies, while “Proper Attire Required: When Clothing Causes a Scandal” (2016), focused on controversies that marked turning points in fashion history.

Nearly all the garments in “Look” were previously featured in their corresponding exhibitions. The one exception is a tricolor bodysuit that Gilles Asquin created for the 2024 Paris Olympics Opening Ceremony (several young designers contributed looks for the momentous event). The garment, which the French National Olympic and Sports Committee entrusted to MAD, is displayed to represent the exhibition “Fashion and Sport, From One Podium to Another,” 2023. Lemahieu said the bodysuit’s inclusion demonstrates how museum exhibitions can open pathways for future donations.

Acquisition, documentation, storage, conservation, and mannequinage (the art of mounting a garment) are some of the internal museum processes discussed in the “How Clothing Becomes a Work of Art: Backstage at the Museum” galleries. Meanwhile, “Backstage: Creating Couture” focuses on inspiration, fabrication, ornamentation, and photography. It’s here where MAD can proudly show the range of its holdings (more than 150,000 pieces from the third century to the present day), which include preparatory sketches, fashion illustrations, embroidery samples, and more. Rarities include a mannequin upon which Madeleine Vionnet draped her fabrics, as well as pleating boards used by Maison Lognon, a historic Parisian pleating atelier founded in 1853.

Running concurrently this fall at MAD are exhibitions dedicated to the Thai court’s fashion evolution, Brazilian photographer Rafael Pavarotti’s cutting-edge imagery, and Marion Delarue’s wearable art created during her residency at the museum. Forty years on, this mix of shows, in scale and subject, has become MAD’s unique strength, as Lemahieu described: “It’s important for us to not just make bigger and bigger exhibitions. We need to be involved in what happens in haute couture, but we also need to be here for young designers and to be aware of what’s happening in fashion socially.” It’s that distinctive cocktail of programming—not to mention all the period-room interiors, jewels, and posters—that still keeps MAD at the top of my Paris museum list after all these years.

#6777. I Got the Love and Dating Life of My Dreams After Transitioning

Forget everything you’ve heard about how hard it is to date while trans. I’m the belle of the goddamn ball.

I’ve been dating since I was 14, several years before my transition and before the guys I dated would see me as a woman. But even back then, I was cognizant of the way men reacted to me instantly—usually it was a cute guy in class who seemed to immediately take a liking to me. The issue was that, as a girl who didn’t present as such, I was often kept a secret, relegated to late-night phone calls and texts or one-on-one hangouts.

As I got older and the men around me became less constrained by the rigidity of small-town surroundings and conservative societal norms, I began to date them more publicly—they’d meet my friends and family and ask me to meet theirs. Still, I knew none of these partners were what I really saw for myself. Now an adult woman who still didn’t present as such, I ultimately wasn’t going out with the kind of men I wanted. Instead, I was dating dudes on the DL—bi men who were keenly interested in the fact that my body was male and others who were in their “experimental” phase.

But I wanted to experience sex and love as a woman—ultimately, I wanted to experience everything as a woman. That would mean not dating men who were trying to repress latent homosexual desires but dating those who were looking for a woman as a partner. I wanted to be courted properly while wearing something fabulous. I wanted autonomy.

During the pandemic, many of us thought about how we wanted to live our lives post-COVID. Trans people came out publicly and began their medical transitions. I happened to be one of them. I came out on my 30th birthday to both my friends and family. I would do the same at work the following week. And once I’d grown my hair and had it braided in an African salon around the corner from my apartment, I decided it was time to come out in my dating life as well—to present as myself on the apps.

That’s when I realized, fairly immediately, something a certain kind of Bud Light–boycotting member of society would hate to hear about trans dating: Men are not only open to but actively pursuing trans women. And no, I’m not talking about the ones who saw me as some kind of novelty—I had zero interest in being an experiment or tourist attraction for dudes who were clearly fetishizing me or looking to recreate a scene from a porno. I’d suffered enough of that already, thanks.

Sure, I encountered a few of those, the ones who’d open with intrusive and inappropriate questions (“Pre-op or post-op?” Block!). But by and large, most men I connected with seemed surprisingly well-versed in being with trans women. These were people who had actual experience dating women like me and wanted more of it, guys who knew how to navigate my body. There’s a stigma that comes with dating while transgender—this idea that it somehow narrows your options or makes you less widely desirable. But as soon as I changed my photos on the apps to reflect my transitioned self, the massive uptick in engagement was instant. In fact, even the dating apps themselves, not just the men on them, were suddenly more interested in me. Raya, which I’d been on a two-year wait list for, let me in the day after I reapplied with new photos in which I presented as my female self.

Not long after the first week or two on the apps, I’d built up a roster of men I was dating regularly—and yes, they all knew about each other (thanks, polyamory). There was Eli the lawyer/writer in an open marriage, Dave the finance bro who lived in a fabulous Upper East Side building and sent Uber Blacks to pick me up, and the NFL player who couldn’t keep his hands off me. Date nights became inventive and impressive, like a food crawl through Chinatown or cocktails at The Carlyle. I garnered attention everywhere I went. Finally, I was dating the way I’d always wanted to date, just like my cis girlfriends and acquaintances.

Pre-transition, I was still getting hit on and my inbox held messages from men on social media, but it always felt like I was something to be embarrassed of. That was no longer the case. Now men were taking me out to crowded, well-known restaurants, picking me up from my apartment, and shooting the breeze with my cis male roommates like a real-life version of New Girl.

I was seeing the way men treated women when they wanted them firsthand. I’d watch the ways my dates would try to impress me—flexing their biceps as I held on, walking to an enviably hard-to-get dinner reservation or the Guggenheim. I’d wake up to music in my Instagram DMs, songs that made an admirer think of me.

What really changed, though, was that these suitors were asking me to be their girlfriend—no more closeted, casual, half-hearted dating. And, eventually, one of them won me over. Nearly four years since my whirlwind dating life began, my now-boyfriend and true love of my life is everything I’d wished for. He’s classically handsome, rugged, tall (in my highest heels, we still aren’t eye level—he’s 6'3"), and while I’ve seen him hoist furniture and move it around like it was nothing (*swoon*), he handles me with such grace and care. We share traditional sensibilities—he wouldn’t let me pay for our meals out for most of our first year together and I always made sure I was in lingerie and coquette-coded dresses when we were together. (Though, of course, he’d be just as happy to see me “in sweatpants, hair tied, chillin’ with no makeup on.”)

I mention all of this to say that I got everything I wanted from transitioning. I live as my authentic self, the one I always pictured somewhere lounging in a man’s lap, a diaphanous dress spread out over my legs, his big arms around me while he kissed me on the forehead. In a world where you can be whatever you want, choose it and chase it.

#6772. Glen Powell Tussles with Country Music Superstars in The Comeback King Trailer

Powell plays a country singer on the rebound in the upcoming Judd Apatow comedy.

Rodney Dangerfield set the bar for return-to-school comedies in 1986’s aptly titled Back to School. He decried that “If a man has no education, he's got nothing” before proceeding to throw money at all of his problems and hilariously ignore his own advice for the next hour and a half. Then Adam Sandler put his own, unique spin on the film when he sent Billy Madison back to grade school a decade later. And when The Comeback King hits theaters on February 5, 2027, Glen Powell will walk into homeroom as a country singer looking to save his career by finishing his degree.

In the first trailer, which debuted on Wednesday, November 18, Powell plays Aubrey King, a country music superstar dating the biggest pop star in the world (played by Madelyn Cline). His life is turned upside down when she cheats on him and then writes a song blaming him for the deed instead, which sends his career down the toilet. So, his manager convinces him to head back to school and rediscover what he wants to say with his music. Plus, fall in love with a teacher (Cristin Milioti) and joke around with The Comeback King’s insane list of guest stars—including Miranda Lambert, Jelly Roll, Brad Paisley, Chris Stapleton, Shaboozey, and Reba McEntire.

Powell and director Judd Apatow mostly wrote The Comeback King as they filmed it—which is normal for Apatow, but not so much for Powell. “For a guy like me, who likes to be prepared, it’s a nightmare,” Powell told Esquire in our cover story last month. The script came together from the best lines of their improvisational takes. Spitfires of one joke after another until Apatow laughs, or says “That’s funny,” Powell says. But for now, there’s little of the actual schooling revealed in the trailer.

You can catch a lot of the jokes from our celebrity cameos, however, like when Jelly Roll tells a disheveled Powell that he “smells like how people think I smell.” There’s also a great line when one of Powell’s managers, played by Kumail Nanjiani, says that fans answered a poll about him and said that his eyes were too close together, which wasn’t even one of the options. “They wrote it in like you were a Libertarian candidate,” he says. Watch the trailer above.

The Comeback King begins a busy 2027 for Powell, who also has the sci-fi film The Great Beyond coming out in October by J.J. Abrams. Also in the works? A Ron Howard firefighter movie that is reportedly not connected to Backdraft; the third season of his Hulu football comedy series, Chad Powers; a Lou Gehrig film with Richard Linklater; and likely the start of Top Gun 3—whenever Tom Cruise is ready. As Powell joked to Esquire, “Hopefully I’m not the age of Maverick in Maverick by the time I make it.”

#6771. Democrats flip the Senate with stunning victories in deep-red terrain

South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews delivers her victory speech at her election night party in Charleston on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Democrats won control of the Senate on Tuesday, sending shock waves through Washington on a historic night that saw them flip seats in deep-red states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

Hours after The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats, the party was projected to flip the House as well. As of 1:50 a.m. Wednesday, Senate Democrats had wrested seven seats from Republicans — a stunning result that gives the party new powers to confront President Donald Trump in his final two years in office.

Winning the Senate was considered an unlikely prospect for Democrats at the beginning of the year, given the number of red states they needed to compete in. But strong candidate recruitment and a favorable political environment put the chamber within Democrats' grasp.

With their majority, Democrats are expected to serve as a significant check on Trump, who could now have a more difficult time advancing his nominees through the chamber.

“Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate, and we have five words for the American people: Relief is on the way,” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said Thursday night in Washington.

“The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks,” the New York Democrat added. “As a result, there is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future.”

The Democratic path to the majority ran through several deep-red states that have proved hostile to the party in recent years and that Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

In Texas, state Rep. James Talarico defeated scandal-plagued Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the Lone Star State since 1988. Paxton had defeated Republican incumbent John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.

In perhaps the biggest shocker of the night, South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, a shocking flip in a state that last elected a Democratic senator in 1998. Graham was appointed to the Senate in July after the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, and ran for the full term with Trump’s strong endorsement.

And the longest Senate drought in the country ended Tuesday when Democrat Adam Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, a state that had not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

Other flips came in onetime battleground states that had turned decidedly red in recent cycles. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to complete the unfinished term of Vice President JD Vance. And in Iowa, Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to succeed retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst.

In blue-leaning Maine, a 30-year Senate career came to a close with Republican Sen. Susan Collins losing her bid for a sixth term to Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

The night began strongly for the party, with key holds in Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff easily dispatched GOP Rep. Mike Collins, and New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas defeated a comeback bid by former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper also gave Democrats their first flip of the night, defeating Republican Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman.

Democrats also held the open seat in Minnesota, with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan prevailing over former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya.

A Democratic majority in the Senate could run into a president who has said he would become “Mr. Veto” against any legislation coming out of chambers controlled by the opposition party.

With Trump in that position, Democrats will likely push “for legislation that may set the agenda for the future in case a Democrat’s elected in 2028,” according to Christian Grose, a professor of political science and public policy at the University of Southern California.

But in a Tuesday night interview with CBS News, Trump also said, “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”

With control of the Senate, Democrats are also poised to block Trump’s nominees, escalating the opposition they mounted while in the minority during his first two years back in office.

“Very few of them are going to get through,” Schumer told Semafor in October. “It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.”

Those nominees would likely extend from the Cabinet to the judicial branch, potentially even hindering confirmation of a Supreme Court pick in case of a vacancy.

Schumer told reporters ahead of the October recess: “The bottom line is, one of the reasons we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices — MAGA justices — on the Supreme Court and the lower courts.”

Other Democrats have agreed with that sentiment and pointed to 2016, when Mitch McConnell led the Senate and blocked the confirmation of President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland. That left the seat open for more than a year, with Trump eventually filling the spot with Neil Gorsuch.

As Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters recently: “We’ve got to do exactly what McConnell did to us.”

Senate Democrats will also gain subpoena power, bolstering their ability to investigate Trump and his administration. Those investigations could include his handling of the conflict in Iran, his family’s business ties and wealth gains while in office, or his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

“We have a real duty to investigate all of this just absolutely blatant corruption that’s so dangerous to our national security,” Senate Judiciary member Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said in September, shortly after reporting emerged about wedding after-party celebrations for Trump’s eldest son, which were financed by a Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin.

While Democrats in Congress could in theory pursue a third impeachment against the president, the appetite to seal the deal in the Senate would likely fall short, given they would need 67 votes to convict.

John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

#6770. What Watch Will Robert Pattinson Wear as James Bond? It's Complicated.

Timepieces are almost as much a part of 007’s wardrobe as his dinner jackets.

Perhaps you've heard? There's a new James Bond in town!

Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next 007, and while most of the speculation has understandably focused on how the former vampire/current Batman might approach Britain's foremost secret agent, watch aficionados are asking another question: What will he wear on his wrist?

Watches, after all, are almost as much a part of Bond's wardrobe as his dinner jackets, Aston Martins, and vodka martinis. Sean Connery famously wore a Rolex Submariner, Roger Moore experimented with Seiko's digital watches, and Omega has been 007's watch of choice since Pierce Brosnan strapped on a trusty Seamaster in GoldenEye in 1995. That brand remains, of course, a paid partner of the franchise.

Yesterday's reveal showed no watch on the newly anointed 007's wrist, and Pattinson's own taste in watches is rather different from the rugged, sporty timepieces traditionally associated with Bond.

In fact, he doesn't seem particularly keen on big watches at all.

"Whenever a watch gets too thick and it keeps your cuff up, I don't really understand the appeal," he told one interviewer as recently September. "A lot of guys really like that, but I don't think I can really pull that off. I need to only have a half reveal."

And when asked what he looks for in a watch, he was even more specific.

"I definitely like really thin watches. That's the main thing. In general, I would probably prefer a leather strap."

Which is quite a contrast with the substantial divers we've become accustomed to seeing on Bond's wrist.

The fact is, until recently, Pattinson wasn't much of a watch enthusiast at all. That changed at this year's Oscars, when he wore a then-unreleased rose-gold Jaeger-LeCoultre Master Control Chronomètre Perpetual Calendar. Other actors apparently began asking him about it at the afterparty, and something clicked.

He subsequently became an ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, although his relationship with the brand goes back much further. As a teenager, he borrowed his mother's Reverso to impress his schoolmates. More recently, he's revealed that Bruce Wayne will wear a Reverso in the next Batman film.

On screen, Pattinson's watch choices have been interesting. He wore a Chanel J12 in David Cronenberg's Cosmopolis, while Christopher Nolan's Tenet, in which he played a mysterious secret agent, featured a Bond-adjacent Omega De Ville.

Meanwhile, the announcement has prompted some entertaining activity on Instagram. Within hours of Pattinson being named Bond, Jaeger-LeCoultre posted pictures of its new ambassador wearing the Master Control Chronomètre Perpetual Calendar. Omega, meanwhile, posted an image of its James Bond Seamaster. And today, Jaeger-LeCoultre has been back with more Pattinson pictures.

It's a little social-media tit-for-tat, although there's no reason the two relationships can't coexist. For now, at least, there's a straightforward distinction: Pattinson can wear whatever he likes. Bond has his own watch.

#6769. Sorry to My Sweatpants, But These 8 Thanksgiving Outfits Are Just as Comfortable and So Much Chicer

Pass the pie and the compliments, please.

Thanksgiving is just a couple of weeks away. Aside from figuring out which dish you’re going to bring to the gathering (Mashed potatoes! Stuffing! Pumpkin pie!), you’re also charged with finding the perfect outfit. Not one look fits all occasions; it’s heavily influenced by the caliber of the celebration. Is the table set with fine china and crystal glassware, or are you watching the football game over finger food? You also have to consider who’s in attendance. If it’s a group of your girlfriends, you might opt for a flirty dress and save the knit sweater for a family brunch.

To take something off your plate and leave room for all that food, we’ve curated a lineup of eight versatile and effortlessly chic Thanksgiving outfit ideas for all types of occasions. Each one can be achieved by reaching for simple style combinations, so keep scrolling for editor-approved inspiration—but remember that the ideal look is one you feel most comfortable and confident in.

Styling a long, draped sweater dress with heeled boots is always a good idea. For an extra cozy look, consider a ribbed style featuring intentional details, like a turtleneck and asymmetrical hemline. Belts, clutches, and jewelry help dress it up.

This is the perfect in-between look for a semi-dressy dinner. The bold coat—whether faux fur, color-blocked, or fringed—elevates the ensemble when paired with sleek, closed-toe pumps. You can fill in the gaps with virtually any other basics, including denim, tees, and slouchy bags.

If a game of football and an afternoon nap on the couch is in your future, then slip on a pullover sweater and track pants. Wear a T-shirt underneath and maybe swap your dress shoes for casual sneakers. In a matter of seconds, you can master a laid-back outfit change.

Thanksgiving is a day meant for cozy vibes, so slip on your favorite fleece-lined slippers or booties. Pair them with a warm-toned flannel, and dress it up (just a smidge!) with relaxed jeans and a suede coat.

Make a scene this holiday season with a bold, printed dress and over-the-knee boots. The shorter the hemline and taller the footwear, the more dramatic the final look.

Sometimes, less is more. A coordinating sweater-and-pants combo looks instantly polished. If your look is light and airy, add visual interest with dark, moody shoes and accessories and vice versa.

When two aesthetics clash, fashion magic is created. A feminine ruffled dress directly contradicts a heavyweight bomber jacket, making it an intentional and trend-forward look.

Slip a pair of sheer tights underneath your favorite skirt to give the outfit a little oomph. From there, you can let your fashion imagination run wild and reach for everything from timeless coats to loud animal prints.

#6768. Frog Closures Are the Unexpected Detail Defining Fall Jackets

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s all in the details, from intricate knots to elaborate braiding

There are plenty of ways to make a statement with your outerwear, from an oversize silhouette to a high collar or bold color. But this fall, designers are turning their attention to a smaller detail: the fastening. Jackets featuring decorative knots, elaborate loops, and ornate toggles have emerged as one of the season’s biggest outerwear trends, offering an alternative to standard buttons and zippers.

In particular, frog fastenings are having a resurgence, bringing a fanciful finishing touch to everything from minimalist wool peacoats to tailored military-inspired jackets. Typically constructed from fabric or braided cord, the fasteners consist of a knotted button and a loop. Originally designed to secure garments, the closures have evolved into a more ornamental role with intricate shapes and floral-like designs.

While they may seem new for the season, frog-fastener jackets have a history that spans centuries. In Chinese dress, knotted closures known as pankou have long appeared on garments such as the qipao and tangzhuang. By the 18th and 19th centuries, frogging had also become a feature of European military uniforms, worn by cavalry regiments whose fitted jackets were adorned with braided cords.

Fashion has revisited the detail since then. Oscar de la Renta incorporated frog fastenings into his designs in the 1990s, while Valentino explored versions for its fall 2015 couture collection. More recently, for fall 2026, designers reinterpreted knotted closures: At Kallmeyer, black toggles punctuated a gilded jacquard jacket, while Kim Shui incorporated the detail into fur-trimmed blazers and opera jackets. Meanwhile, labels like Khaite and Ann Demeulemeester embraced military-inspired looks featuring ornamental braiding and embellished fronts.

Today’s store-rack versions range from collarless blazers with understated knots to dramatic outerwear designs featuring detailed cording. Brands like Róhe have introduced contemporary takes on frogging, while Hong Kong–based fashion label Sau Lee has reimagined traditional Tang-style jackets with modern silhouettes.

Rather than reinventing jackets entirely, designers are proving that something as minuscule as a fastening can make a familiar silhouette feel new again for the season. Ahead, shop our favorite takes on the look.

#6767. Inde Navarrette Credits Actresses Who Gave Her ‘Permission to Be Free’

For ELLE Women in Hollywood honoree Inde Navarrette, playing Nikki in Obsession was about far more than landing her first leading role. In her acceptance speech at our annual event at the Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles at Beverly Hills last night, the actress spoke about putting everything that she had into playing the character. “I needed to break through every glass ceiling either school, peers, society, or even I put on myself,” she said. “I needed to be connected with that rage that I used to find solace in. I needed to be reminded that my voice, whether soft or loud, holds weight and creates tension that I get to be in control of. I can play a girl who has an internal world—crazy!—whom is the lead of a film and whom is not the perfect victim. Nikki was my opportunity to show the world what I knew I could do and to that, I have to say thank you.”

She went on to thank Obsession’s writer and director Curry Barker, along with all actresses who inspired her early on (including Bryce Dallas Howard, who presented Navarrette with the award). “Thank you not only to Curry Barker for writing a role that allowed me that chance, but thank you to all of the women that took that chance before me,” she said. “Thank you to Jessica Lange for showing me and all of her work that there is beauty in madness and to just give it to the world. Thank you to Natalie Portman for Léon: The Professional. It was the first time I got to see a kid in a movie being more than a kid. She was me. Thank you to Sally Field and Steel Magnolias for daring to portray grief honestly and the hardships of motherhood gracefully. Thank you, Bryce Dallas Howard and The Help, for portraying how intersectional womanhood can divide us and that women who look different than ourselves are no different than ourselves. Thank you to Florence Pugh, Carrie Coon, Julianne Moore, Elizabeth Debicki, Samantha Morton, Rosalind Eleazar, Penélope Cruz. Thank you for daring to be wild. Thank you. Incredibly, you have all given me permission to be free. Let’s all shine a light in each other.”

#6766. Brad Pitt Wants to Play a James Bond Villain

The announcement finally arrived this week: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. But before we could even come up for air about Amazon MGM and director Denis Villeneuve’s decision to have arguably the busiest movie star in the business today follow Daniel Craig as 007, the Internet had already moved on. Fans started asking more questions. Who will costar as the next Bond girl? Who’s performing the song? And, most importantly, who would play opposite Pattinson as the villain?

Well, how about Brad Pitt? The F1 star likely didn’t expect a James Bond question when he stepped on the red carpet for the premiere of his latest film, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. The spinoff sequel of Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood sees Pitt return as stuntman Cliff Booth under the direction of David Fincher, which couldn’t be further from the life of a British MI6 hitman. Still, Pitt was excited to hear for the first time that Pattinson landed the role when a reporter for ExtraTV shared the news. “I love this idea,” Pitt said. “He’s the real deal.”

Would he ever think about playing the villain? Pitt winked at the camera and said, “Robert? Denis? You know what, I’d like to do that. My man Javier [Bardem] did it so well [in Skyfall] It’s tall shoes, but I’d take that on.”

Later down the red carpet, Pitt answered the question again when Complex asked if he had any advice for Pattinson. “Sign me for the villain,” he said, coming around to the idea even more. “Get Denis Villeneuve on the flip phone. Let’s go!”

Elsewhere, Pattinson’s fellow Dune: Part Three costar Florence Pugh is already pitching herself as a potential villain and/or Bond girl. When Villeneuve presented her with an honor at Elle's Women in Hollywood event on Monday, Pugh congratulated the director on finding the next James Bond. “Nice catch,” she said. “Any villains the size of a five-foot-four-inch female?" I’m sure this is just the beginning.

I’ll admit, Pitt wasn’t my first choice for the next Bond villain. If anything, Pattinson was. But I love how enthusiastic he is about the possibility. Now, I kind of feel like I need to see it.

Did you know you can get in-office beauty treatments on sale during Black Friday? In fact, it’s my secret for getting a good deal on things like Botox, skin lasers, and facials that I would already be buying full-price later in the year. And there’s no time like winter to get your beauty treatments, when your skin is out of the sun and mostly hidden beneath thick layers of coats and scarves.

One of the best deals I’ve seen so far this season is for Milan Laser, a spot that our editors just started trying in NYC that’s available with 400+ clinics across 38 states in the U.S. Right now, through November 28, Milan Laser is offering 60% off all body areas for laser hair removal. In all my time as a beauty editor, I’ve never seen such a good deal on laser hair removal in general, let alone an in-office service.

Let me explain laser hair removal first. In a laser hair removal session, your provider will use a handheld laser device that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) all across your skin where you want less hair to grow. The laser uses concentrated beams of light to target the melanin in your hair follicle and destroy it using heat. This slows down hair growth and can even prevent future growth for a limited time. IMO, laser hair removal is the key to super-smooth, clear-looking skin from head to toe.

Although the lasers are stronger and don’t require as much upkeep as an at-home laser hair removal device, they can be pretty expensive. But with this solid 60% off deal, it really cuts down on the cost. To get the deal, sign up with your name, phone number, and email address and make an appointment at your nearest location (reminder: there are more than 400 around the country, so there’s likely one wherever you are, not just in big cities!). At your appointment, you’ll have a consultation about the right package and treatment for you based on your skin type and goals.

What’s super cool is that Milan Laser offers something I’ve never seen before: an Unlimited Package, which gives you a lifetime guarantee and unlimited sessions per body area and free touch-ups for life. You won’t have to worry about not having enough to get the desired effect you want, because remember, laser hair removal isn’t truly permanent and will require touch-ups. You also need quite a few appointments depending on your hair type. Some with thick, coarse hair could need up to 16 appointments, while those with fine, thin hair might only require eight. It’s really personal, which is where an unlimited package can take away some of the stress.

I usually shy away from recommending deals with providers you’ve never tried before (like grabbing a cheap Groupon), but because you get a free consultation first, it takes some of the stress out of figuring out if this is the right place for you. And Milan Laser is more than just a random med spa. They perform more than 90,000 laser hair removal treatments every month across all of their locations, so it won’t feel like you’re walking into a place that isn’t experienced. They also use only licensed medical professionals (and have a physician overseeing everything) to ensure safety.

If you were ever considering laser hair removal, now is the time to do it too. In the summer, it can be difficult to keep up with treatments when your skin is inevitably exposed to the sun. While you’re bundled up and stuck inside this winter, laser hair removal treatments can make you feel one step closer to warm days.

This deal only lasts until November 28, so make sure to book your appointment ASAP at one of Milan Laser’s 400+ locations.

#6764. Carrie Coon Speaks Out About Women’s Representation at ELLE’s Women in Hollywood Event

Carrie Coon had a question for her fellow Women in Hollywood honorees: “Can we start a studio?”

On Monday night, the actress took the stage at ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood celebration in Los Angeles, where she called for women in the entertainment industry to come together and create more opportunities for themselves.

Coon was introduced by her Gilded Age co-star Louisa Jacobson, who celebrated her recent career achievements.

“Carrie is a crusader, always fighting tirelessly for artistic integrity in a landscape that seems to value high gloss and profit over honest, nuanced storytelling,” Jacobson said. “And if you know Carrie, you know that she is completely allergic to superficiality.”

In her acceptance speech, Coon reflected on the importance of women’s stories, drawing inspiration from feminist literature and End Times Fascism, a book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor.

“Patriarchy, capitalism...these are hierarchical systems of domination that rely on fear,” she said. “And in this paradigm, women and girls, like our natural resources, are a disposable commodity—and as such, according to philosopher Kate Manne—our stories are interchangeable and of equal power. But of course, they’re not. That’s not true. And we’re not a monolith.”

Coon went on to discuss the performances of her fellow honorees, arguing that their work represented something extraordinary. “In these women, I see the fight for the living world. I see moral clarity. I see imagination. I see courage,” she said. “And these are, in fact, the antidotes to fascism. That’s how important this storytelling is.”

Toward the end of her speech, Coon questioned how women in Hollywood could create lasting change beyond events celebrating their individual achievements.

“How do we forge our collective safety and solidarity in an ethic of communalism?” she asked. “Okay, so this is the part of the speech where I don’t actually have the answer to that question, but I make the appeal that nights like these shouldn’t be one-off nights.”

She concluded with the aforementioned proposition for her peers: “And so I’m going to start with a really stupid question, but I’m not afraid to ask a stupid question: Can we start a studio?”

#6759. Trump made midterms about himself, and voters rejected him

President Donald Trump dances to "YMCA" after speaking to a Republican midterms convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas on Sept. 9. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump consistently told voters this midterm campaign to pretend he was on the ballot.

Voters responded by making election night a disaster for the Republican Party the president has spent a decade remaking in his own image. Trump spent his first two years back in the White House focused almost exclusively on his “Make America Great Again” base.

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, called the election results for Trump a “2006-style massacre,” referring to President George W. Bush’s second midterms when Democrats picked up a combined 37 House and Senate seats amid frustrations with the Iraq war, the economy and other issues at home.

“This is much bigger than a couple of candidates here and there. … The issues were Americans prefer cheap gas and not the Iran conflict, and [Trump’s] tariffs were … an issue given grocery prices,” the GOP strategist said in a text message as midnight approached Tuesday in Washington, D.C. “What’s going on in Texas … could be the shot heard around the world.”

That was a reference to Texas going blue on Trump’s watch, his handpicked GOP Senate nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, losing his race to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, and Trump-backed GOP Gov. Greg Abbott losing to Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. Trump blamed Abbott, whom he had long praised, in a late-night post, calling the three-term governor a “RINO,” or Republican in name only.

For 21 months, multiple public opinion polls charted the independent voters who pushed him to a second nonconsecutive term in 2024 steadily leaving his coalition. Many of the same polls showed an electorate fed up with the high prices of groceries, health care, travel and other everyday items.

Even as voters already were casting votes Tuesday, Trump continued to dismiss the country’s “affordability” crisis, which he for months dismissed as a Democratic-manufactured lie. The president who long sold himself as the one true messenger of the forgotten American man and woman dismissed voter concerns as a “hoax.”

Down went Senate candidates he rallied for in the homestretch of the campaign, including Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, GOP nominees Ashley Hinson in Iowa and Michael Whatley in North Carolina, and Paxton in Texas.

Several media outlets called Democrats winning control of the House before or just after 10 p.m. Eastern time. In South Carolina, Trump backed Graham over veteran GOP Rep. Ralph Norman, and in Texas, he put his grudge against longtime Sen. John Cornyn — who didn’t endorse him to be the GOP presidential nominee in 2024 — over Paxton’s baggage.

Former GOP Rep. Charlie Dent said “the president's support among Republicans has been slightly diminished leading up to this point, and I suspect it will become more diminished after the election.”

“Over the next two years, many Republicans will be looking forward, not backward, and I think that the president will be less of a factor in the party. He’ll still be a factor, don’t get me wrong, but I think less of one,” Dent said in a telephone interview. “The [2028] presidential nominee, whoever that is, will be the one who will be trying to determine the future of the party.”

An ever-defiant Trump took to social media Tuesday night as the results rolled in and blamed GOP candidates, writing: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Except, he had pleaded with voters for a month to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

One White House official tried to deflect blame away from the boss, writing in an email that “candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.”

But Marc Short, who worked in the Trump 1.0 White House, on Tuesday night said the blame fell squarely on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. “It’s hard to think of a WH that’s sabotaged House and Senate candidates more than this one,” he wrote on X.

Leading up to election night, however, Trump was dug in on defending his second term’s record.

“The inflation is solved. … I mean, everything’s going good,” Trump said Tuesday morning on “Fox & Friends” on Fox News Channel, calling his unpopular tariffs “tremendous.”

“I mean, we have a thing going that nobody has ever seen before, and that includes China and other countries, and they will let you know,” he said.

Trump’s campaign-trail economic message was further complicated by his decision to join Israel in striking Iran. The conflict, which started Feb. 28, defied his pledge of no new prolonged military conflicts, which had been a hallmark of his foreign policy for a decade.

Even as polls showed majorities of Americans placing high gas and diesel prices atop their lists of most-concerning issues, Trump for months shrugged them off, predicting oil prices would plummet, eventually.

“The onus and the blame is going to be right on the president of the United States, which of course he is going to resist,” Dent said. “At his rallies, there were these never-ending comments on things that were just really not connected to what most voters care about, which was inflation and the cost of everything and how challenging their lives are, from a financial standpoint. And the president just didn’t focus on those issues and talked about all these other things that, frankly, were irrelevant.”

Trump would not allow his party’s candidates to put distance between their campaigns and his unpopular second term.

As some House and Senate GOP candidates attempted to run on messages that downplayed Trump, he announced the first-ever Republican midterms convention in Dallas. The primetime spectacle spanned two nights, with Trump as the headlining act on Sept. 9 and Sept. 10 at the American Airlines Center.

During his lengthy appearance on the opening night, Trump got pushback from even some Republican lawmakers when he pledged he would send every U.S. citizen $5,000 — but only if his party retained control of the House and Senate.

On night two, Trump’s loyalists in the large arena — home to the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks — agreed to his demand that they raise their right hands and declare allegiance to him.

The convention made clear Trump would not ease his grip on the GOP.

Then came his October campaign rally blitz, with the president continuing to dismiss voters' economic worries and issue cryptic threats about the accuracy of American elections and what he called Democrats' collective intention to “cheat.”

By the end of his midterm rally sprint, Trump increasingly went for laugh lines, a striking contrast to his fire-and-brimstone events in 2016. Audiences of his supporters from Gastonia, N.C., to Corpus Christi, Texas, to Dalton, Ga., to Salina, Kan., to Wasilla, Alaska, chuckled along at times.

His closing-argument event Monday at the Reflecting Pool that sits between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II memorial on the National Mall offered another example of Trump’s predilection for talking about matters relatively unimportant to voters. He talked about pool liners, his White House ballroom and other non-election issues.

By late Tuesday night, Trump appeared to have moved on, telling The New York Times he would accept the outcomes of the election results.

In other media interviews, the GOP president said he was ready to meet congressional Democrats at the negotiating table but that he had his veto pen ready.

“We’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country,” he said on a Politico livestream Tuesday. “They've already called and they want to work with me.”

Niels Lesniewski contributed to this report.

#6756. The AI Police Are Going After Black Writers

The white powers that be have always doubted our intellect. Now they have a new tool.

Picture a waifish enslaved teen—a girl named Phillis, after the slave ship that Middle Passaged her from present-day Senegal and Gambia—trembling before a room of incredulous, austere white men, the most esteemed thinkers and politicians of colonial Massachusetts. The reason: The gifted girl wrote a book manuscript, and the family that owned her journeyed all the way to London to find a publisher for it. That prospective British publisher, a bloke named Archibald Bell, promised to publish the manuscript if the Wheatleys could prove Phillis had written it herself—an attestation tantamount, of course, to whether an enslaved African soon-to-be American possessed the intellect requisite to producing exceptional creative work.

Present at the trial, which has been described by historian Henry Louis Gates Jr. as the nascent scene of African American letters, was Thomas Hutchinson, the governor of the Province of the Massachusetts Bay; Andrew Oliver, the province’s lieutenant governor; and Mr. John Hancock himself, the future first governor of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Per Gates, almost all the men forgathered to pass judgment on Phillis Wheatley were both Harvard graduates and slaveholders. No record exists of what transpired, but oh how brilliant Phillis must’ve been as she convinced those 18 eminent Bostonians that she’d indeed written the poems. The confirmation was printed in the front matter of Phillis’s poetry collection—the first book published by an African soon-to-be American—Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773):

We whose Names are under-written, do assure the World, that the Poems specified in the following Page, were . . . written by Phillis, a young Negro Girl, who was but a few Years since, brought an uncultivated Barbarian from Africa, and has ever since been, and now is, under the Disadvantage of serving as a Slave in a Family in this Town. She has been examined by some of the best Judges, and is thought qualified to write them.

As my great-grandmother Edith Larkin Jackson, a woman not two generations removed from chattel slavery, used to say, “There’s nothing new under the sun.” Mama Eddie was a schoolteacher, and I imagine she’d be astounded by artificial intelligence. However, she’d have no trouble whatsoever fathoming a world that called into question the creativity or intellect of her people.

Here we are in this brave new world of AI, an age hurtling headlong toward the peril of superintelligence. Here we are in the 21st century, a time when the ivory-tower panjandrums are engaged in a sinister pattern, if not conspiratorial scheme, of incriminating Black and brown writers with even the suggestion that their work is AI assisted.

For example: In March, Hachette Book Group rendered kaput the U. S. publication of Mia Ballard’s Shy Girl over claims of AI usage.

When Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir’s story “The Serpent in the Grove” was named the regional winner of the Commonwealth Prize in May, Ethan Mollick, a Wharton Business School professor who serves as the codirector of Wharton Generative AI Labs, ran it through the AI-detection software Pangram, touted as the industry standard, and reported that the platform flagged it at 100 percent. Once Mollick shared his findings on social media, several others joined the chorus bemoaning Nazir’s work as a product of AI.

In July, academics studying AI accused H. M. Wolfe of having used a large language model to write her best seller Daggermouth (though its publisher Simon & Schuster has, thus far, stood by the book). Later that month, writer Jerry Falade had a $2 million book deal with Macmillan collapse after his agents withdrew the submission of his debut crime novel citing AI concerns.

In September, Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça ou Mourir (It Was Either That or Die) was proclaimed a standout of the French literary season, won France’s Prix du Roman FNAC, and was long-listed for the Goncourt, the country’s most prestigious literary prize. But then an anonymous X account (later revealed to be owned by a conservative columnist) posted that Pangram had identified all 34 chapters of the book as having been written with AI. That claim spurred accusations that Orélien plagiarized earlier work, leading the Goncourt to nix the book from its long list.

In October, The Atlantic accused writer Simbarashe Kundizeza of using AI to write “The Blue Fighter,” which won the Caine Prize, Africa’s most prestigious short-story accolade.

Germane: While Nazir is Trinidadian, Ballard, Wolfe, Falade, Orélien, and Kundizeza are all Black.

Although all those writers have denied claims of using AI to produce their work, I’m not here to dispute whether they did or to what degree they used it, nor the epistemological paradox of using AI to determine whether a writer used AI to write a story. Of equal importance is that, if we ain’t reached the point where all published writing is scanned for possible use of an LLM, what’s the logic informing which writers are investigated for AI use and which aren’t, as well as the attendant issue of which accused writers suffer the most severe fallout, including the scarlet letter of damaged credibility?

The plight of Black and brown writers in the age of AI must be judged in light of what’s being described as an era of postliteracy. Of the specter of AI sloptimism becoming so ubiquitous it overruns human output. Of the cataclysmic doom of superintelligence approximating the creative work of a human brain to such a degree that the difference will be negligible to the undiscerning masses.

The plight of Black and brown writers in the age of AI must be apprehended against the beef between the publishing industry writ large and AI. Against 10,000 authors having copublished an “empty” book in protest of their work being pirated to train its models. Against America’s Big Five publishers suing Meta for copyright infringement. Against the recent unsealed documents that reveal OpenAI executives knew they were training their AI on copyrighted material and, furthermore, that AI-authored books were apt to displace in the market ones authored by humans. “There will be a point where a bunch of artists express worry about what we’re doing here, and we’ll likely ignore their concerns and release anyway,” OpenAI policy director Jack Clark wrote in an internal memo back in 2020. The predicament of Black and brown writers should be weighed against the long and calculated history of portraying them as lesser intellects.

Casting doubt on the possibility of Black literary brilliance is in the spirit of a hubristic Saul Bellow asking, “Who is the Tolstoy of the Zulus?” Of 45/47 portraying beaucoup Black people as “not that bright.” Of attacking DEI to paint us as unworthy or incapable, less we are sanctioned by people in power. The same insidious forces—linked to right-wing Cambridge professor James Orr and conservative billionaire Peter Thiel—stoked the allegations that ended in Cambridge professor Jason Arday dying by suicide. (Arday has been posthumously cleared of plagiarism.)

In stark contrast, best-selling novelist and screenwriter Anthony Horowitz has admitted using AI for his work. Best-selling biographer Katie Prescott extolled AI as invaluable in writing her book on Mike Lynch, the late British tech entrepreneur and AI pioneer. And while she’s been called among other things a “grifter” and a “villain,” South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books using artificial intelligence since 2025 and defended her use of LLMs despite criticism and threats. While she later clarified she used it only for research, Nobel laureate Olga Tokarczuk caused a ruckus revealing she queried AI for writing help. Other than Santiago Schnell, a white Latino, resigning as the provost of Dartmouth for using AI in his published articles and The New York Times cutting ties with Alex Preston for an AI-assisted book review, beyond vocal to tepid criticism, white writers aren’t suffering material consequences on par with those of their Black peers.

Poor Phillis Wheatley never published a second book. Despite advertising six times in the newspaper to find a publisher. Despite announcing she’d dedicate it to Benjamin Franklin. Despite General George Washington extolling her as “favored by the muses.” In fact, in 1784, Phillis died at 30 years young, destitute, having placed the last advertisement for her second manuscript just a few months prior.

Because Big Tech is big-time thriving and race is evermore an oppressive tool, critics are bound to keep casting the work of Black writers as AI assisted, in effect electing themselves nouveau versions of those privileged 18th-century Bostonians. Best believe their indictments are a tacit way to portray the work of Black people as unworthy of patronage, acclaim, awards—aka inferior. But be forewarned: If Big Tech succeeds at AI turning the creative work of human brains passé if not obsolete, it’s near foregone that most writers will lose their ability to earn a living. Indeed, the sad-ass upshot is that if AI prevails, all writers—race be damned—will be fated a Phillis.

#6755. Fall Is Almost Over, So I Rounded Up the 7 Celebrity Outfits I Still Want to Copy

Like much of the TikTok generation, I spend way too much time looking for style inspo on social media. While that sometimes means letting the dishes pile up in favor of a few extra minutes of scroll time, I rarely miss a street-style moment. Whether it’s Hailey Bieber in a date-night outfit or Taylor Swift in this season’s hottest color combination, I’ve been stowing away fall outfit inspiration for the final stretch of the season.

Hollywood’s cool girls are squeezing every last wear out of fall, wearing silk midi skirts, sheer tops, and cape-like scarves. Beyond fall essentials like trench coats and dark-wash denim, they’re also reaching for this year’s breakout trends, including maraschino-cherry-colored accessories and striped pullover sweaters, keeping their seasonal rotation fresh before winter takes over.

While I can’t recreate every ensemble on the internet, I can round up the seven autumn outfits most on my mind, ranked by how eager I am to make them my own before the temps drop for good. Keep reading for late-fall outfit inspo to carry you into the holiday season.

On the set of Die Alive, Zoë Kravitz made a case for laid-back elegance and an unexpectedly bright fall color choice. The slinky midi skirt is polished, while the basic gray tank is casual. The trench coat makes the outfit perfect for chilly weather, with a pair of chocolate pumps elevating the style. Consider this your go-to look for weekend brunch plans and cocktails with the girls alike.

Selena Gomez put a fresh spin on the capsule wardrobe, creating a monochromatic outfit using closet staples, including sleek capris, mesh pointed-toe heels, and a quilted cinched bag. However, instead of a basic black tee, she reached for a sheer iteration, turning the simple ensemble into a fresh and fun look. To pull it off for a chilly night, I’d add a leather bomber jacket.

Kristen Bell managed to wear just about every style trend at once—without it looking like a slop wardrobe. Her striped pullover served as the base, with coordinated fall-coded colors sprinkled throughout the rest of her outfit. Her dark-wash, wide-leg jeans reminded me why denim is an autumn classic, and I officially want her glove flats. However, it was Bell’s cherry-red beanie and merlot Chanel handbag that injected personality into her look.

I’m all about a cozy fall wardrobe, but when date night rolls around, I want something a bit more elevated and sleek. Ashley Graham understood the assignment, wearing a silky plunge halterneck top and draped, gray trousers. While she opted for open-toe sandals, pointed, closed-toe pumps can beat the chill.

Karlie Kloss’ chic look is a nod to office wear. Her polished autumnal look features closet basics, including a white button-up shirt, above-the-knee skirt, and ballet flats. Kloss added an extra dose of flair by intentionally draping a black shawl across her shoulders, making it the perfect look for strolling Fifth Avenue and museum hopping alike.

Sometimes the best looks are the simplest. Daisy Edgar-Jones layered a classic white T-shirt underneath a sapphire-blue trench coat, taking a closet basic and elevating it with an unexpected twist. Light-washed, straight-leg jeans elongated her frame, and timeless black pumps turned a casual look into a polished ensemble.

Elizabeth Debicki played with fall textures, reaching for a bold leopard-print turtleneck sweater and slick leather pants. Leopard print is both timeless and trendy, which makes it especially easy to style. It’s the ideal outfit for a night on the town, perfectly cozy yet fashion-forward.

#6752. Samantha Morton on Being a Woman in Hollywood: ‘We Are Here as a Family’

The Odyssey costume designer Ellen Mirojnick delivered some of the actress’s remarks on her behalf.

Yesterday evening, The Odyssey star Samantha Morton was unable to attend ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood celebration, remaining at home in London instead. But the honoree had the film’s costume designer Ellen Mirojnick deliver some of her moving remarks on her behalf. Morton reflected on the honor of playing Circe in The Odyssey—and the greater lesson she has learned about what being a woman in Hollywood means, decades into her acting career.

She wrote, “Thank you so much to Nina and ELLE for this amazing honor. And to Ralph Lauren and Bulgari for supporting this wonderful event. My huge thanks to Alex White, Norman Jean Roy, and the wonderful team who made me feel so fantastic at the cover shoot. To Jenny, Nicki, Kat, Billy, Scott, and Ashton for being there for me every step of the way and for helping to make my dreams come true.

“To be even a small part of a phenomenon like The Odyssey was an experience that cannot be matched. Circe is a role that I felt deeply blessed to play, to bring her voice to life for Christopher and Emma and their incredible team, John Papsidera, Ellen Mirojnick, Luisa Abel, and Andrew Jackson.

“And to get to work with my favorite actor in the whole world, Matt Damon, the peerless Matt Damon…the most suave, sophisticated, talented, handsome, generous, kind, and gifted Matt Damon. Thank you for helping me to find Circe on that Scottish hillside and for standing in for me this evening. It takes a village and I am certain this wouldn’t have happened without all of these wonderful people and more…I am so desperately sad not to be able to be there with you all to celebrate.

“I want to congratulate the other amazing women being honored tonight. What an incredibly talented and formidable group. Rosalind, my Harlots sister…you inspire me so much.

“And as women in this industry, we know what we do isn’t easy. Yes, we love it, we are passionate about it and we are fortunate to do it; it’s great when it all comes together. But we know this isn’t always the case and there can be many obstacles and pitfalls along the way in an ever-changing and sometimes cruel business.

“I keep asking myself what it means to be a ‘Woman in Hollywood.’ It was a childhood dream for me to be here. To work in this business. To act in films that would travel the world and be remembered forever. For almost 30 years I have visited and worked here and for a time I called this city home, returning every year to the same house in Beechwood Canyon, a house built by Dolores del Río, the first Mexican movie star, yet I never fully felt that I belonged, that I had ‘made it.’

“Tonight shows me that to truly be a woman in Hollywood is not about location but community. It doesn’t matter where you come from…your race, your faith, your sexuality, your social or economic background. We are here as a family, a community of creatives, and we must support each other, help each other, and fight for our right to work in a safe environment. To be treated fairly and respectfully. To keep pushing for fair and equal pay and parity for female actors and filmmakers. We will get there.

“And ultimately to pass on the baton and because of this I want to thank my beautiful daughters Esmé and Edie for their brilliance and support and the difference their outspoken and courageous generation is making to our glorious industry.

“I dedicate this award to all the women in our community, fighting to carve out their own path and to create, free from fear and exploitation.

#6751. How ‘Rivals’ Created an Age-Gap Relationship We’re Actually Rooting For

R ivals has returned to our screens, and Rutshire’s residents are hornier than ever. But Rutag fans might have to hang on a little longer to see them enter their relationship era. Frustrating? Not necessarily, as maybe this intense slow-burn is exactly the reason Rivals has managed to create an age-gap relationship we’re actually rooting for.

There is a lot of awareness around age-gap couples in pop culture right now, and audiences seem very done with the classic younger woman, older man dynamic. Movies like A24’s Babygirl and Amazon’s The Idea of You have gone some way toward challenging outdated tropes around age-related power dynamics, but that still doesn’t erase how Hollywood handled things in the past (Pretty Little Liars and Fifty Shades of Grey come to mind).

Rivals is a bit of an anomaly in how it has tackled Rupert and Taggie’s age-gap relationship so far, and the slower pace seems to have played a very necessary part in that. Rutag’s slow-burn underpins the entire foundation of their connection. What’s working for me personally is that Rupert hasn’t been rushing Taggie emotionally or physically to match where he’s at in his current stage of life. In fact, even though he seems besotted with her—she’s sort of become his moral touchstone—he’s doing his best to stay away from her. He seems to find the idea of letting her down (or fully letting her in) absolutely terrifying, despite how much he clearly cares.

Rivals gains further grace from viewers for its willingness to openly acknowledge Rupert and Taggie’s age gap as being an obstacle to overcome in their relationship, rather than just glossing over it or choosing to pretend it doesn’t exist. Rupert even acknowledges the age gap as being an issue himself by making a promise to Declan in season 1 that he’ll stay away from Taggie. By showing us these hurdles early on, it gives deeper insight into what a relationship would eventually mean for these two and what they’d be up against.

Watching Taggie gain life experience and have her own adventures of self-discovery—not everything has to involve Rupert—has helped them remain exciting to us as a potential couple. Her catering business seems to be thriving, for example. The slow-burn gives Taggie the opportunity to forge her own identity and ambitions, which would be important to have going into a relationship with Rupert, given their differences in life experience. Taggie is slowly blossoming into herself, without falling into that cliché trap of trying to change who she is to impress a man, and that’s empowering and necessary.

As long as Rivals continues to explore the age gap with care and consideration, I think fans will keep rooting for Rutag’s romance, no matter how long the slow-burn takes.

The upgraded dual-voltage design ensures great hair days all over the world.

I’ve gotten compliments on my hair my entire life. (I mean, I am a redhead.) But I noticed a significant uptick in flattery once I mastered the art of the bouncy at-home blowout. As a beauty editor, I’ve tried nearly every blow-dry brush and multi-styler on the market—yes, even the pricey Dyson Airwrap and beloved Shark Flexstyle. Neither of those viral tools comes close to my beloved T3 Aire 360, though.

I’m not the only one obsessed with this hair tool. When the Aire 360 first launched in 2024, my colleagues raved about how it expertly smoothed their hair, how easy it is to use, and the fact that it comes in a cute, convenient carrying pouch. T3 has since come out with an upgraded dual-voltage model that can be used all over the world. (As an avid traveler, that detail is essential!)

Could the upgraded T3 Aire 360 be the right multi-styler for you? Keep reading to discover everything you need to know about the tool and get first-person intel from two editors who can’t live without it.

T3 has all the bells and whistles you could want in a multi-styler. The tool comes with four attachments: A blow dryer, two curling wands (for each direction), and a smoothing round brush. The barrels stand out from other models because they’re ceramic, meaning they conduct heat beautifully, smooth strands, and produce impressive style longevity. (Just be careful because these can burn your hands if you touch them while using.)

Another cool feature? It’s designed with “SoftAire,” which is the dryer’s unique mechanism to help speed up drying time. The brand boasts “zero” heat damage, but obviously, there is some heat. However, it’s much cooler than a normal curling iron or hair straightener, so using this tool can protect your hair in the long run.

My hair is very fine, but I have a lot of it. It has also changed texture and become more curly over the past two years (thanks, birth control!), so I’ve had to relearn how to style and take care of it. Overall, though, I don’t have many issues with it. Stylists often say my mane is very “obedient” because it responds well to heat and is easily styled. I try to wash it two times a week and will always blow it out with a round brush.

This is a much smaller kit of attachments than I’m used to, but I actually prefer it. I don’t need all that. One of my favorite aspects is the chic leather carrying case that holds everything inside, making storage a lot easier. (So many multi-stylers don’t come with a storage bag, FYI!) Also, it’s pink. Love that.

Let me preface this by saying I’ve religiously used the T3 Aire 360 for the past two years, and the upgraded dual-voltage model functions just as beautifully. When I wash my hair at home, I blow it out with the round brush attachment. The tool is so easy and intuitive to use, and it makes my hair look incredibly smooth and sleek. I’ve perfected my at-home blowout routine with it, and most days I don’t feel the need to use a separate device—like a curling iron or flat iron—to zhuzh my hair.

When it comes to the curling wand attachments, these produce the best results out of all of the multi-stylers I’ve tested, probably because they’re ceramic. Do they get a little hot? Sure, but not at temperatures as high as your standard curling iron. The conductive ceramic material ensures my curls last for days. They might not be as defined on day two or three, but I don’t feel the need to touch them up either.

“I don’t say this lightly: My hair has never looked so good. I walked into the office with a level of confidence that should probably be studied. The dual-voltage upgrade, along with the chic pink leather carrying case, make this the ideal choice for avid travelers. If you’re a jet setter (like me), this is the multi-styler to purchase because you’ll never experience a bad hair day, no matter where you are in the world.
