#6715. Robert Pattinson’s Hair Is Already 007 Material

Whether you like it or not (or placed bets on Kalshi), Robert Pattinson is our next James Bond. During the years-long process in casting 007, we used our best detective skills to narrow down the field to who would join His Majesty’s Secret Service. And if you were going by hair type alone, well, Pattinson makes a rather compelling case.

Let’s review the canon for a moment. In the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Bond creator Ian Fleming describes the spy’s mane thusly: “The hair was black, parted on the left, and carelessly brushed so that a thick black comma fell down over the right eyebrow.”

Pattinson’s hair might be naturally light brown, but a darker ‘do is hardly out of the question for the actor’s upcoming transformation. For his turn as Bruce Wayne in The Batman, he dyed his hair to a darker, almost pitch-black hue. The rest of Fleming’s description fits the actor nicely, particularly the bit about being “carelessly brushed.” In real life, the actor’s hair is rarely anything approaching immaculate. Even at more formal engagements, it tends to retain a certain studied dishevelment, with stray strands escaping an otherwise respectable comb-through. Fleming’s famous “comma,” after all, isn’t a carefully sculpted curl. It’s simply a lock of hair allowed to fall where it pleases, which just so happens to be very on trend in 2026.

We got our first glimpse of the 40-year-old actor taking on the role in a video posted by the official James Bond X account where he’s seen stepping out of the shadows pointing a gun at something (or someone) just outside the frame. It’s hard to tell whether the golden lighting is playing tricks on his hair color, but the accompanying promotional image certainly seems to suggest a shade of black. Plus, his hair’s parted on the correct side.

It’s worth noting that Daniel Craig’s casting as Bond was initially met with considerable resistance, much of it centered on one detail: He’s blonde. Fleming’s Bond, after all, was famously dark-haired, and Craig represented a departure from the physical template established by the novels and previous screen incarnations. We know how that turned out. Craig went on to deliver one of the most celebrated interpretations of 007, proving that a little deviation from the source material needn’t be a deal-breaker.

Pattinson will still need to prove himself to be agile in a tuxedo, nimble behind the wheel, and thirsty for a martini or two, but one thing’s sure: He's got the hair down pat.

#6712. Mike Johnson won’t seek top GOP spot as House flips

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 3. He will bow out of next week’s leadership race. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek to serve as House minority leader in the next Congress.

A source familiar with the speaker’s decision confirmed that the Louisiana Republican would not seek the post after Tuesday’s midterm elections saw Republicans lose their narrow majority in a Democratic tsunami.

Other candidates were already lining up. Fellow Louisiana Republican Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, is expected to launch a bid for minority leader Wednesday, according to a person familiar with his plans who described him as a “proven and tested leader.” And House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio is also throwing in his hat, according to multiple reports.

The Republican conference is set to hold its leadership elections next week.

Johnson held an election night event in Shreveport, La., after crisscrossing the country trying to protect the GOP majority, arguing throughout the campaign that polling favoring Democrats would not be accurate.

“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson said in a statement after Democrats claimed the majority. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”

The blame game had already begun Wednesday morning, as Republicans reeled from losses that cut deeper than expected.

“The polls were not wrong. You were,” Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., wrote on social media, referring to his party’s leaders in the House and Senate. “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6711. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

There’s a certain kind of guy who’s impossible to shop for. Pleasing him might seem hopeless, but there’s a cheat code, and it’s called Todd Snyder. The brand has spent more than a decade quietly perfecting the American wardrobe: the sweaters, cords and jackets that look like they’ve been in his closet forever, only better.

Consider this your shortcut. I went shopping the way I always do and pulled the Todd Snyder gifts I’d be thrilled to unwrap. All that’s left for you to do is pick one and maybe hide the receipt, since he won’t be needing it. Fair warning: there’s a good chance you’ll end up buying something for yourself, too. ‘Tis the season.

A barn jacket gets an upgrade. Flocked denim gives it a velvety, suede-like surface, and the leather collar adds a nice bit of contrast. It’s rugged enough for a weekend upstate and polished enough for a swanky dinner in the city.

Cords are back in a big way, and it’s not just vintage obsessives wearing them: they’ve become the go-to cold-weather pant for guys who want something softer than denim. This straight leg camel pair is an easy way to add some warmth and texture to his wardrobe. He’ll wear them just like his favorite 501’s.

Every guy needs one great flannel, and this blue-and-cream plaid is it. It’s soft enough to wear on its own and sturdy enough to layer as a light jacket on milder days.

A cashmere sweater is the gift that never misses, and this rich red version is perfect for the holidays without screaming “Christmas sweater.” It’s the kind of thing he’ll pull on every December for years.

Colorful flecks of Donegal yarn take a simple black beanie somewhere much more interesting. It’s cashmere too, so he’ll actually want to wear it instead of stashing it away in a coat pocket in case of emergency.

Supple leather on the outside and cashmere on the inside: this is a cold-weather essential done right. It’s a grown-up upgrade over the gloves he’s been losing every winter since college.

An olive wool bomber with a plush shearling collar hits the sweet spot between a flight jacket and a proper winter coat. It works with everything from cords to tailored trousers. Bonus points since it will look better every season after some wear and tear..

For the guy who lives in dark denim, black cords are a smart switch. They’re just as versatile, much cozier, and dress up easier than you’d think.

Brushed cotton turns the camp collar into a fall shirt. The muted plaid and relaxed fit make it a great layering piece over a tee, or something to wear buttoned up on its own when the heat’s cranked indoors.

The waffle knit gives this navy sweater a depth and texture that a flat knit can’t match. It’s understated in the best way: the kind of piece that gets compliments without trying too hard.

Joshua Ellis has been weaving cloth in Yorkshire since the 18th century, and it shows. This bold red tartan is the coat accessory that does the most work, brightening up even the gloomiest January commute.

Pleats, a roomy leg and a flecked silk-Donegal fabric from Italy make this the dress pant for guys who don’t like dress pants. It’s sharp enough for the office party and relaxed enough to wear with a sweater the next morning.

#6708. It’s the Season of the Statement Glove

Vivid colors, lush leathers, and fingerless styles: Gloves have never been bolder.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If the late, great, legendary fashion editor Diana Vreeland were still alive, I believe she would incorporate a question like, “Why don’t you replace your ring stacks with statement gloves?” into her famous “Why don’t you” column, where she rhetorically mused on ridiculous and often opulent situations. A good glove is a winter staple, yes. But lately, fashion has been having a love affair with embellished, stylized gloves. We’ve now seen the opera glove in all of its forms. But what about gloves bedecked in crystal cuffs, neon hues, faux fur effects, and beyond? They’ve already arrived, on the runways and at retailers.

Consider Givenchy’s leather wonders, which come in ballooning silhouettes that envelop the hands and wrists. Or Prada’s spring/summer 2026 silky satin opera gloves in shades of pale yellow or olive green. With delicate ruching throughout, the formal opera glove gets an ironic, modern, slouched, and louche makeover. Elsewhere, Khaite has shown the power of an opera-length glove in python. Clearly, texture is an embellishment all its own in these kinds of extreme examples.

In some cases, the gloves become the jewelry. In others, jewelry further accents the statement glove, like for Mugler’s fall/winter 2026 show in which models wore kelly green and royal purple scrunched leather gloves up to their elbows, sometimes styled with a big chunky bracelet over top. Elsewhere, some gloves were mismatched: vivid yellow on one hand and brilliant blue on the other. The brand called it a new take on power dressing, which melded codes of the 1980s, 1940s, and 17th-century aristocratic court coats. “Ultimately, this show intends to acknowledge that self-empowerment is the most potent antidote of clarity to the oppressive forces and grey political climate that surrounds us at this very moment,” Mugler creative director Castro Freitas was quoted in the show notes, “and most of all, it’s a manifesto of the highest power that we should never forget to reclaim: FREEDOM.”

Most of all, the statement glove dresses up any neutral wool coat or adds an extra layer of over-the-top theatrics to a statement coat. When in doubt, you could also simply opt for a colorful glove, which the runways have loved in droves lately. Take, for example, Valentino, which has been pumping out short and statement-making silky gloves in shades of ’80s neon pink or dreamy cobalt blue.

Sometimes, all you need is a change of silhouette, too. At Chanel, the fingerless glove has long been a staple, and it’s now become a favorite of superfan clients during street style moments between shows. Elsewhere, the fingerless glove has forever been a celeb favorite, especially when it comes to style legends like Madonna.

“We’ve got every color under the rainbow of gloves and/or a sheer opera-length glove that is in either a matching color or an opposite color of whatever the look is,” Madonna’s stylist Rita Melssen told ELLE in August 2026.

One thing is clear: Statement gloves are the new power accessory, equal parts practical, theatrical, and impossible to ignore.

#6706. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6705. How the Grocery Store Became Travel’s Hottest Destination

It’s about so much more than just a snack haul.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Last winter, for a friend’s birthday, a large group of us rented a chalet in Courchevel, France. There were the usual Alpine excesses—elaborate supper-club dinners, après-ski that stretched well into the evening—but, as with any ski holiday, there came a point when somebody had to buy groceries. This responsibility fell to me. I approached the task with all the enthusiasm I usually have for making my bed or taking out the garbage.

I ended up at Sherpa Supermarché, an unfussy grocery chain with 116 locations across the mountains of France. I expected to be in and out in five minutes. Instead, I found myself standing before a cheese section that puts the Library of Congress to shame—there were varieties of Comté I had never heard of, some aged longer than certain marriages, others washed in wine or wrapped in herbs. The chocolate section was equally impressive. I had not known there were so many ways to make chocolate, or that I would, like a kid with eyes bigger than his stomach, start shoving them by the armful into my basket.

Sherpa wasn’t particularly fancy or large. It was an ordinary shop serving ordinary people, only its definition of “ordinary” happened to feel particularly French, and unlike anything we have back home. I returned to the chalet with way more chocolate and cheese than anyone had requested, and the sense that I had just experienced something meaningful.

Apparently, I’m not alone. According to Hilton’s 2026 Travel Trends Report, 77 percent of travelers said they enjoy visiting grocery stores abroad. Grocery store tourism has become one of travel’s more unexpected obsessions in recent years, with visitors increasingly building supermarket stops into itineraries once reserved for museums and monuments.

Looking back on my travels, the grocery store was always there. I’ll never forget my horror when I went to an IGA in Montréal for the first time and learned that Canadian potato chip flavors are vastly superior to our own. (If you ever find yourself north of the border, All-Dressed, Ketchup, and Poulet Rôti-flavored chips are a must.) Or on a trip to Seoul, where Lotte Mart introduced me to a wide variety of truly restaurant-quality instant noodles and elaborate packaged desserts. I’ve heard similar stories about Big C, a grocery chain in Thailand, which even offers hands-on workshops where visitors can indulge in tastings of Thai curry pastes. Doesn’t that feel a step above the free samples at Costco?

Grocery stores shape the way you see a destination. One friend keeps telling me about a to-die-for babka from Panama City’s Super K, billed as the world’s largest kosher supermarket. Would I necessarily think of kosher food in a destination best known for its beaches and tropical rainforests? Probably not. But that’s precisely the point: a supermarket can reveal an entirely different side of a place.

We’re seeing grocery store tourism get increasingly luxe, too. In Los Angeles, Erewhon has become a destination in its own right, where visitors can observe the city’s wellness aristocracy paying $22 for a celebrity-endorsed smoothie. New York City’s Meadow Lane opened in Tribeca last year with beautifully packaged pantry staples and artisanal chicken fingers so good that you don’t care about the $17 price tag. And in Tokyo, Kayanoya, a Japanese brand known for its hard-to-find seasonings and traditional ingredients, just opened a new flagship in Ginza designed by Kengo Kumba. It honestly looks about as luxe and appealing as a Prada boutique. Grocery tourism is increasingly becoming something you experience, not just a utilitarian shopping stop.

But the alpha and omega of grocery store tourism remains French butter. For years, bringing home a few blocks of Maison Bordier was the ultimate edible souvenir from Paris, and La Grande Épicerie makes the process seamless, vacuum-sealing purchases for the journey home. (I’ve also learned from TikTok that you can take your butter back to your hotel, ask for it to be frozen overnight, and, by the time you land in the States, it should be just about thawed.) And this year, Paris got another dedicated butter destination in Le Butter Shop, a retailer within walking distance, specializing in du beurre and all its regional varieties.

Which brings me back to the cheese case in Courchevel. I went in expecting a quick chore and came out with a better sense of the town than I’d gotten from any of its chi-chi, Champagne-drenched supper clubs. The monuments and must-dos tell one side of a place’s story, but the supermarkets show you another. I’ll be packing an extra bag for butter next time I’m in Paris.

#6704. Denis Villeneuve on Finishing ‘Dune,’ Casting James Bond, and Why ‘Reality Is Unbeatable’

The last days of the making of the Dune trilogy take place on an unassuming Hollywood side street in September, in a dark, mostly silent room. “We were about to have a quick look at reel one because they did some adjustments, and it’s without sound,” Denis Villeneuve says, apologetically. “So it’s a way to discover the film that is a bit brutal for you.”

Villeneuve, the director and cowriter of Dune, Dune: Part Two, and Dune: Part Three, is tall, slender, and bearded, with deep-set eyes. He has a disarming effect. Many directors of Villeneuve’s stature—Christopher Nolan or James Cameron—lead their productions with a kind of remote but dazzling competency: They can do everything better than you and are used to the deference that comes with that fact. Villeneuve’s charisma is closer and more mischievous: He speaks quietly and playfully, in Quebecois-accented English, and commands loyalty via the protective instinct he inspires in nearly everyone he meets. His method is emotional; his instructions are conveyed with sincerity and praise. When presented with the results he is seeking, he will let you know with an almost childlike enthusiasm: I deeply love it. Or: Wow.

Today, Villeneuve and his cinematographer, Linus Sandgren, are at the postproduction facility Company 3, where they have been the past weeks and months, color-timing—the process of adjusting and balancing a film’s many colors and contrasts—the 150 minutes of Dune: Part Three. For my sake, and because there is still work to be done on it, they have started, once again, at the beginning of the film. “So here we could have fucked up the Warner Brothers logo if we wanted,” Villeneuve says, gesturing at the screen at the studio’s iconic WB, “but we are nice guys.”

Then he leans forward: “No, but seriously, without joking, are they too rich, the colors? A little bit? Or is it the original to your eyes?” Sandgren—a calm Swede in Birkenstocks—and Matt Wallach, the film’s colorist, chime in to agree and to tone down the blue. “Their logo is a little cartoonish,” Villeneuve says, still staring at it. “It’s not their best work, I will say. But that feels better. Thank you, Matt.”

Villeneuve and his wife, Tanya Lapointe, who is a producer and second-unit director on Dune: Part Three, disagree on how long they have been working on Dune: Villeneuve tends to say nine years, and Lapointe says 10. (It’s 10.) Frank Herbert’s Dune books, which are notoriously complex and hard to adapt, have stymied directors as talented as David Lynch and Alejandro Jodorowsky. But Villeneuve seems to have found a way. The first two Dune films—Part One came out in 2021—have grossed over a billion dollars, been nominated for 15 Academy Awards, and helped make stars of Timothée Chalamet (who plays Atreides, the film’s complicated messiah figure and main character) and Zendaya (who plays Chani, a native Fremen warrior and the lover of Atreides) while still capturing the uniquely strange and surreal texture of Herbert’s novels. (Multiple people in the Villeneuve films imbibe what one character describes as “worm piss.”)

Right now Villeneuve is feeling the last decade acutely. “I’m at that stage of the process where all my body hurts,” he says. On Dune: Part Three alone, the production shot for nearly a hundred days, in three countries: Hungary, where the film’s main stages were; Iceland; and the Liwa Desert, in the United Arab Emirates, which doubled for the sand planet of Arrakis. They wrapped last November, and Villeneuve went directly into the film’s edit and postproduction process. “It’s a feeling of some kind of deep melancholia to finally come to the conclusion of this long journey,” he says. “Because it has been nine years of my life dreaming about Arrakis, about sandworms, about the adventures of Paul Atreides. I’m pretty emotional about that.”

In the history of Hollywood, there have been only a handful of directors who have had the ability to work, again and again, at the highest level of the art form while also connecting with audiences at the widest possible scale. Villeneuve is one of them. His signature films—2015’s cartel thriller Sicario, or 2016’s science fiction film Arrival, which was nominated for eight Academy Awards—are knotty and severe and not always easy to follow; they are also beautiful and seem to play well anywhere, whether on an airplane, in an HBO rerun, or at an IMAX theater. Villeneuve’s reward for all his success is his next project: the 26th James Bond film. “It’s a blessing,” Villeneuve says. “Because to leave Arrakis, I need some kind of strong rocket, something that will grab me and pull me away from the orbit of that planet. I’m leaving a childhood dream. I need something so powerful to pull me away from it. And Bond is the one that will do it.”

In the dark screening room, Wallach lets the first minutes of the final Dune film play. We watch soldiers on a dimly lit warship prepare themselves for battle. Sandgren and Villeneuve discuss trying to bring out one of the actor’s features more concretely. “I guess what we’re fighting is we could have lit him more,” Sandgren says, “but also what Denis really wants here is the realism and the sort of incidental light—like he just happens to sit in a shitty light here, and gets what he gets, which adds to the realism, which is nice. But you still want to see him. So it’s a balance.”

“What Linus says, in a very polite way, is that it’s my fault,” Villeneuve says, smiling, while Wallach finds a little more detail in the actor’s face.

“I deeply love it,” Villeneuve pronounces, when he is done. “Thank you. The scene is at the beginning, and becomes claustrophobic. In French, we say they are chair à canon.”

“Cannon food, we call it in Sweden,” Sandgren says.

Villeneuve watches his own film as it plays on. “Wow,” he says. “Fantastic. Fantastic. That’s beautiful. Nice work on the highlights here. Thank you, guys. Wow. Great work. It looks real now. Wow.” His voice is full of emotion as he turns to Sandgren: “It’s beautiful, my dear friend.”

In the Dune movies, you can feel Villeneuve’s desire to go deeper into the desert, to shed all the big, loud machinery of his own films, and to get to the places out near the horizon. This is one of the reasons his trilogy works where others have failed: Despite Villeneuve’s talent for spectacle—his Dune is full of menacing, chromed-out oblong shapes and eerily familiar war machines—his true gift is finding the uncannily quiet spots in the worlds he creates, the lonely places where his characters are tested against themselves.

“That was the main condition when I agreed to make these movies,” Villeneuve says, about the way all three Dune films were shot in the desert, on location. “I said that it was deeply important for me to shoot it in the real environment.” The Liwa Desert was so mind-bendingly hot while shooting Dune: Part Three that the director had to incorporate a midday break into the crew’s daily schedule. Robert Pattinson, who joined the cast for the third film, has talked about the set being so intensely warm that he basically disassociated for most of shooting. But being there is one of the main things Villeneuve is after. “I love reality,” he says. “I love to be in the environment. It’s like a pleasure that I give to myself to be in the crew with a camera in the desert. I feel that there’s all these shots that we did, the realism, that I think you cannot achieve otherwise. And you cannot feel the power of the desert if you’re not there. There are some shots you can cheat sometimes. But in general, reality is unbeatable.”

Villeneuve on the set of Dune: Part Three with Timothée Chalamet.

Villeneuve and Zendaya on location in the Liwa Desert, Abu Dhabi.

Villeneuve, 59, grew up in Gentilly, Quebec, a small town right next to a river. From that place he emerged with “a relationship with horizon and silence,” he says. “I was in contact since my birth with incredible gigantic skies, very dramatic, operatic skies. And colors as well. I grew up in a world that has a black-and-white winter, which has a tremendous, beautiful, precise palette of black and white and blue and grays.”

Villeneuve likes to point out that the two main structures in his town were a church and a power plant. “I grew up melancholic, a child that was dreaming big alone in his corner and fascinated by the engineers that were working in that nuclear power plant,” he says. “I was raised as a Catholic, and I was raised going to the church, and those chants and the passion of religion [are] all that mixed together with incredibly powerful grandmothers. I think that’s the background of Dune right there.”

Villeneuve was a reader, a dreamer. It was only as an adult, when Villeneuve became a documentary filmmaker, that he began to discover a larger world outside his own mind. “I think that there’s something about Paul Atreides in the way he’s introduced at the beginning, the way he is like a kid that has been protected in a small bubble all his life and suddenly finds himself confronted to a new reality where he has to consolidate his identity in another culture,” Villeneuve says. “I think it’s something that I, at the time when I was a kid, I really connected with. And early on when I became a young adult, I traveled a lot, a lot. I went a lot to Asia and was spending a lot of time there doing small documentaries and being in contact with so many perspectives, so many points of view on reality.”

Villeneuve made his first feature, August 32nd on Earth, in Canada in 1998. He would go on to make three more films in French, before making his first English-language film, Enemy, in 2013. “I consolidated my identity as a filmmaker,” Villeneuve says about the time before he came to Hollywood “through documentaries and movies with less commercial pressure where I was free to express myself and find my own voice.” Partially, he learned by failing. “I will say that I don’t see my first feature films as...they had some clumsiness in them. I was a beginner. I learned my craft. I made mistakes and I learned from those mistakes, a lot more than from my successes.”

Villeneuve, as a young filmmaker, was wary of Hollywood, even as he was pointed at it like an arrow. “Hollywood has always had that kind of dichotomy, to be a paradise for a filmmaker and hell at the same time,” he says. “Since the birth of Hollywood there has been a struggle between the art of cinema, the idea that you want to express yourself—and for that you need a lot of money, and somebody will write the check, and you have a responsibility. Since the birth of cinema, it has been like that.”

In 2012, Villeneuve found himself facing a rare opportunity: He had two films greenlit at more or less the same time. One was Prisoners—an in-demand Hollywood script about the abduction of two children and the vigilante efforts of one father to get them back. The other was a coproduction between Spain and Canada called Enemy, about a college professor who becomes obsessed with another man with whom he appears to be physically identical. Both were English-language films, which Villeneuve had not yet done. Both films starred Jake Gyllenhaal. But to Villeneuve, they were very different propositions: Enemy was a deeply personal film about identity and the unknown nature of the self. And Prisoners, which also starred Hugh Jackman and Viola Davis and which would be largely distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures, represented Villeneuve’s first true chance to make a real Hollywood film.

Villeneuve decided to make both. But he made Enemy first. “I did convince the studio, Alcon”—the producer of Prisoners—“to wait a few months for Prisoners because first I wanted to make a first film in English in a smaller environment. And the real reason is that I wanted to make sure that I will shoot something that will be so close to me that if ever I was smashed and destroyed by Hollywood, there will be something. If people say, ‘What’s that? Oh, Denis’s there. He’s flying over there.’ Because I did feel that I was afraid.”

I remember watching Enemy in a small screening room the year it premiered, in 2013 (the movie was distributed in the United States by a then upstart studio called A24), and being increasingly unsettled and haunted by the film. Sometimes, in quiet moments, the final shot of Enemy still comes to me, unbidden. Who is this guy? I wondered then.

Enemy and Prisoners were both stylish, morally ambiguous films that showed the extremes of human behavior without ever venturing into sadism or pure spectacle, and this style of filmmaking—brutal, unresolved, lush, and heartbreaking—would become Villeneuve’s signature as he made progressively bigger, and bigger-budget, films in Hollywood: 2015’s Sicario, 2016’s Arrival, 2017’s Blade Runner 2049. “I always did projects I [felt] ready to do,” Villeneuve says. “I was ready to do Dune after Blade Runner. I would have not been ready to do Dune after Prisoners. I slowly learned my craft one step at a time—my skills with actors and then to work with more and more background action and increase the technical difficulty slowly. I just felt secure. And when I started Dune, I knew I could not go in front of people and ask them to invest $200 million [until I was ready]. I need to feel deep inside me that I can do that.”

Villeneuve says he only recently stopped feeling like a tourist in Hollywood. “I think that feeling of having the right to be here in some ways came from other filmmakers, colleagues that wanted to reach out and share thoughts about cinema with me or some friendships that began and that I accepted,” he says. He’s coy about who exactly he’s talking about. But part of it, surely, has also been the acceptance of the films, which despite their increasing size and scale and sometimes exotic source material are consistently deeply personal.

“My work is all about me,” Villeneuve says, helplessly. “If you don’t like Dune, the movies, I’m 100 percent responsible because I made every single decision. I brought them to the screen, and they are very personal films. Even for me, it’s like—scope is not something that is contradictory with the ownership of a movie. These movies have been brought to life by me, and I say that without arrogance. I mean, I’m the one who brought them to life. And yeah: It’s my Dune.”

A few weeks later, Villeneuve and Lapointe, who is shorter but equally warm and charismatic, are at the North Hollywood warehouse of Legendary, the production company behind the Dune films. The warehouse is full of costumes from past productions: Pacific Rim, Crimson Peak, Godzilla. In the back, transported from another continent entirely, is one of the ornithopters—a helicopter-like vehicle—from Dune: Part Three. Soon this prop, which is the size of an actual helicopter, will join a bunch of others in an upcoming exhibition of work from the Dune films. But right now it is here, in a parking lot under the glaring Los Angeles sun. Its paint—an homage to the specific color of a 1981 Porsche—glows in the light. “The last time I saw this vehicle, it was in a deep desert,” Villeneuve says, looking on. “We had brought it to Abu Dhabi, and it was, I remember vividly, at the top of a cliff of sand. This thing I’ve seen a lot. It’s like an old friend.”

Later in the day, Villeneuve tells me he is set to approve a final handful of effects shots. And then Dune: Part Three, and the director’s work on the trilogy, he says, will cease. “I do feel that I have to stop,” he reflects. “I don’t think I should spend another minute on it. Because I’m still curious, I’m still alive, and I do it for artistic reasons, not because I see that I’m comfortable or I see that it’s going to be good business-wise or for my career. I think it’s good for me to stop artistically.”

As Villeneuve’s star has risen, he has increasingly had to think through the question of how to remain an artist at the very high tier of the business that he’s in. “In the past 25 years, there’s a tendency to try to find the perfect formula to make a film, and to try to reproduce, reproduce, and make sequels,” Villeneuve says. “I’m responsible. I just made three Dune movies. I’m about to make James Bond 26. So I’m a sinner. But the idea is that as an artist, I feel that there’s an urgency, and you feel it in the young filmmakers, which I deeply love—the idea to bring new stories, original stories to the screen. It’s very important. And that we have to try to, at the end of the day, we need to take risks.… I want to say that we, as humans, as artists, if we want to be better than AI, we have to be unpredictable.” Only humans, he says, “can step into the unknown and go deeper into the dream. That is the strength of a human being. And I think that no computers can do that.”

It’s the end of September, and the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger is about to close. “I think that consolidation, I mean, less players in the business is never a good idea,” Villeneuve says. “Those studios are historical studios. And I hope, I truly hope, that the people in power will have the wisdom to protect the legacy of both studios. There’s a limit to profit. I mean, if the only goal is to make money, it’s really sad. Those things are historical gems of American culture and they have a duty to—I hope and I pray that they understand the responsibility that they have and that they will take care of both of these entities.”

Villeneuve, for his part, is already turning his attention toward Bond—another character, and another world, he grew up fascinated with. “I adore James Bond,” he says. “I adore Sean Connery, the Sean Connery years, the verve of James Bond, his panache, his drive, his charisma, his unapologetic way of living the strength and what it says, good and bad, about masculinity. There’s something about James Bond that deeply inspires me.” He says the previous producers of the franchise approached him with the idea of directing the film a few years ago, right as he was beginning Dune: Part Three. Villeneuve says he hung up the phone and actually screamed out loud when they offered the franchise to him. Then he told them they’d have to wait. “I said to them, ‘Yeah, I’m up for it, but I have something before called Dune: Part Three. I’m shooting in two weeks.’ And the only way I can do things in life is to fully commit to something. So I said to them, ‘If you want to work with me, you will have to wait many months because I will be entirely focused on Part Three.’ And so that’s why I’m sorry for everybody, but it took more time for the casting because I’m busy.”

Now we know: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. Villeneuve’s decision, albeit in consultation with his producers and the studio. He is incredulous that I am even asking. “I am the director!” he says. And then softens a bit: “I’m doing cinema because I love to share the creative process,” he says, about the conversations that led to Pattinson. “Otherwise, I will do ice sculpture in my basement. I love the idea to share creativity. But when it comes to casting, it’s something that—I’m doing the casting. But, of course, it will need to be accepted and approved by a ton of people, including you, the pope, my mother, my brother, who has a strong opinion about who should be James Bond.… I think Donald Trump wants to be James Bond. Everybody talks about James Bond. So yes, I will choose James Bond with my friends, producers, and hopefully everybody will.…” He pauses. “You know what? At the end of the day, the truth is, no matter who I choose, some people will be excited and others will be disappointed.”

Now Villeneuve has a gleam in his eye, talking about what he was looking for in the part. “The first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer, because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin,” he says. “I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It’s not everybody who has that. I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that when he comes into the room, everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma and someone that has a lot of sensuality as well and that people are attracted to and that someone who expressed some kind of pleasure, someone who has width, sometime who has dark humor, sometimes that has pleasure into being in deep shit, someone who is not afraid to put his hand in the mud. I need someone that is strong, muscular, someone that is a force. And someone, of course, who has a deep intelligence in the eyes, someone that is always ahead of us.”

He is grinning. You can feel Lapointe, in the nicest possible way, willing him to say less. But Villeneuve, as is typical, is swept away. “Every time I’m thinking about James Bond,” he says, “there’s an electricity that goes into my vein that is the electricity of pleasure. It’s like: For me to do that is just a pure cinematic pleasure. Incredible pressure, stress, yes. But the pleasure is bigger.” ✦

#6702. Which Ultra-Processed Foods Are the Worst for You? A Dietitian Breaks It Down

From hot dogs to whole-grain breads, here are the ultra-processed foods worth limiting first.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Research over the years has shown exactly how ultra-processed foods (UPFs) negatively affect the body. What’s still being studied is how many of these specific foods, and how much of them, impact the rise in certain cancers and other diseases. Although the internet is rife with stats showing an uptick in certain cancers among younger adults, a recent study conducted among a massive 460,000 Americans debunked one of the many fear-mongering rumors that ultra-processed foods are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk specifically. But before you place your next fast food delivery order, Caitlin Hosmer, MS, RD, LDN, a registered dietitian and co-founder of MenoPantry alongside Mark Gilbert, nutritionist from The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Plan, explains which parts of the meal are potentially the most harmful, and what you should know about the study’s findings to understand which ultra-processed foods are actually the worst for you.

Most researchers use a system called NOVA, developed by a Brazilian epidemiologist, Carlos Augusto Monteiro, who coined the term “ultra-processed foods.” Hosmer explains that NOVA sorts foods into four groups based on how much they’ve been processed and not by their nutrients.

Gilbert argues that the system is questionable. “Even nutrition experts were unable to categorize foods reliably or consistently into one of [these] four categories, from unprocessed to ultra-processed. Other systems, including IFIC, Nutri-Score, and the proposed CHIPS system, exist but are similarly controversial,” says Gilbert.

To better understand what these foods are exactly, Hosmer says the simplest way to put it is that a processed food is still recognizably food that’s been preserved or prepared. An ultra-processed food has been taken apart. “These foods are designed to be cheap, shelf-stable, convenient, and very easy to overeat. The key caveat is that NOVA describes how a food is made, not how nutritious it is. So the Ultra-processed category can hold both a hot dog and a packaged whole-grain bread,” says Hosmer.

Gilbert further explains that the processes many of these foods undergo often reduce healthy, essential nutrients, remove fiber, and make the resulting food easier to consume, absorb, and digest, leading to untoward blood sugar levels, less satiety and, in the longer term, poorer metabolic health.

Gilbert notes that it’s difficult to deem any one type of UPF as “worst” simply because genetic and environmental risk factors to various diseases and ill health vary so vastly. “So, just like no single diet is ‘best’ for everyone, no single food is necessarily worst. For instance, if someone has a high heart and vascular disease risk, they might benefit from less saturated fat. If someone has a high risk of diabetes, they should avoid sugar and other refined carbohydrates that raise their blood sugar levels,” Gilbert explains.

However, Hosmer points out that when researchers break ultra-processed foods into subgroups, processed meat consistently comes out on top. The aforementioned study of more than 460,000 adults, conducted by the National Cancer Institute (NCI), found that ultra-processed food intake overall wasn’t linked to colorectal cancer—but higher consumption of meat from ultra-processed food sources was. Hosmer references a 2024 Harvard analysis in The British Medical Journal that found the same pattern for mortality.

“Across more than 30 years of follow-up, meat-, poultry-, and seafood-based ready-to-eat products showed the strongest and most consistent associations, followed by sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened beverages, dairy-based desserts, and ultra-processed breakfast food. That category includes processed meats such as hot dogs, deli meats, bacon, sausages, and many frozen breaded meat products,” Hosmer summarizes.

Second to processed meat are sweetened drinks—both sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened. “Sodas, sweet teas, energy drinks, and diet drinks give you sweetness and calories (or the expectation of calories) with no fiber, protein, or real food structure. They show up consistently across heart, metabolic, and mortality research,” Hosmer notes.

Sugar-laced and dairy-based desserts alongside sugary breakfast foods follow on the list. “Many sugary cereals and pastries are basically dessert dressed up as breakfast,” says Hosmer.

These foods won’t necessarily give you cancer or lead to other diseases; Hosmer explains that the more useful message is that “worst” means low in what the body needs and high in what it doesn’t. In the NCI study, higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium from ultra-processed food sources was linked to a lower incidence of colorectal cancer. “A packaged whole-grain bread and a package of bologna are both “ultra-processed,” but they are not the same choice,” she adds.

Many UPFs are often made to be irresistible, meaning you’ll likely eat more than the recommended serving size. Gilbert explains that this leads to large spikes in blood sugar and doesn’t reduce satiety as much as most whole foods do. UPFs can also increase overall calorie intake. “Increased calorie intake and excess blood sugar spikes cause weight gain, high blood pressure, inflammation, diabetes, unhealthy blood lipids, generally poor metabolic health, and a variety of other effects which increase a person’s odds of the most common serious health conditions and diseases, reducing health span and lifespan,” Gilbert warns.

To illustrate, Hosmer points to what she calls a small but elegant 2019 National Institutes of Health (NIH) trial led by Kevin Hall, which she says has the strongest causal evidence. Twenty adults lived on a metabolic ward and ate either an ultra-processed or a minimally processed diet for two weeks each. The diets were matched in calories, sugar, fat, fiber, and sodium, and people could eat as much as they wanted. On the ultra-processed diet, participants ate about 500 more calories a day, ate faster, and gained weight—about two pounds; on the minimally processed diet, they lost about the same amount. “That points to something about the food’s form, not just its nutrients: it’s soft, energy-dense, quick to eat, and slow to trigger fullness,” says Hosmer.

Considering these results, she says there are multiple mechanisms present that likely work together:

Turn the package over and read the ingredient list. That tells you far more than the front of the box. Some signs:

Context matters too. A whole-grain bread with one dough conditioner is a very different food from a toaster pastry, even though both may technically count as ultra-processed. Ask two questions: how processed is it, and what is it actually giving me? Fiber, protein, whole grains, and added nutrients count for a lot.

This depends greatly on the specific foods in question. “That’s what makes this new study that differentiates between the different kinds of processed foods particularly important,” says Hosmer. “The clearest evidence is for processed meat. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen for colorectal cancer. That’s the category for strong evidence that something causes cancer, though it says nothing about how big the risk is,” Hosmer clarifies. More practically, she further explains that the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) estimated that eating 50 grams of processed meat every day—about one hot dog or a few slices of deli meat regularly—is associated with roughly an 18 percent increase in baseline colorectal cancer risk. “That’s a relative increase: for an average person, it moves a lifetime risk from approximately four to five percent to roughly five to six percent,” says Hosmer.

For ultra-processed foods as a whole category, Hosmer says the picture is less clear. The new NCI study is one of the largest ever done on this question. When the team looked by food group, whole grains and dairy were linked to lower risk and meat to higher risk. The researchers note possible opposing effects of some ultra-processed foods on colorectal cancer etiology—mainly that the helpful and harmful foods cancel each other out in the total. More specifically, the total consumption may matter more than the specific foods or food groups.

According to Hosmer, there’s also an indirect pathway. “Diets high in ultra-processed foods are linked to obesity, and excess body fat is an established risk factor for many cancers, including breast cancer after menopause, endometrial cancer, and colorectal cancer,” she notes. Hosmer warns, though, that this study’s findings shouldn’t be read as ultra-processed foods are fine. “Read it as a reminder that it’s hard to make a single recommendation about such a large and varied category of food.” When the researchers broke ultra-processed foods down by type, the results lined up with what we already know: whole grains, fiber, and dairy were linked to lower colorectal cancer risk, and processed meat to higher risk. Hosmer’s challenge is to check the new data against well-established research. “Headlines alone can be misleading, especially on topics as emotionally charged as what we eat.”

Turn the package over and read the ingredient list. That tells you far more than the front of the box. Here’s what to look for:

Context matters too. A whole-grain bread with one dough conditioner is a very different food from a toaster pastry, even though both may technically count as ultra-processed. Hosmer says to ask yourself two questions: “How processed is it, and what is it actually giving me?” Fiber, protein, whole grains, and added nutrients count for a lot.

Hosmer explains that the risks associated with ultra-processed foods include two things: how much of someone’s diet comes from these foods, and how much room their body has to absorb the negative effects.

One caveat from the new study that Hosmer points out is that participants were mostly older white Americans, so results may not generalize to younger or more diverse populations. “That matters because colorectal cancer is rising in adults under 50, the group that has grown up recently, and with the most ultra-processed food available,” she cautions.

Gilbert adds that knowing your family’s health history and getting various tests can offer some indications of individual risks, but predicting these risks is by no means foolproof. “Ultimately, those who have prediabetes, diabetes, high blood pressure, cardiovascular disease or cancer, or are living with overweight or obesity are the most at risk because these conditions can often be avoided or improved with better nutrition,” says Gilbert.

Both Gilbert and Hosmer agree here. “Some foods can be intentionally processed to increase and improve their nutritional profile rather than reduce it,” Gilbert explains. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, plain yogurt, canned salmon, and bagged salad are strong examples. They are processed and still very good for you. Processing often makes healthy food more affordable and accessible. Gilbert’s 1:1 Diet is designed to align with this. “The products we produce are processed, but instead of reducing the essential nutrient content of the products, we actually increase it, adding vitamins, minerals, essential fats, and quality protein,” Gilbert notes, adding that extensive research has shown his diet improves blood sugar, blood pressure, inflammation, metabolic health, cardiovascular health, and reverses diabetes in about half of dieters.

Myth: This new study proves ultra-processed food is safe.

Hosmer says explicitly that it doesn’t. “It looked at only one disease, colorectal cancer, in a mostly older population, and participants reported their diets just once, back in the mid-1990s. The authors themselves point out that ultra-processed foods became far more common and varied over the following two decades, so the study likely underestimated how much people were actually eating,” she clarifies. “The fairer reading is that which ultra-processed foods you eat matters more than the category itself: a whole-grain bread and a hot dog may both be “ultra-processed,” but they don’t affect the body the same way.”

Myth: It’s only about nutrients, and processing doesn’t matter.

Kevin Hall’s controlled feeding trial suggests otherwise. People ate significantly more on the ultra-processed diet even when nutrients were matched, so a food’s structure and how fast you eat it matter too.

Myth: Organic, plant-based, or “clean label” means it isn’t ultra-processed.

Myth: You have to completely eliminate ultra-processed foods.

Perfection isn’t the goal. Hosmer points out that in the NCI study, replacing 10 percent of the total weight of ultra-processed foods with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2 percent lower incidence of colorectal cancer. “We don’t yet know exactly what that looks like on an individual’s plate. The study measured diets statistically, not swap by swap. But the direction is clear, and it fits decades of nutrition research: incremental shifts away from ultra-processed foods appear to matter, even when they’re modest. Start with categories that matter most: processed meats and sweetened drinks,” she concludes.

#6701. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6700. More Men Are Getting Penis Filler Than You Think

In Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life, Eric Idle sings, “Isn’t it awfully nice to have a penis?”

But, according to the new documentary Manhood, the feeling is not universal. In the film men look between their legs with nothing but shame, regret, and self-pity. The subjects’ members—particularly their perceived smallness—are problems to be solved.

Enter Bill Moore, a Dallas-based med spa operator, whose PhalloFILL penis filler procedure can supposedly add meaningful girth without surgery. The film follows his eager patients, including Ruben, an aspiring comedian and father of five, and David, a gay ex-OnlyFans star whose penis was botched by a previous filler procedure.

Director Daniel Lombroso spent years filming Moore and his patients, , slowly building trust until they opened up and (quite literally) bared all to the camera. Watching Manhood, it is clear that getting penis filler is never just about being bigger. To the patients, this procedure represents an escape from middle-aged ennui, a break from a difficult past, or a life preserver for a sinking marriage. The fast-growing, nationwide penis enlargement industry is happy to help, at $6,000 worth of filler injections per dick.

GQ sat down with Lombroso, fresh off Manhood’s breakout premiere at SXSW, to find out how he convinced a male enhancement spa to let him film inside, why the penis filler industry is booming, and who’s already getting rich off it. Manhood is available to stream on November 17.

Daniel Lombroso: That’s a great question. I think the most squeamish moment is Ruben bombing at stand-up on stage, more so than the botched penises. But, it’s funny. In real life, I am incredibly squeamish. It’s hard for me to look at surgery. It’s hard for me to look at someone using the bathroom or throwing up. There’s something about when you’re making a film, when you’re behind a lens, it gives you a level of separation. It’s sort of a mediator between you and the world. I shoot a lot of my own work, and on this project I shot some and worked with an incredible cinematographer, Vittoria Campaner. So there’s something about having that intermediary between you and the world that gave me comfort and helped me get through it. The hardest moment was the penile reconstruction, but we did not put most of that in the film.

Yeah. David, the person who gets botched, had his penis fully degloved like a banana. They had to peel back the layers and scoop out the permanent dermal filler that’s living in nodes in the shaft of his penis. That was one of the most gruesome experiences of my life. We decided to spare the audience that horror. And David is okay, thank God.

It’s tough. That was the toughest one. I also used to work at The New Yorker and I made a film on the Brazilian butt lift, which was similarly gruesome. I mean, that is one of the most gruesome cosmetic surgeries in the world. It’s a fat transfer procedure. They suck out the fat from where you don’t want it, your stomach or your arms, and stick it in where you do want it, your butt.

I filmed and watched that, and edited it on my New Yorker computer in The New Yorker newsroom for six months, and I would see David Remnick walk by and be curious and confused, and continue with his day. So it’s not my first time being in those environments, and they are hard for me personally. But something about making a film, it just gives you this level of separation that helps you get through it.

I think it’s important for people to be braced with these images. It is shocking to me how difficult it is for people to look at just a regular penis, especially straight men and older straight men. Gen X and above feel like they’re getting hit with an atomic bomb when they see a penis. Younger men, queer men, and women have always been fine, but I cannot tell you how many pitch meetings we went into where, like, the female executives love the film, the queer executives love the film. Then it gets to a straight guy at the top who is hit with one dick, and certainly one botched dick, and is out. Or he has to make sure on the record that everyone knows that he doesn’t have that problem. That happened in quite a few meetings. So I think it’s important to confront people with those images.

My business partner Kerry [Mack] joked that this is the first time I don’t have a Holocaust connection. We were looking for a penis enlargement-to-Holocaust connection, but we couldn’t find one.

I started this film three and a half years ago. At the time, we were all inundated with stories about the male loneliness epidemic. It felt almost like a cliché. I know you’ve covered it super well, and I’m sure we both grew up on Vice. It’s also something that’s really hard to show, because you don’t necessarily want to… “Condone” is the wrong word. “Platform” is also the wrong word. I hate when that word is used. But it is a cultural phenomenon that needs to be covered and discussed, and it’s very hard to do it.

I couldn’t really find a good way. Around that time, I read about the explosion in penile enhancement, and specifically, penile girth enhancement. I was less interested in penis enlargement than using that as a canvas to explore this burgeoning cultural discussion. So I called, like, every urologist in the country doing versions of it. There’s the Penuma, which is a really gnarly implant.

Yeah, Ava Kofman wrote a great story about the Penuma, which, like, pokes through and makes you bleed. I spoke to the creator of the Penuma. I spoke to people doing more permanent dermal fillers. And all of them were reticent. You know, the way I make films is I embed for many years in these environments. When I made [the alt-right documentary] White Noise, I lived on the road with white nationalists for three or four years. And for this film, I lived in clinics for two years.

So I had to find a practitioner who was open. And finally I got to Bill Moore, this very classic American character. He’s a businessman, not a doctor, and he said, “Come on down to Dallas.” So I booked a one-way ticket, and I would just sit in the waiting room and introduce myself to different patients. With a story like this, it’s really the only way. These men are so ashamed, they’re not gonna open up to a random reporter who calls them. So I knew I would have to put in a lot of time. I would just sit there, usually with my camera in a different room, and introduce myself. Sometimes they’d say, “Come back,” some would say no, some would say yes.

On those first two shoots, I met a megachurch pastor getting his penis enlarged. He’s very famous, and I cannot say who it is. A border patrol agent in the film. A father of five, an OnlyFans star, someone with brain cancer.

Super hard, and I try to be very patient. You want to push your way in at the right times and with the right people, but this is not the kind of project where you want to be coercive in any way. The last thing you want is someone saying that they were forced to appear naked in a film. So all of these men consented in different forms. Some said, “Change my voice.” Some said, “Anonymize my face.” Some said, “Just shoot my dick.” Some said, “You can shoot my face, but not my dick. I can talk about having a small dick, but don’t show it.”

There was kind of every version and permutation. But when I started to look for the main characters who could carry a film, I needed someone who was comfortable with me filming their family. Usually I’m doing vérité, like direct cinema. Really in their lives for at least a year and a half. I feel like this is front of mind for everyone now because of the Lance Oppenheim Nathan Fielder movie [You Can See Everything]. But you need someone who’s willing to invite you into their home and play the game with you, and Bill was willing to do that from the beginning.

Ruben was the next person who signed on. He’s a father of five on his second marriage. And it doesn’t go the way he might have hoped. The hardest one, I think, which speaks to your question, was David Smith. David is a pseudonym. He’s an OnlyFans star, and he had never told his story before. You would not know this from watching the film, but it actually took the entire production to get him to show his face. It was such an incredible story. I’ve never heard someone talk so openly about their botched penis and growing up evangelical and the horrors of being a male porn star.

We had a very small budget, but we saved a tiny bit of money up until the SXSW deadline. We were about to work with a face replacement company in France because that was his wish, and we thought it spoke to the theme of shame. We were starting to explore, do we hire an actor? And around that time we said, “You know what?” I used to work at The New Yorker, where you don’t really screen things. But I said, “Let’s just take a chance.” So we flew David to New York. We said, “You have no editorial control.” None of the subjects in any of my work ever have any editorial control, including my grandmother. But let’s just show him the film and see what he thinks.

And he was so blown away, he cried in the room. He called his brother, and has since opened up to his family about everything. He’s touring with the film. He came to SXSW. That took until literally a week before the premiere at SXSW, and it’s an ongoing process. He continues to become more and more open.

Yeah. I mean, it’s funny. He was a porn star. You’d think that he had such a level of exposure that he would be comfortable with this. But I think this speaks to the film. Somehow talking about your body is easier than talking about your feelings. Having to talk about his shame, his insecurity, his issues with faith, and with his parents is super, super hard for him. He needed to see the final cut to decide to go forward with it. It was the biggest gamble of my career and, thank God, it paid off.

That’s a great point. So many of the men—this takes me back now—like, I was more nervous than them. I felt like I was being potentially intrusive. I didn’t want to appear coercive in any way, as I mentioned. I wanted them to feel comfortable. But many of them felt grateful to have what you might call a third space to talk about how they feel, because most of them are not opening up to their partners, believe it or not. I don’t know how they come home with a soup can and explain that. And many of them are paying cash. There’s no credit card transaction fee. Many of them are finding ways to anonymize what they’re doing.

But at the same time, they want to talk to someone about it, which is so strange. They just don’t want the people that are part of their daily life to know, but they want Bill to know, and I think Bill deserves a lotta credit for that. He’s a queer man treating these oftentimes right-wing Texans, holding their dicks and enlarging them and making them feel comfortable.

And they wanted to talk to me, and if they wanted it to be off record, that was fine. If they wanted to be on record, that was fine. I think for many of them that was a relief. It’s so common when you work on intense stories that people start to see you as a friend or a collaborator. People see you as someone who understands their plight, and I think whenever I felt like it was starting to get there, I would remind them I’m a journalist. The world is gonna see this. Anything that is private or uncomfortable, just make sure you’re comfortable sharing before it goes in front of the world.

These guys feel so alone. Going back to White Noise, my first film, the single biggest motivator for joining those white nationalist movements wasn’t ideological conviction. I mean, some of them are gnarly racists or antisemites, but a lot of them just, like, want to be part of a club. I saw that in a lot of these men too. They just feel isolated. They want someone to talk to, and felt relieved that Bill was there to listen and that I was there to listen.

I think men, and particularly straight men—I say this as a straight man who probably struggles with this myself—have an underdeveloped sense of self oftentimes.

I’ve done these types of stories for ten years now. When I’ve interviewed women or gay men, they’ve had to think about who they are and their place in the world from such a young age. Especially queer men, from their earliest memories or certainly when they started to understand their sexuality, have had to grapple with who they are and how they appear publicly. I think that because there’s this lack of communication or lack of internal dialogue in a lot of these men, they’re internalizing so much constantly, and they’re not reaching out to those around them.

The reason I got so excited about Tuben as a character is he felt emblematic of everything we were talking about during Trump’s last re-election. You have the. disaffected conservative man who maybe voted for Trump. He would never tell me. He wouldn’t say whether he did or he didn’t, but he thinks all politicians are corrupt, and he’s living in this world on his phone that goes from Andrew Tate to porn to Nick Fuentes.

And, then here comes along a doctor, or not even a doctor, that says, “All of the things that you’re feeling can be fixed with this shot.” If you’re Ruben and you’re already feeling so alone and you haven’t spent your life thinking about who you are and your place in the world, you see a chance to fix all of your problems.

And when Ruben and Lana, his partner, had deep conversations, or when Ruben is on stage doing comedy, connecting with an audience, he feels so much better about himself. But then when he’s back to his phone, he’s feeling horribly alone, like he needs to change something. I think that’s something we all feel.

When I’m talking to my fiancée about how I’m nervous about this or that, I feel great. I feel connected. But then I go back to my phone, and I feel like shit again. So yeah, the ones who have those conversations are in a much better place.

That was by design. Every kind of man is getting this. Anecdotally speaking, Bill says that about two-thirds of the patients are straight and one-third are queer, which is surprising. Sometimes he even says three-quarters are straight, and anecdotally from my experience, that’s accurate. I’ve seen patients as young as early 20s. I mean, David was in his late teens when he got botched, or maybe right around 20 years old. He’s 24 in the film.

Yeah. I also filmed with men in their 70s. I’ve spoken to practitioners who’ve done penis enlargements for men in their 90s.

Men have been trying to enlarge their penis all the way back to the days of the cavemen, as the movie says. But now there’s this extra layer of social pressure, and technology makes it possible. It doesn’t mean that it’s safe, but it makes it possible. Every kind of man is doing this, and I felt like I needed an avatar for both.

You have the guy who’s completely seduced by bullshit online. We all know that guy. I have friends I went to college with who are that guy now. Certainly people from high school who are that guy. And then David is a little bit more heartfelt coming from OnlyFans and dealing with the scars of his experience.

There’s always something bigger. No pun intended. I really tried not to be reductive. For Bill, it was a partner who called him a “little dick motherfucker” 15 or 20 years ago, and then he started changing every part of his body. He has fake balls. He has silicone balls. He has his [fake] pecs, all of it. For David, it was growing up evangelical. For Ruben, it was dealing with abuse and being Mexican-American and things like that.

But there are ordinary people. Believe it or not, the most ordinary person I met was the megachurch pastor. He claimed he was just doing it for his wife, who he loves very much. I hope that that’s true. But almost everyone else would start that way, and then you know how it goes. It’s the old Errol Morris trick: you just kind of stay quiet and let them continue. Then they’d be like, “Oh, and also it’s this, and that, and this kid who said this fucked up thing to me 15 years ago. And by the way, my wife and I don’t have sex anymore.”

Look at implants. Whenever Dolly Parton got hers, they were sort of the medical frontier. I’m sure whoever was the version of me and you at the time was dealing with the same sort of fun, gonzo stories.

And there was probably a Dr. Loria at that time [a penis enlargement provider in the film] who was botching breast implants. It’s a lot safer now, and we know how those work. This is a—maybe unregulated isn’t the right word—but under-regulated frontier. You have people like Dr. Loria operating with impunity in Florida.

This is a guy who designs his own proprietary blend of who knows what. He literally will not tell me. It’s some kind of silicone oil. He says he’s “a hobbyist pharmacist,” and he likes to come up with his own proprietary solutions which he creates in Florida at his office. And the results you see in the film are egregious. I have yet to talk to a Loria patient who has had a positive outcome, and he is still practicing in the state of Florida.

The movie intentionally tries to leave that in a gray zone. But even the better technologies like hyaluronic acid, which is lip filler, the FDA has never said that you can inject that into someone’s dick. [But] it hasn’t said you can’t. It’s fine for off-label use. It’s all sort of the Wild West right now, and I think people don’t realize that the American medical system has all these gray areas and openings.

Bill is not a doctor. He just has to be under the supervision of a doctor, meaning a doctor came to his facility at some point and sanctioned it. Where I see the trouble is that all of these urologists who are trained to do really important medical procedures, like someone struggling with ED or who has issues after prostate cancer, they see a way to make money doing this. I saw literally dozens of urologists flock to Bill because they realize they can make a few thousand dollars in twenty minutes doing penile enhancement. Is that what they should be doing with their time? Probably not. Is that a way that they can make a lot of money? Certainly.

Business looks good. And sorry, one last point is that the penis is different also because it’s invisible. Men already don’t talk about their feelings, as you and I know. But other types of female work are visible. The media has been objectifying women from the beginning of time.

This is something that almost feels personal to men. They’re not telling their partners. Many of them say they’re doing it for themselves. Some of them literally tell me they just want it to poke bigger through their pants at the gym, or they want to show it off in the locker room. So it’s a personal choice, I think, in a way that I’m skeptical of, that’s also different from other medical procedures or kinds of plastic surgery.

[Long breath] I don’t know if you can put “long breath” in the transcript, but… I believe in a kind of documentary filmmaking that doesn’t impose a takeaway. I think we now live in this streamer era where movies are designed to be “two screen” documentaries. It’s a Netflix term, where you can fold laundry [while watching], and they tell you every third of the movie what it’s about and what the takeaway is. The movie is not pro-penis enlargement. It’s not anti-penis enlargement. It’s using that as a canvas to explore all of these things and I think that’s where I like to start. That said, I would not recommend my friends do it. Bill tried to get me to do it, by the way.

Many times. And I am willing to do anything for my stories, like be in bed with Nazis for years or whatever the fuck. I was not willing to do that. The simple fact is that this is a medical gray area. No one knows how safe it is. Filler migrates, and the problem is in your penis.

Whoever that friend is, I would be like, “What issue are you having in your marriage, with your kids, with your self-esteem, with your body?” And I would really welcome the chance to get close to that friend again, you know? As you get older, people are around less, people have kids, people are also more isolated. They’re in their family. And those moments actually can lead to incredible breakthroughs when your friend is like, “I’m scared that my dick is not good enough.”

I would have just been gifted with the most exciting conversation that I’ve had in months, and I would welcome that. We would go on a hike, or have a beer, and talk about why he doesn’t like his dick. I think we as a society would be better if we did that more often.
