#6699. New Senate class includes experienced lawmakers, ex-governor

Former Sen. Sherrod Brown is once again a senator-elect, after winning a special election in Ohio. Above, he talks with voters during a campaign event in Athens, Ohio., on Oct. 20. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The new Democratic majority in the Senate will feature a number of top recruits with significant government experience both on and off Capitol Hill.

None is more familiar than Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown, who unseated appointed Sen. Jon Husted just two years after losing Ohio’s other Senate seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno.

Having prevailed in a special election, Brown is expected to be seated before the end of the year.

Brown, who rose to be the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs chairman during his first stint in the Senate, does not reclaim seniority under Democratic caucus rules but will surely have influence above and beyond that of a typical newly-elected senator.

Speaking to supporters after his victory Tuesday night, he said he would make it a priority to ban members of Congress from trading stocks — one of the popular campaign messages of Republicans and Democrats alike in 2026.

“We will fight to end these tariffs,” Brown said of his other priorities. “We will end this war. We will fight to lower your costs, and increase your paychecks and open up paths to the middle class.”

Brown will be joined in the Senate by several first-timers with outsize profiles and experience, led by Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, D-N.C.

“I am determined that no matter the challenges that confront me, I will be an independent voice ready to work with anyone to do what’s right for this amazing state that has given me so much,” Cooper said in his victory speech.

With his history of winning statewide elections, Cooper was a top recruit for Democrats and expected Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., with Republican incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis opting to retire at the end of the current term.

Cooper’s the only former governor in the Senate freshman class, though he is not alone among the newcomers with significant public sector experience, being joined by several House members.

New Hampshire Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate, blocking the comeback bid of former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Illinois and Minnesota are sending their Democratic lieutenant governors, with Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton set to succeed Minority Whip Richard J. Durbin and Minnesota voters choosing Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan as the successor for retiring Sen. Tina Smith.

Minnesota’s other Senate seat will be filled by an appointee after Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., won the state’s governor’s race on Tuesday.

“The American people have now entrusted Democrats to fight for them and to put a stop to the most corrupt administration in our nation’s history, and with this new majority, we are ready to turn the page,” Stratton said in a statement. “With a new majority in the Senate, Democrats are prepared to stand up to the Trump administration while fighting to lower costs, protect our rights and democracy, and deliver progress for the American people.”

The smaller Senate Republican Conference picks up new members from a number of particularly red states, with Alabama Rep. Barry Moore winning the open seat contest to succeed Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who was elected governor on Tuesday.

Rep. Julia Letlow, R-La., who had defeated Sen. Bill Cassidy in the primary, prevailed in the general election and will move over to the Senate. Also heading to the Senate is the at-large congresswoman from Wyoming, Republican Rep. Harriet Hageman.

“We are about to engage in a battle for the future of this nation, and as we all recognize, the looming fight with the left is about much more than just policy differences. It’s about the very survival of this country as it has been and as we know it,” Hageman posted on social media after her victory.

Rep. Andy Barr, R-Ky., won the Senate seat being vacated by the retirement of longtime Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell.

Another House member crossing the Capitol is Republican Rep. Kevin Hern, who won comfortably in Oklahoma. While his contest was not a special election, Hern is also likely to be seated early, after the state attorney general released an opinion last week that he can take over for appointed Sen. Alan Armstrong as soon as the results of the election are certified.

The unusual scenario came about because Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vacated the Senate seat earlier this year to fill the spot in the president’s Cabinet.

Hern, speaking with reporters before polls closed on election night, highlighted a relatively straightforward set of legislative priorities, including government funding legislation, the annual defense authorization, a surface transportation bill and the farm bill.

“The Senate hasn’t really done anything since last July, and that’s one of the reasons I think the Senate’s in trouble right now. They really haven’t passed any bills over there,” Hern said.

#6698. An Up-Close Look at The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power’s Twisted Love Triangle

Morfydd Clark, Jamie Campbell Bower, and Charlie Vickers unpack that tree nest scene.

This story contains spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.

After sleeping alone, it takes some getting used to sharing a bed with someone. This is a challenging proposition in the third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power for the recently reunited Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband, Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), when they use a tree nest as a makeshift bedchamber, as the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers) hunts them down. But Elves are not mere mortals, and after centuries apart, they slip back into slumbering beside each other as if not a day has passed. On set, however, things were much more awkward: Galadriel’s sword gets in Clark’s way, she struggles to roll over in chainmail, and the couple’s moss pillow is too small.

It is mid-September 2025 at the legendary Shepperton Studios just outside London, and there has been another request for more real moss to elevate Bower’s head. (He likens this grassy pillow to the mattresses in The Princess and the Pea when we talk a year later.) The mood up in the tree nest, as Clark and Bower rehearse a scene from the fifth episode, is much lighter than what plays out on screen. Under the watchful eyes of director Sanaa Hamri, the actors figure out the logistics of spooning in this confined space, mimicking sleep so the camera can see their faces, and allowing Clark to shift to her side, then quickly back away when Galadriel imagines Sauron lying beside her. Later in the day, Vickers will switch in. The shock sends Galadriel falling backward out of the tree and straight into danger. This is not your run-of-the-mill love triangle or burgeoning throuple.

To put it mildly, Galadriel has been going through it in the adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien’s history of Middle-earth. After she rejected Sauron’s offer to be his queen (again) at the end of season 2, he has since taken much of Middle-earth, and his quest to create the One Ring—and thereby rule over all—continues. In the previous episode, he attempted to locate an elf being held prisoner in Gundabad who knew the secrets of forging the One Ring. It turns out the last Elven-smith was already dead, but Galadriel’s long-lost husband, Celeborn, was locked up in a neighboring cell. Celeborn likely knows those same secrets that Sauron needs, making him invaluable. During their escape, Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) is slain, and Sauron comes face-to-face with Galadriel for the first time this season. Well, other than popping into her subconscious.

When Sauron appears in Galadriel’s dreams again in the fifth episode, “The Lady of Lórien,” the safety of the tree canopy is immediately shattered as Galadriel’s sleeping mind pictures Sauron lying inches away where she expects to see Celeborn. When I catch up with Clark on Zoom a year later in September 2026, her face lights up when I mention this scene. “I loved being up there [in the tree nest],” she says. “It was so cozy.” While the episode ends with Celeborn being captured by Sauron—separating the couple once again—there is a brief respite from the horrors of this war-torn land. “There’s a real unabashed lean into the gorgeousness of fantasy,” Clark says of this season, including the foray into swoon-worthy romance in the cocooned foliage.

While the Elves have only just reunited, Clark and Bower had already established the foundation of Galadriel and Celeborn’s relationship during a dance sequence in the season 3 premiere episode, revealing a far lighter Galadriel than we have seen for some time. This also gave the actors an opportunity to get to know each other. “There is a magic about him,” Clark says of Bower. “We did get to rehearse that together, which also took away a certain type of magic in that learning a dance with someone is pretty vulnerable. We got to know each other doing that, which was really nice. He was so lovely, and he is elf-like.”

As we learned in season 1, Celeborn left to fight in the war during the First Age and never came home—Middle-earth is now in its Second Age. Galadriel and Celeborn share battle stories, but it is Sauron informing Celeborn that they have previously met (Celeborn claims he has no memory of this) that throws more fire onto this already sizzling dynamic. But before Sauron storms in like a jealous ex, Celeborn and Galadriel manage some K-I-S-S-I-N-G in the tree. “It was a tight space,” Bower laughs over the phone earlier this month. “Towards the end of that scene, there’s that beautiful moment of physical reconnection, and our intimacy coordinator [Sophie Cooch] was so helpful in finding a beauty and almost like a dance and a grace within that physical reconnection into the falling down [together], and being able to lie side by side,” Bower says.

Having just played Stranger Things’ big bad Vecna, Bower (who is a huge fan of Tolkien’s work) said he was looking for a character who represented love, and Celeborn radiates light even in the darkest circumstances. In the episode, Celeborn senses Galadriel is holding back, but doesn’t press too hard about what. “She definitely feels like she’s lost a sparkle, and he’s a mirror to her,” says Clark. “She can’t ignore the parts of it that have changed.” Clark recalls discussing with Bower that there should be zero “feeling of ownership between them.” When I mention this to Bower, he references the line from Breakfast at Tiffany’s to sum up this dynamic: “We belong to nobody, and nobody belongs to us. We don’t even belong to each other.”

Tolkien’s marriage and experience in World War I provided inspiration for this union, but it was The Magnetic Fields song “Abigail, Belle of Kilronan” that Clark says she became obsessed with while filming. “It’s about someone going off to war, and it’s like, ‘And when I come home, if I come home, you’ll be a grown woman. And when I come home, if I come home, don’t be alone, Abigail, Belle of Kilronan,’” Clark says. “That’s almost been her biggest betrayal of him that she allowed herself to be lonely for so long, which I found really beautiful.”

One person Galadriel was close to before knowing his real identity was Sauron. Although she vocalizes that she doesn’t want Sauron present in this moment—not even uttering his name—the image of him lying next to her is a jolt back to reality, even if he is a figment of her imagination. “Even though in many ways her dreams are coming true with being reunited with Celeborn,” Clark says, “they can’t live in a simple vacuum of happiness. The world is still out there, and she’s part of the world.” Unfortunately for Galadriel, as she quickly backs away, she falls from the tree, alerting the nearby orcs to their presence.

The vision seems to be Galadriel’s own doing; Sauron is living rent-free in her mind instead of intentionally popping into her dreams. Vickers discussed this approach with Clark. “The way I play it was determined by what she [Clark] had in her mind—because it’s Galadriel’s experience, it’s not Sauron’s experience—and that was to be the scariest I could be in Galadriel’s mind,” Vickers says.

When I met Vickers on set, he was in costume, grabbing a juice from craft services before joining Clark up in the tree nest. Having spent a lot of time on a nearby soundstage, where Sauron’s bleak Barad-dûr lair is located, the Australian actor was happy to experience this change of scenery. “Barad-dûr this season is incredibly intense. It was 35 degrees [95°F] on the days we were filming there,” Vickers says over Zoom. “There was a lot of sweat. It was wonderful to go into the forest on a soundstage.” Still, there were some logistical issues for Vickers up in the nest, first finding the same eyeline to match Bower’s sleeping position and then trying not to stab Clark with Sauron’s pointy gloves. “Lying down in all that stuff is incredibly challenging,” Vickers says.

Of course, you don’t see this human behavior in the final cut. “It’s a very particular thing to film something fantasy in this way because the look is so important,” Clark says. “It does matter that their hair looks absolutely lovely in that light, and they move like they’re artists with their bodies.” This includes scenes that might require a stunt double, like the one I observed. “Your stunt double is always a huge part of creating the character, but I think more so than ever with an elf, because she’s got to be excellent,” Clark says. “We do as much as we can with me being as excellent as I can be.” For everything else, Clark’s stunt double Hannah Grant (who has a ballet and martial arts background) steps in.

While the version of Sauron in this scene is a figment of Galadriel’s imagination, the real Dark Lord is traveling to the Eryn Galen woodland. Celeborn sacrifices himself to stop his wife (who is lying unconscious nearby) from being discovered. What comes next will likely be incredibly unpleasant, but Bower enjoyed going head-to-head with Vickers as the twisted trio enters its next phase.

“It’s where sparks can fly,” Bower says. “You need to build a rapport, have a friendship, a comfortability, and a trust in one another. Charlie made that so easy from day one.” However, Sauron won’t be as accommodating. “Celeborn has something that Sauron really needs,” Vickers says. “It’s the key to his whole existence up to this point, so you have all the emotional interplay, but then beneath that you have this real psychological drive, which is, ‘I will do anything. I will not stop. I will do all I can to get this secret out of you.’” It seems unlikely that Celeborn, Galadriel, or Sauron will get any sleep anytime soon.

#6697. Aman Essentials Creative Director Kristina Romanova on Collaborating With Kim Jones

“I think the most successful collaborations are the ones that feel a little unexpected at first, but completely natural once you see the result,” the creative director told Bazaar

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Kim Jones is, in his own words, an “Aman junkie.” Over the years, the designer—known for his work as artistic director of Fendi (2020–2024) and Dior Mens (2018-2025) and who recently announced his own soon to be launched namesake label—has turned to the luxury hospitality group for its suite of exclusive resorts, hotels, and private residences, traveling the world and experiencing more than 30 of the company’s destinations. It was this, even more so than his longstanding career in fashion, that made creative director Kristina Romanova declare him the “perfect” choice for retail subsidiary Aman Essentials’s debut collaboration.

“He knows exactly what makes the brand special,” says Romanova, who first met Jones at a masked ball in Venice, where the two creatives bonded over a shared love of travel, fashion, and art—all pillars of the broader Aman ethos. “We didn’t need to explain the Aman philosophy to him; he already lived it. When the idea of a fashion collaboration came up, I had absolutely no doubt that it had to be Kim.”

“For me, I’m not interested in collaborations simply for the sake of creating something new or generating attention. There has to be a shared sensibility, mutual respect and something meaningful that both sides bring to the table. At the same time, I don’t want someone who simply repeats what Aman already does. The whole point of collaborating is to introduce a fresh perspective, perhaps even challenge us a little, while staying true to who we are.”

With this trust, Romanova and the Aman Essentials team gave Jones full creative reign, asking the designer to offer his own interpretation of the Aman world through a line of knitwear, silks, accessories, and more. The result was “Lines of Passage,” a capsule wardrobe that could take a traveler from airplane to adventure, with an emphasis on practicality, timelessness, and high-quality materials. In colorways that might blend into the blues of an ocean getaway or the greens of hiking retreat, Jones designed windbreakers and pullovers alongside silk pajamas and slippers, everyday polos and T-shirts, and swimwear. And to celebrate, travelled to one of the Aman’s most famed locations, Aman Tokyo for not only the campaign’s stirring visuals but a bespoke trip that included an itinerary that showcased the finest of Japanese craft and culture as well as a dinner that was attended by the likes of Claire Waight Keller and Yoon Ahn.

“Aman has always been more than a hotel brand. It represents a particular way of living, one rooted in a love of travel, nature, culture and the freedom to be completely at ease,” Romanova adds. “The collection is a natural extension of that philosophy.”

#6696. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6695. Joaquin Phoenix Wasn’t Thinking About 'Her' When He Filmed This Intelligent Eyewear Campaign

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

“Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner says. “It could be any language.”

The idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix says was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across New England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”

Phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor says. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”

In an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director said.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

When I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he says. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”

#6694. Leighton Meester on the New Blair Waldorf Novel—and Whether She’d Play the Character Again

The former Gossip Girl star has already read part of the book.

In February, news broke that Gossip Girl author Cecily von Ziegesar was writing a new standalone novel about Blair Waldorf, aptly titled Blair, that would capture the iconic character’s life 20 years after the original novels took place. Leighton Meester, who famously played Blair in the 2007 show, is well aware of the project, which is tentatively set for a summer 2027 release. In fact, she told ELLE in a new interview that she has already read the first seven chapters.

When deputy editor and features director Kayla Webley Adler suggested that she could play the role again if the book was adapted into a show, she simply smiled.

She is open to revisiting the character, though. “I’ve been asked this exact question forever, but I never have a good answer because I just am always like, ‘I never say never because I don’t know,’” Meester said. “Obviously that character meant something to me. And I’m grateful that it meant something to other people. So you never know, but I really just don’t know.”

Of course, the actress didn’t share any details about Blair. Deadline wrote in February that its plot is “still under wraps, but it’s expected to follow the former NYC socialite as she returns to the Big Apple to climb her way back to the top of Upper East Side food chain.”

For her part, Meester is just happy to keep acting. “I’m sure that this is cliché at this point, but every time I finish a job, I don’t know what my next job is,” she said. “There’s nothing that’s guaranteed, so every time you get a role, you’re like, ‘I get to do this again. Here we go.’”

It’s a privilege to have a career in the industry, she said: “To be an actor is such a dream, and it’s never lost on me. I’m almost nostalgic about it because I can’t believe I still get to do this. Not to sound like a crazy person, but sometimes before I do a scene, I will tell myself, ‘This is my dream, and my life, in one way or another, has led to me being able to be there when they yell ‘action!’”

#6693. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6692. Only Murders in the Building Season 6: Everything We Know So Far

Though Only Murders in the Building wrapped its fifth season in October 2025, the Hulu hit is hardly slowing down. The series is heading toward its next chapter with awards-season momentum after earning Golden Globe nominations for Best Television Series – Musical or Comedy, as well as best performance nods for stars Selena Gomez, Steve Martin, and Martin Short.

The final episode of season 5, which ended with the suspicious death of Cinda Canning, left fans on a major cliffhanger that begs for a deeper investigation. Here’s everything we know so far about the future of the show.

Yes! The news came shortly after the season 5 finale premiered. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the forthcoming season will officially switch locations and be filmed in London. The previous season’s finale ended with the trio listening to a new Cinda Canning podcast set across the pond. That, along with Canning’s mysterious death at the end of the episode, may hint at why the group could travel to the U.K.

Selena Gomez previously stated that she hopes Only Murders continues for many seasons to come. “I really hope that I can just keep evolving Mabel as I get older, because I want to do this for a long time,” she told USA Today in September 2025.

Steve Martin also felt optimistic about a sixth season. “We believe we’re doing another season,” he said. “We think so. But you have to live season by season. And even if it was canceled tomorrow, we would have to say, ‘We had a great, great run. We loved what we were doing. It was a great way to spend five, six years.’”

In May 2026, Gomez shared that filming had officially begun when she reposted a photo from the show’s Instagram account to her Instagram Story. The image, showing Gomez alongside some of the cast members together in London, was captioned, “Season 6 🇬🇧 Day 1!”

Just like previous seasons, season 6 is confirmed to have 10 episodes.

Only Murders in the Building season 6 is taking place in London, as well as a select few countryside locations in England. In an August 2026 interview with Vulture, showrunner Josh Hoffman teased, “one of the more signature episodes is called ‘The Country House,’ and that sits in a very specific vibe and look, and quite a collection of characters.” He added, “We got about an hour outside of London…and into some of the stately homes.”

Season 5 concluded with Cinda Canning (Tina Fey) dropping dead in front of the Arconia, the same night that her new U.K.-set podcast The Girl With the Curls aired. Given the proximity, Charles, Oliver, and Mabel set out to solve her murder. “It was technically a murder in the building because she did it with her last gasp,” Hoffman told Vulture. “But the question is, what was going on with her? That is what our trio is off to investigate.”

Specific plot points will remain under wraps until its premiere, but Hoffman revealed that Charles’s Brazzos television show is getting a reboot in the U.K. “Martin Freeman will go toe-to-toe at some point with Charles as to who’s the better Brazzos,” he shared.

The show will also be taking place during the holiday season. “With the show airing at the top of December, it was impossible to avoid,” Hoffman added. “Within the story, we are moving towards the end of the year. The end of last season was fall, so we had to carry through on that.” The sixth season was shot in an uncharacteristically hot summer, but the show did its best to capture an English winter “that feels a bit rainy and a bit cloudy. There will be a bit of a lean into the holiday season by the end of it all.”

Selena Gomez, Steve Martin, and Martin Short have returned for another season. Season 5 featured newcomers Renée Zellweger and Logan Lerman, while Keegan-Michael Key was elevated to a recurring role. It’s not yet clear whether these supporting characters, along with Meryl Streep and Da’Vine Joy Randolph, will return for season 6, but we’ll stay tuned.

Season 6 has also added several notable new faces. In June 2026, Deadline reported that David Tennant, Nicola Coughlan, Jodie Whittaker, Jim Broadbent, Richard Ayoade, Adrian Lukis, and Kathryn Hunter had joined the cast in recurring roles. By August 2026, Deadline reported that Doctor Who star Peter Capaldi will also be joining the upcoming season—Whittaker, Tennant, and Broadbent have all had roles within the Doctor Who universe.

Olivia Colman was added to the cast days later, with Gomez, Streep, and Short announcing the news via an Instagram video. “We have had so many amazing guest stars for Only Murders in the Building,” Gomez said in the short clip, with Streep adding, “We’re just missing one.”

Short jokingly pops into the frame before making way for Colman to appear alongside the trio.

Colman’s character will be a writer, Hoffman revealed in the Vulture interview. “The U.K. is the home of Agatha Christie. This is where Cinda Canning might have met her maker in some way,” he said. “And all of them are following along in the tradition of the cozy murder mystery. Olivia is in that line as well as a memoirist.”

Jennifer Saunders will also have a role in the sixth season, with Hoffman telling Vulture that her character takes significant inspiration from Vivienne Westwood. “I had an incredible time many years ago working on a screenplay with Brian Grazer and Ron Howard on the life of Vivienne Westwood,” he said. “So I spent a lot of time here in London developing that screenplay with her.” Though that movie never materialized, Hoffman used his research to inform Saunders’s character, which will “lean into the fashion design world in great British style, with a tip of the hat to the great Vivienne.”

Queen Camilla was extremely close to having a role in Only Murders in the Building season 6, with Hoffman telling Vulture, “We almost got Camilla...I know it’s insane, but yes, there was a moment.”

The Queen Camilla cameo never materialized because of logistics, but Hoffman “did pursue it a little bit, until I realized it’s going to be a whole thing.” Hoffman isn’t ruling out Prince Harry and Meghan Markle cameos, though—“When is she traveling? We’re leaving in three days.” He added, “I wouldn’t rule anything out.”

Season 6 of Only Murders in the Building will arrive on December 8. Gomez and the rest of her castmates revealed that filming wrapped in an August 28 video shared to the show’s social media platforms.

Yes. First look photos arrived on August 25, and feature Gomez, Martin, and Short back in costume as Mabel, Charles, and Oliver in winter-approved wardrobe staples.

The trailer for Only Murders in the Building season 6 arrived on November 17. In the trailer, Mabel, Oliver, and Charles try to find out the truth about Cinda’s death after seeing her leave her hand on the gates of The Arconia in her final moments. “Cinda died dropping a hand on our gate,” Mabel says, to which Oliver adds, “She clearly wants our help.” After discovering that Cinda was in London just before her death, the trio travels across the pond to London with the hopes of finding out who did it.

The trio struggles with getting used to how life works in England. Simple things like drinking tea prove to be a challenge when Mabel suggests that Cinda could have died from a poisonous pot of tea. The suspects—aside from Gemma Joyce, Coughlan’s character—aren’t immediately clear, but there are a host of individuals who could be guilty of the crime as the first glimpses of Streep, Ashley, Colman, and more characters are revealed in the trailer.

#6691. The Governors Awards Marked the Official Start of the 'You Can See Everything' Oscars Campaign

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

Start your engines: the 2027 Oscars race is officially underway. Awards Season always starts in earnest with the Governors Awards, a ceremony held in a smaller ballroom in the same Dolby Theater complex where the main event will take place early next spring. It’s where they give out honorary Academy Awards (and the esteemed Irving Thalberg Award) to the legends who, woefully, have yet have won a competitive Oscar—last year’s marquee honoree was Tom Cruise, this year’s were Glenn Close and Ridley Scott. But it’s also where Best Picture and the other awards narratives we will discuss endlessly for the next four months really begin to take shape.

Dune 3, Artificial, and Misty Green all had big presences in the room, which, duh. (Tim and Kylie in the cut, mostly sitting and not mingling, but it was interesting that he showed up this year but not last for the big Marty Supreme push.) But there were a few other films represented whose presence made their campaign intentions clear. Mahershala Ali presented the first award of the night to Floyd Norman (a 90-year-old trailblazing cartoonist who worked with Walt Disney and later Pete Docter) but the Your Mother 3x squad was deep, from director Bassam Tariq to John Cho. Jesse Eisenberg, Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore put on for A24’s The Debut, Eisenberg's second directorial effort. (Watching Jesse and Andrew Garfield reconnect made for a beautiful Social Network reunion.) And Curry Barker and Inde Navarette being there would certainly imply a real push for Obsession. The duo with the most motion in the room, though, was unquestionably Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The only time they didn’t seem like the big dogs that everyone was gassed to chat with was when they were talking to King Big Dog himself, Christopher Nolan, front and center receiving will-wishers at The Odyssey table. Nolan and Fielder is a crossover that needs to be cemented on wax, a drum I will continue to beat. But it was cool to see Zendaya talking intently with Oppenheim; her collaborator curation has been pretty elite—imagine her in whatever Oppenheim chooses to follow Primetime with?

When I asked Fielder about embarking on the campaign trail and how far the doc can actually go, he sighed and said “one day at a time,” in that Fielder monotone where you can’t quite tell if he’s being earnest or not. But he laughed off the idea of being too invested in any nominations either way.

But most importantly: the Governors Awards is just a really fun room in which to be an interloper or fly on the wall. I spotted Shawn Levy and my brain immediately started spamming the word “sublime.” Daniel Kaluuya started cracking up at the mention of his great airport interview with Tyriq Withers. Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Ed Norton joined ranks for a brief Invite huddle. Everywhere I turned, there was either a person so famous or certified that it startled me to see them walk by (like Zendaya breezing in right as the show started, or turning around to find myself face-to-face with personal favorite Carla Gugino. (Karen Sisco mentioned!) Unlike some stuffier award ceremonies, the Governors Awards is kind of like the cocktail hour before the big sit-down dinner in March.

Ambling around the room with a stiff glass of Johnnie Walker in hand—“Did you just get carded”? an exec asked me incredulously; the bartender replied that he thought I was “like, 14"—I briefly caught up with David Corenswet, who, true to form, was unfazed by the forces beyond his control as ever. When I said “weird week huh?” he didn’t even realize I was referring to James Gunn’s DC exit, then laughed when it dawned on him and said “above my pay-grade” with a genuine shrug. We should all be so blissfully unbothered.

Later, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II told me he was excited for this week’s Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth red carpet premiere, noting that this film will be the first time he only read his scenes for a project and no other part of the story. Without wanting to give too much away, Yahya said Tarantino’s script is structured in a way where he could comfortably read his parts and get enough of the gist to stay in the dark about the rest, because the only thing better than starring in a new Tarantino joint is getting to still experience it like a fan.

Other notable sightings, interactions, and crossovers: Travis Scott doubled down on what he told me at our Men of the Year party: he wants that golden statue for his original Odyssey song, and he’s willing to play the campaign game for it, dutifully sitting through the whole night (and jetting off immediately after the ceremony ended to go catch Future’s 10 pm set at Camp Flog Gnaw up at Dodger Stadium.) Speaking of Odyssey collaborators, James Blake was also in attendance—I watched him meet H.E.R. and talk about potentially collaborating. Tom Cruise was the belle of the ball at last year’s ceremony but played it super lowkey this year, to the point where I didn’t actually realize he was there until I saw him sneak out of a secret side exit after briefly talking with Tessa Thompson. Digger’s divisive reviews and reactions have evidently not knocked Tom off of his Best Actor pivot.

As for the actual awards, after Floyd, John Malkovich charmed the room with a great toast to Glenn Close, and King Storyteller Matt Damon regaled everyone with a great impression of triple-OG crank Ridley Scott from their time together on The Martian. (Matt was hesitant to do another movie about a loner astronaut right after Interstellar, to which Ridley apparently replied “No one gives a shit.”) Both tributes and subsequent speeches were expectedly emotional; Damon pointedly said that "it’s about time we see Ridley Scott with an Oscar in his hand,” but Ridley’s remarks were all about how much the late great Tony Scott would’ve deserved one too, leading to misty eyes and standing ovations. Close addressed going 0 for 8 but said the work is the real reward as her daughter tearfully watched on. But there were great moments of levity, too, like Todd Haynes presenting Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with an award by revealing that he and Christine both slept with the same guy back in college.

Either way, a narrative of being long overdue seems to be emerging. An Awards Season where the Tom Cruises and Glenn Closes of the game finally get theirs, while upsets like You Can See Everything shake the table. What more could you ask for?

#6690. Stylist and Creative Director Akari Endo-Gaut’s Guide to Tokyo

Perhaps no city juggles the past and the future as nimbly as Tokyo. Sleek skyscrapers meet centuries-old shrines; a rich culinary tradition blends with contemporary innovation (it’s no accident that this is the city with the most Michelin starred-restaurants in the world). The fashion, of course, exists in a similar dichotomy, expertly blending traditional techniques with the avant-garde. There’s never a wrong time to visit the Japanese capital—but in winter, when ski resorts a quick day trip away are in full swing and New Year’s celebrations are on the horizon, it feels particularly special. All you have to do is narrow down your itinerary.

In fact, there’s so much to discover that you could spend an entire trip dedicated to shopping alone—according to Akari Endo-Gaut, a Japan-born, New York-based stylist and creative director who studied in Tokyo, it may be worth bringing a second suitcase just for souvenirs. From the vintage shops to put on your radar to the best place to stop for a glass of natural wine, here’s a glimpse at Endo-Gaut’s Tokyo little black book.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Since I was student in Tokyo, one of my favorite areas to hang around was Minami-Aoyama. We used to have amazing Corso Como store there; now, the Comme des Garçons store, the Issey Miyake Pleats Please shop, and the Auralee store there are still where you can go to find a special piece.

For vintage gems: There are so many good vintage shops in Tokyo, and it goes deep. BerBer Jin is always my first stop, and I also check luxury resale shops like Komehyo.

For unique souvenirs: You can find the best curated products, from ceramic bowls to German knives, at Arts and Science. And beautifully wrapped sweets at Higashiya are the best gifts.

For a worthwhile investment piece: Wako Arts and Culture is a new space conceived by artist Hiroshi Sugimoto in the basement of a prestigious department store in Ginza. It’s all specially curated, a great spot to find a special piece from fashion to Japanese craft.

For the magpie: My very talented friend Charlotte Chesnais from Paris recently opened a shop in Tokyo; it’s a must-visit. Or, if you’re looking for best-condition vintage watches, you can go to ECW Shoto.

For your next great read: Japan has a big book culture—go to Komiyama bookstore for vintage books, or spend a full weekend browsing at Tsutaya Daikanyama or SKAC.

For stylish home goods: You can find traditional but beautiful kitchen goods at Kiya and, of course, at Muji. Or, spend a fun day exploring all the kitchen goods stores in the Kappabashi area, which is a shopping street dedicated to restaurant owners.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Hakujitsu houses a beautiful collection of ceramics in an old dentist building. My secret favorite is Yanaka Matsunoya—it has the best baskets and tote bags.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Japanese-Chinese food or yakiniku, so I go to Chugoku Hanten with local friends or to Jojoen with my sister. If I have foreign guests, they usually have fun dining experience at Narukiyo.

For a bakery treat: Sawamura is our best local bakery cafe in Hiroo. After a soba lunch at Kanda, stop by Omiya Western Sweets Shop for the cutest pastry; for traditional Japanese sweets at an upscale, architecturally beautiful spot, go to Toraya Akasaka.

For the art-lover: Taka Ishii and Tomio Koyama are the best fine arts galleries in Tokyo. I like the artists from Kosaku Kanechika too, and at Licht gallery, you can see the best design pieces.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: For the architecture lover, a drink at Imperial Bar, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, is a must. When I’m hanging out with local friends, I’d go for a natural wine at Le Cabaret or Tabac.

For your packing list: Honestly, you don’t need anything, since you go to Tokyo to buy the best of all items! Bring flat shoes for walking, and an extra suitcase for shopping. An eye mask and melatonin for the 13-hour time difference will come in handy, as will a handkerchief; it’s part of local etiquette to carry one. And I always like to bring a running outfit for the famous Imperial Palace run.

#6688. 15 lessons from the midterms as Democrats rebound with historic wave

Democratic staffers cheer Tuesday as results roll in during an election night watch party in Washington with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS — It wasn’t exactly a surprise that Democrats did well on Tuesday, but the breadth and depth of their victory was stunning. Votes are still being counted, but it’s looking like a massive blue wave with very few Republican survivors.

Just two years ago, Donald Trump delivered one of the biggest Republican victories in recent history. The GOP won back the White House, finished ahead in the national popular vote, recaptured the Senate majority and held on to the House. But what Republicans thought was a permanent realignment of the party coalitions crumbled under the weight of an unpopular war in the Middle East and voter frustrations over the economy and president’s economic policies.

The complete analysis will come in the weeks and months ahead, but here are a few initial thoughts.

Trump is a political mortal. Despite the pervasive narrative that normal political rules don’t apply to the president, election night showed that is simply not true. Sure, he was a surprise victor in 2016, but as an unpopular sitting president in 2018, his party lost a net of 40 House seats. When he ran for reelection in 2020, again as an unpopular president, he lost. When he got to run against an unpopular Democratic administration in 2024, he won again. And when his job approval rating sank to historic lows, his party was routed in the midterms.

Polls pointed in the right direction. Despite a decade of ridicule and abuse, the polling industry had a good cycle. Of course, there were a few outliers, but much of the public and private data (at least on the Democratic side) pointed to a good midterm for Democrats. Surprise outcomes on Tuesday were likely more due to a lack of data than poor data. And, if anything, some surveys underestimated the support for Democratic candidates. Pollsters still have methodological challenges, particularly with low response rates, but it’s time to ditch the narrative that polls always underestimate Republicans.

Democrats captured the Senate. Democrats are going to gain at least seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. They might gain up to nine with wins in Alaska and Mississippi. (Both races haven’t been called as yet by The Associated Press). They needed to gain four seats for a majority. Our projection of a Democratic gain of four to six seats was directionally accurate but will fall at least slightly below the final tally.

It could have been worse for Republicans. While it’s almost hard to believe, the night could have been a bigger catastrophe for the Senate GOP. Louisiana Rep. Julia Letlow won the open seat by 2 points; appointed Florida Sen. Ashley Moody won by 3 points; and Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts was leading by 7 points as of Wednesday morning. If Sens. Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi or Dan Sullivan of Alaska survive, they’d do so by narrow margins. Meanwhile, Democrats didn’t really have any close calls, as they held Michigan (6 points as of Wednesday morning), Minnesota (10 points), New Hampshire (14 points) and Georgia (18 points).

Democrats captured the House. While dozens of races remain uncalled by the AP, Democrats will gain the House majority as expected. But the size of the wave is going to be bigger than expected. Democrats will likely clear our projection of a net gain of 20 to 30 seats and could approach their 40-seat gain during Trump’s first midterm.

Redistricting flopped for Republicans. Republicans are struggling to gain any of the seats they intentionally redrew to elect new members of their own party. Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas ended up as debacles for the GOP with near total domination by Democrats up and down the ballot, all in states Trump won just two years ago. North Carolina Republican Tim Moore is on track to lose a district that he helped draw for himself.

It didn’t have to be this way. Even though Republicans are placing the early blame on history and inevitability, Tuesday’s results were not a foregone conclusion. Things could have been very different had Trump not started the conflict with Iran, which resulted in domestic economic hardship, or waged a tariff war with friendly countries. Or if he had limited his immigration policy to closing the border and deporting violent criminals in the country illegally. Republicans would have held the Senate, and it would have been an extremely close fight for the House. No matter who or what Republicans choose to blame, the party is here because of Trump.

Sometimes history repeats itself. Twenty years ago, there was an unpopular Republican president in the White House with a war in the Middle East that was driving up fuel prices. Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress as Republicans lost 30 House seats and six Senate seats — a remarkably similar outcome to this cycle.

Midterms portend the future, except when they don’t. Democrats had a great night this week but that’s no guarantee the success will continue. In their best-case scenario, 2026 could be the first part of a two-cycle wave, similar to 2006 and 2008, when Democrats expanded their House majority and won the White House. But 2028 could also look like 2012 in reverse, with Republicans bouncing back from a disastrous midterm as Democrats did after the 2010 tea party wave.

Candidate quality is only a fraction of the story. Republicans can try to blame their candidates or campaigns, whether it’s Hyde-Smith, Ken Paxton in Texas or Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, but all of them would have won in a political environment in which the president was even modestly popular. Without Trump’s self-inflicted policy wounds, candidate quality would not have mattered as much for Republicans, and they could have exploited Democrats with vulnerabilities, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. Gina Hinojosa’s victory over GOP Greg Abbott in Texas, where Democrats also appear on track to sweep every other statewide race, is proof that Republican problems in the Lone Star State extended beyond Paxton’s baggage.

The Trump coalition collapsed. The coalition that brought Republicans to the mountaintop didn’t stick around very long as the party lost ground among a host of key demographic groups that were supposed to be a permanent part of its voter bloc. Trump finished behind Kamala Harris by just 11 points among voters aged 18-29. Republican candidates lost those voters by 47 points on Tuesday, according to the exit polls. Trump finished 5 points behind Harris among Latino voters, but Republicans lost them by 27 points this year. Trump lagged Harris by just 3 points among independent voters but Republicans lost them by 17 points this week. Trump bested Harris among male voters by 12 points in 2024, but Republicans ran even with Democrats with this group on Tuesday. Republicans even lost ground among voters without a college degree. Trump was +13 against Harris in 2024, but Republicans were just +4 in the midterms.

Personal brands matter until they don’t. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania’s 1st District came into the cycle with stellar reputations about bucking partisan trends, but both Republicans went down to defeat. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York’s 17th could join them. It’s just evidence that voters have a limited tolerance for voting against their own partisan tendencies.

Pay attention to special elections. For two years, Democratic candidates significantly overperformed in special elections and regularly scheduled off-year elections. Republicans dismissed the results as “special,” finding excuses to explain them away. But that was a mistake. Their turnout problem was right in front of everyone for more than a year.

Elections are humbling. Losing twice to Trump was a humbling experience for Democrats. Seeing most of those gains wiped out in a single night should be humbling for Republicans. But we’ll see what lessons each party chooses to take from these results.

White evangelicals couldn’t save Republicans. White evangelical voters continue to be one of the most reliable pieces of the GOP coalition. After supporting Trump with 76 percent in 2020 and 82 percent in 2024, and Republican candidates with 83 percent in 2022, white evangelicals supported GOP candidates once again, with 82 percent. But turnout did not keep pace. According to the exit polls, white evangelicals made up 17 percent of the midterm electorate after consistently comprising around a quarter of voters for more than a decade.

#6686. Jewelry Designer Keri Ataumbi’s Guide to Santa Fe

Santa Fe is a perennial favorite for avid hikers and art lovers alike—but visit in winter, and you may just have some of its famed galleries and museums to yourself. Crowds thin out, skiers populate the trails, and glowing farolitos take over every public space. (Abiquiú, the onetime home of Georgia O’Keeffe where you can now visit her studio, is a short car trip away.) “Santa Fe has a lot of day hikes, lake trips, and soaks at the local hot springs,” says Keri Ataumbi, a Kiowa artist and fine jewelry designer based in town. You won’t run out of things to do on a winter trip out West; even the non-adventurer will find plenty to delight in.

It’s an excellent shopping destination, too: Santa Fe has a strong Native American artist tradition, and jewelry lovers especially will want to take note. We spoke to Ataumbi for all her best recommendations on where to find the best of it all—plus, a really good cocktail after a day of exploring it all. Just don’t forget the sunscreen; even in winter, the high altitude makes the UV glare intense.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: I’m a big fan of owning fewer, quality pieces that last. One of my current favorite tops came from Workshop and Wildlife; it’s an oversized, loose knit, hand-painted cashmere sweater by Avant Toi. Chocolate and Cashmere carries locally knit fine cashmere and locally made beautiful chocolates—I just bought one of their cozy serapes as a birthday present for myself last week. They have a large assortment of colors in the store.

For unique souvenirs: I think the best gifts are consumable, and Kakawa Chocolate House makes both beautiful and unusual chocolates. I love their elixirs, which range from historic pre-Columbian and old European recipes to contemporary creations.

For vintage gems: Double Take is great for treasure hunting, with everything from western boots and statement jewelry to vintage coats and kids’ clothing. Santa Fe Vintage is also fun, but it’s by appointment only.

For a worthwhile investment piece: I wear glasses everyday all day, so they are an essential part of how dress, and I’m an avid collector. Ojo Optique is locally owned and carries handcrafted frames you won’t find everywhere; plus, the owners are wonderful at choosing styles that flatter your face.

For the magpie: There’s so much amazing jewelry in Santa Fe! For Native American jewelry, I love Shiprock Santa Fe and the Case Trading Post. For something not Southwestern, The Golden Eye on Don Gaspar has been making high karat gold jewelry since 1971.

For your next great read: I just picked up a copy of American Bread by Andrew Coe at Garcia Street Books. Then I grabbed a coffee next door at Downtown Subscription and happily lost far too much time reading in their garden under the autumn sun.

For stylish home goods: For something special and unique, I head to the farm store, Los Poblanos Norte.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Take a day trip to Truchas to visit Eight Million Gods, where owner Heywood Simoneaux curates a perfectly eclectic store. Back in town, I love Gray Matter. On my last visit, they were unpacking medieval winemaking tools from a French museum; the Cooper’s adzes were my favorite.

For a bakery treat: I love everything at Dolina Bakery and Café, but the gingerbread tiles are my favorite. Owner Annamaria O’Brien is from Slovakia, so the locally sourced menu has Eastern European flavors.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: For a special dinner that’s still relaxed, I go to Izanami. It’s tucked into the mountains and serves small Japanese plates meant for sharing.

For the art-lover: Cara Romero Studio is a photography studio that also hosts group shows, run by my dear friend Cara, an internationally recognized Chemehuevi artist. Her work is deeply thoughtful, with beautifully saturated theatrical compositions.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: Last month when a friend visited from New York, we had gorgeous cocktails at As Above, So Below, a local distillery that uses local ingredients. Mine was made with fragrant juniper and piñon Sigil gin, butterfly pea flower tea, and a 24k gold garnish.

For your packing list: Do not forget a water bottle and electrolytes—it’s 7,000 feet and very dry, so staying hydrated helps with possible altitude sickness. I love Larroudé sneakers for practicality in Santa Fe, where there are a lot of rocky and uneven surfaces to traverse around town, and my go-to cotton travel trouser is a barrel-leg pair from Nili Lotan. The high desert is extremely dry, so I also recommend the piñon body oil, which is locally made from Dryland Wilds.

#6684. David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

One of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

#6682. Where to Stay in Antwerp, Belgium’s Design-Filled City

Antwerp isn’t a loud city. You don’t come here to be awed by ancient ruins or to tour record-breaking skyscrapers. There are no leafy stoops with picturesque brownstones enshrined on TV. Antwerp’s charm unfolds quietly alongside its cobblestoned streets and narrow brick townhouses; I’d argue it’s a place most stumble upon when traveling through Europe, rather than specifically seek out. Those who do make it a point to visit, however, will easily be won over by its unassuming beauty and artistic milieu—after all, there’s a reason why it’s long attracted a certain kind of creative. (Painter Peter Paul Rubens called it home in the 16th century, fashion designers Raf Simons and Pieter Mulier do so in the 21st.)

Winter is an especially lovely time to visit—even when it drizzles (trust me, it will), Antwerp feels delightfully festive: Christmas markets take over the Old Town square, with glowing lights strung up all over the city. The ongoing Antwerp Six exhibit at the MoMu makes a trip this holiday season particularly timely; the group’s first major retrospective closes on January 17, 2027.

The best places to stay in Antwerp offer a chance to adjust to the city’s quiet rhythm—whether that means finding calm in a former convent, or slowing down in one of the many well-appointed Airbnbs that dot the center. Like most major European towns, you can confidently skip the car rental; much, if not most, of Antwerp, can be comfortably discovered on foot and by bike.

An Augustinian convent transformed into a design lover’s dream, the work of famed Belgian architect Vincent Van Duysen makes for a serene refuge after a long journey. Modernist touches and an earthy color palette underscore the property’s monastic qualities, and the rooms are thoughtful but efficiently put together. (The artfully rumpled bed linens are one highlight; the exposed timber beams in the larger suites, another.)

Couples wishing to explore the grounds can unwind with a treatment in the spa—which includes an intimate swimming pond—then dine in the on-site restaurant. (If weather allows, try to book a table in the outdoor terrace.) While the hotel is located in one of Antwerp’s quieter neighborhoods, het Groen Kwartier, you’re still within walking distance from most of the action, including two local favorites: Bar Vert for a low-key lunch, and Funk (an essential personal bookmark) for breakfast pastries.

Photo: Courtesy of Antwerp Botanic Sanctuary

It doesn’t get more central than this. Antwerp’s Botanic Sanctuary, the sole five-star property in town, gets its name from its location: It’s a former monastery nestled besides the city’s Botanical Gardens. Rooms are awash in calming neutrals with multiple large suites available for families—some of which overlook the adjoining 15th-century chapel. Food-motivated travelers are spoilt for choice: Start with drinks at Henry’s Bar, then take your pick of one of three Michelin-starred restaurants for dinner. (Ed note: The property’s marquee wellness facilities are currently temporarily closed due to a recent fire.)

Hotels in European Old Towns aren’t exactly known for their modern charm—and yet, Hotel Julien is brimming with exactly that. Set across two former historic buildings, it precedes the opening of its sister property August, but remains a worthwhile destination for its location alone. Rooms are cozy but pared back, punctuated by touches of red, and you’ll appreciate all the sightseeing there is to do, starting with the rooftop terrace that overlooks the Cathedral of Our Lady—an exalted edifice of Gothic architecture. It’s the ideal cozy home base for a trip spent exploring: “Antwerp is a very historic city, so it’s worth spending a day wandering through its streets, admiring the old architecture, and stepping into the many independent boutiques and antique shops,” adds de Geyter.

Originally a mansion built in 1890, Boulevard Leopold has found new life as a bed and breakfast since 2006. It’s very much no-frills—the aforementioned breakfast, a daily spread that includes croissants and fresh orange juice and is served each morning in the orangerie, is pretty much the only standard “amenity”—but that doesn’t mean it’s sparse. On the contrary, this jewel box of a space is full of charming little touches everywhere you look, the effect of which is a collected feel akin to that of a slightly eccentric aunt’s home.

To wit: crystal chandeliers that play against antler mounts, taxidermy birds that mingle with ornate, gilded candlesticks, a large bamboo fan moonlighting as a headboard that sits above a spartan cot. There are just five bedrooms to book, one of which is a gold-painted suite that takes up the entirety of the first floor. If you’re looking for a quiet, design-forward spot, this B&B is it.

Art is the main motivator at Hotel Pilar, a stylish boutique stay in Antwerp’s hip Het Zuid area, where each of its 21 rooms is designed around unique works. Oil paintings and glossy photographs contrast exposed brick and raw concrete in some; colorful prints juxtapose stainless steel and marbled tiles in others. Lively cafés and bars surround the property, which also happens to overlook the Royal Museum of Fine Arts (KMSKA). For the intrepid gallery hopper, the Museum of Contemporary Art (M HKA) is similarly close by; so is the Ann Demeulemeester flagship if you’re down for a side quest. An art-filled salon adjoins the hotel’s ground-floor restaurant—you’ll want to bookend the day here on one of its velvet couches, no matter where you dined that night.

Set in a 19th-century building in the heart of Antwerp’s fashion district, this light-filled apartment is a more than comfortable base from which to explore the city. It sleeps up to four, with a large dining room and sweet little kitchen that encourages culinary creativity. Original features, like a marble fireplace and antique wood floors, mix seamlessly with modern amenities; you will feel instantly at home.

Stained glass windows, zellige tiling, gilded mirrors… there are more than enough special decorative touches in this home to keep the eye busy. This stay is ideal for a family: It sleeps 10, with five distinctly designed bedrooms (the flamingo pink one, complete with a crystal chandelier and brocade drapes, feels especially grand). It’s well-located, too, with a green park nearby and several main tramlines on your cobblestoned doorstep.

#6681. Nike Made an Air Jordan 1 for Guys Who Love Japanese Denim

Menswear guys love Japanese denim. Menswear guys also love sneakers. So why not make some kicks for the people who can tell you exactly which artisanal mill produced their selvedge? That seems to be the thinking behind the new Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko.’

Social Status is a North Carolina-based sneaker and streetwear boutique owned by the Whitaker Group, the same company behind A Ma Maniére. Over the years, it’s worked with Nike on everything from milk-inspired Dunks to Air Pennys. The shop’s last proper Jordan collab was an extremely hairy Air Jordan 6 from 2019, but now the pair are back with something a little easier to wear.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’

Social Status’s take on the AJ1 Low starts with the classic ‘Chicago’ color palette. The toebox is white, the overlays are red, and the Swoosh and collar are black. But rather than keeping everything box-fresh, Social Status has roughed up the leather so it arrives pre-scuffed, as though you’ve owned these shoes for years.

The big switch happens across the sidewalls. The usual white leather panels have been replaced with mismatched patches of indigo fabric covered in white sashiko-style stitching. Sashiko is a traditional Japanese embroidery technique used to reinforce, repair, and extend the life of clothing. It’s particularly associated with vintage workwear and denim, which is why these Jordans look like they’ve been mended using a very expensive pair of jeans.

There’s also an old-school nylon tongue, a slightly aged sole, and a custom shoebox wrapped in the same blue pattern.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’

While you might normally expect this sort of big Jordan release to land on the High, it’s nice to see the Low silhouette get some love. Some dudes prefer it, after all—it’s less bulky around the ankle and works better under wider trousers. You still get all the bits that make an Air Jordan 1 instantly recognizable, only without half the collar.

The Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’ is set to drop on December 18 for $155 through Social Status, with a wider release via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists expected to arrive later on. Japanese denim guys, get your credit cards ready.

#6680. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.
