#6679. House GOP races to lock down new leadership after blue wave

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, left, is seen in a House Republican Conference speaker election meeting on Oct. 13, 2023. Now he has his eyes on the minority leader post for the next Congress. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A sweeping tide of Democratic wins Tuesday left Republicans preparing for a new face atop the House GOP leadership ranks as the party gears up to defend President Donald Trump from a list of investigations.

It’s shaping up to be a battle between sitting Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio, pitting two lawmakers Trump has publicly praised against one another.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana had been trying to stay the course before Republicans dropped a stunning amount of seats, including ones considered deep-red. The cascade of losses, which will give Democrats a sizable majority in the 435-member chamber, forced Johnson to stand down. He told his staff on a Wednesday morning call he would not seek the minority leader job for the next Congress when the GOP conference votes behind closed doors next week.

In a possible sign of what’s to come when the often-raucous conference meets to hear from candidates and vote, some GOP insiders were split Wednesday on which lawmaker should take over as leader.

“It might be Jordan’s for the taking. I think the real fight will be at whip and conference chair,” said one GOP source with ties to each member’s office, granted anonymity to be candid.

In a letter to colleagues Jordan circulated Wednesday, he pitched himself as “battle-tested on the oversight front,” which could help as Democrats go full-tilt on probing the Trump administration. “For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority,” Jordan’s letter reads.

But another person familiar with Scalise’s thinking said “his No. 1 goal will be to lead the conference back into the majority,” describing Scalise as a “proven and tested leader who is ready on day one.”

“The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he’s a trusted leader,” the person said.

Spokespersons for Scalise and Johnson did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment on their plans.

Heading into the midterms, it appeared Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the sitting majority whip, had been working behind the scenes to shore up his standing with House GOP members in a bid to become the No. 2 Republican in January.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger of Texas has also pitched himself for minority whip, writing in a Wednesday letter to colleagues that he believed his conference needed “fresh ideas” and had “missed many opportunities.”

The scope of Tuesday’s losses had some calling for a completely clean slate, with Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., posting a message on social media to House and Senate brass: “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”

“Having Jordan and Emmer in as leadership won’t be much of a change at the top,” the first GOP source said. “But President Trump should want a warrior like Jordan with impeachment experience in charge, given the Democrats will inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

To that end, Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, likely the incoming House Judiciary Committee chairman, said in a brief interview before the chamber adjourned in September to campaign that “there’s a long list of potentially impeachable offenses” to look at from the president, his family members and inner circle.

An aggressive investigatory push by Democrats could make Jordan, in Trump’s eyes, an attractive candidate to lead the conference. Jordan fought hard against Trump’s two first-term impeachments, including with fiery cable news hits that were praised by the TV-focused chief executive.

Whatever happens, it will cap off a rocky ride for Johnson, who claimed the gavel in the tumultuous weeks after Kevin McCarthy was ousted as speaker in October 2023.

In a statement released early Wednesday morning, Johnson did not reveal his next move.

“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson said. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”

Notably, during a phone interview with Politico late Tuesday night, Trump was asked about Johnson — but did not endorse him for minority leader.

“I think he’s done a very good job,” the president said, his voice hoarse from an October-long rally blitz that did not pay off for his party. “I mean, they’re going to have to make that decision. He’s going to have to make that decision. But he’s a good person and a good man.”

On Wednesday Trump told reporters at the White House he intended to stay out of the coming House GOP leadership race.

While Republicans are eager to avoid repeating the bitter public battles of the past, the fight for minority leader is in some ways a rerun. Both Scalise and Jordan tried for the speaker’s gavel back in 2023 after McCarthy’s sacking but neither landed the job.

A former high school and college wrestler who later coached grappling, Jordan was once considered too much of a firebrand to lead the entire caucus.

“Early on he wasn’t really given the opportunity to show what he’s capable of because of his steadfast conservative positions,” Ray Yonkura, who was Jordan’s chief of staff for a decade and has done political work for him, told CQ Roll Call in October 2023. “He was oftentimes pushed to the side, or different Republican leaders tried to keep him down.”

“Once he was given an opportunity to show what he’s capable of, I think a lot of people realized that this is somebody whose skill set can actually be good in a leadership role,” Yonkura said then.

Jordan has faced questions over the years about what he knew about sexual abuse by a doctor at The Ohio State University when he worked there as an assistant wrestling coach starting in the 1980s. He has repeatedly denied knowing of the abuse, and multiple Republicans told CQ Roll Call in 2023 that it hadn’t factored into their support for Jordan.

As for Scalise, he went through a public ordeal in 2017 when he was shot by a gunman at a GOP baseball practice, sustaining serious injuries. He later was diagnosed with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, and in 2024 said he was in remission.

Beyond the House leadership shuffle ahead of the start of the 120th Congress, G. William Hoagland, a former Senate GOP leadership aide, said there would be a broader battle among Republicans as they analyze their losses and look ahead to 2028.

“I take Steve Bannon’s comment recently seriously that the Republican Party will be engulfed in a civil war over the future of the party,” he said, referring to recent comments from Trump’s former chief 2016 campaign and White House strategist. “Expect that civil war to play out over the next couple of weeks in the midst of all the other legislative issues they have to deal with in the lame-duck session.”

Niels Lesniewski, Savannah Behrmann, Paul Krawczak and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6678. The 8 Best Hotels in Santa Fe for a Winter Escape

Whatever expectations you might have for Santa Fe, nothing really prepares you for the magnitude of its beauty. The blue sky is enormous—with impossibly fluffy clouds—stretching on and on until it melts into the distance. The surrounding Sangre de Cristo (“blood of Christ”) mountains are especially striking, named by the Spanish who were spellbound by the peaks that turned a vivid red during sunrise and sunset. There’s the traditional adobe architecture the Southwest is famous for, earth-toned and low-slung, and the piñon-juniper woodlands that add to the landscape’s dreamlike quality. It’s a magical place where chiles and pine nuts are on every menu, and the craft scene is so prolific the city was designated a UNESCO Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art. For travelers who have their sights set on New Mexico’s capital city, the best hotels in Santa Fe celebrate its many riches.

The city’s high-elevation desert climate makes visiting throughout the year a distinct experience. In winter, Santa Fe puts on its party hat and transforms into a holiday snow globe with glowing farolitos and city streets perfumed with piñon pine drifting from kiva fireplaces. Whether you choose to position yourself downtown in proximity to galleries and restaurants, or on the outskirts with wild acreage as your backyard, a winter spent in Santa Fe is certain to be a memorable one.

As you plan your upcoming travels, let Vogue’s guide to Santa Fe’s best hotels, below, serve as motivation to spend the cozy season in the Southwest.

Originally settled over 150 years ago by Jean Baptiste Lamy (the first Archbishop of Santa Fe), this property is now home to a luxury retreat surrounded by 317 acres bordering the Santa Fe National Forest. Guest rooms occupy adobe-style structures, with interiors that lean into the southwestern aesthetic—think, kiva fireplaces, wood beam ceilings, and decor sourced from local artists. The resort’s Adventure Basecamp acts as a meeting point for the day’s excursions, which range from horseback riding and guided hikes to a dedicated Ski Santa Fe experience in the winter.

For travelers who prefer a hotel amidst all the action, Vogue’s Senior Fashion and Style Writer Christian Allaire suggests Rosewood Inn of the Anasazi. “If you’re looking to explore around downtown Santa Fe, there are few better locations than here,” he says. “Situated right on the plaza, it's just steps away from all the action—but you may not want to leave, given how cozy the hotel is! The rooms come with wooden beams and fireplaces, and the restaurant serves up classic New Mexican fare with a modern twist.”

Despite its central location, the property feels like its own world once you step through the hand-painted, carved-wood doors. The interiors pay tribute to ancestral textiles and works by local indigenous artists, and chef Cristian Pontiggia (a James Beard Award semifinalist) blends New Mexico ingredients with global influences.

Set on 57 acres in the Sangre de Cristo foothills, Four Seasons Resort Ranch Encantado is a destination for travelers who want to be completely surrounded by nature (yet still situate themselves a convenient 10 minutes from the downtown area). There are 65 casita-style rooms designed with traditional materials like stucco exteriors, wood beams, and kiva fireplaces—plus private outdoor spaces for taking in bird chirps and the afternoon breeze. Thanks to the surrounding wilderness, activities run the gamut, from jeep tours to snowshoeing. Once you’ve worked up an appetite, head to Terra for roasted poblano leek bisque and an Ember & Adobe reposado cocktail.

With its convenient Barrio de Analco location and jewel box interiors, it’s no surprise The Inn of the Five Graces has won several prestigious design and travel awards over the years. “Each room is a feast for the eyes,” Abbas says, “a tapestry of colorful textiles, mosaic tiles, and handcrafted antiques that combine Southwestern decor with East Indian and Tibetan influences.” (If you fall in love with the decor and want to bring home a souvenir, the owners are also behind the furniture store Seret & Sons, which houses their grand collection.) For travelers staying on the property this winter, don’t miss seasonal activities like holiday tea time, fireside cocoa, and a holiday makers market.

This is not your average motel. This adobe roadside motor court was originally built in 1936 and is now home to one of Santa Fe’s most compelling boutique hotels. El Rey Court sits along old Route 66 and offers 86 rooms on five acres of old-growth gardens. No two adobe rooms are identical, and amenities like a heated outdoor swimming pool, a tree-lined lawn, and al fresco fireplace offer plenty of opportunities to soak in the natural surroundings. Be sure to spend at least one of your evenings at Le Reina, their mezcal and tequila bar that serves up a mean margarita.

This legendary hotel on Santa Fe’s iconic plaza sits on land that has played host to an inn since the early 17th century. La Fonda’s current structure dates back to 1922, and is now a member of the Historic Hotels of America association. Original details like hand-carved beams, terracotta tile, and stained glass skylights set a thoroughly romantic tone, while guest rooms keep it cozy with hand-painted headboards and earth tone decor.

For a home-away-from-home kind of getaway, this welcoming bed and breakfast offers eight rooms tucked among lush gardens. El Farolito is close to the city’s best attractions—to name a few: the historic plaza, farmer’s market, and Georgia O’Keefe Museum—yet sits on a tranquil street away from the bustle. The inn features original artwork throughout, as well as handmade furnishings like wood-carved headboards. And be sure to set your alarm for breakfast: It’s served from 7:30 to 9:30 every morning and can be blissfully enjoyed on the patio next to a gurgling fountain.

Unlike local lodging that leans into Southwest design aesthetics, the ryokan-style accommodations at Ten Thousand Waves offer a distinctly Japanese perspective. The spa is surrounded by 20 acres of piñons and junipers, and guest rooms are situated within a historic ranch house. This retreat is best for wellness-focused travelers, as the private hot tub suites and shared soaking environments are just a few steps away from the rooms. (Don’t sleep on the myofascial facial or shiatsu massage, either.) For cuisine, Izanami is an upscale izakaya serving seasonal small plates meant to share.

#6677. Sam Heughan and Stephanie Bullock Make Their Red Carpet Debut in Coordinating Looks

Sam Heughan is making things red carpet official with his girlfriend, model Stephanie Bullock. On Sunday, November 15, the Outlander actor brought his partner to the BAFTA Scotland Awards in Glasgow for their first joint appearance.

The couple’s red carpet debut coincided with a significant moment in Heughan’s career. At Sunday’s ceremony, he accepted the Outstanding Contribution to Television award on behalf of Outlander.

“I think actors before social media were pretty elusive,” he said. “I love to people watch. I don’t like standing out in the crowd…I love sitting in a café or a bar and just watching people.”

He prefers not to share much about his private life because “I just think it’s who I am.” And keeping a little mystery helps with work, too. “I think an actor should disappear behind the character,” he said. “You shouldn’t be like, ‘Oh, there’s Sam Heughan onstage playing a character.’”

#6676. Joseph Zada of The Hunger Games Is Still Getting Used to Being a Movie Star

Joseph Zada is doing “very, very, very good,” he tells me, with a heavy emphasis on the third very and an audible exclamation mark. And why shouldn’t he be?

His much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week. Zada and I spoke the morning of his New York City premiere, while he was being shuttled from one press obligation to the next, already go-go-go before actually hitting the red carpet Monday night in custom Louis Vuitton, punctuated with a pair of gold-toed cowboy boots from Pharrell’s first collection for the brand.

In the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy. When asked about the movie, the 21-year-old Australian demonstrates palpable care and excitement, even a bit of sadness that it’s over. “I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes,” Zada says. “And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.”

Since being cast, he’s barely had a second to stop and reflect on joining one of the biggest franchises in the world—and this comes right on the heels of East of Eden, too, in which Zada played another haunted young man. He laughs when I note the comparison: “I guess I just pride myself on my ability to show my vulnerability.”

Below, read our full conversation with the emerging star as he reflects on his Hunger Games journey, talks red carpet style, and shares his thoughts on Robert Pattinson playing James Bond.

Joseph Zada: Yeah, I wonder if I’ll be nervous.

Maybe towards the start. It doesn’t get old… but it gets familiar.

Well, I did SiriusXM this morning, and then, I mean, it’s basically just been like, "Hey, do press all day and then go to your premiere." So there’s not much time for a ritual, so I guess I go a little bit nonverbal and half-dissociate.

No, it’s so much fun. I have a lot of fun at these premieres. It’s always like a crazy, crazy crowd. The way they’ve set it up has just been otherworldly, and I’m not sure if I’ll ever have it again, but I distinctly remember each stop and the feelings that I’ve had thus far, and it doesn’t get old. It’s always crazy to see this many fans and the passion they have for this project. I mean, it’s not every day that you get to step into something with a built-in fan base where people are already coming out and supporting it before they’ve even seen it. So it’s a really special experience, and I don’t know when I’m going to be able to get that again.

Where did I have the most fun? I had a lot of fun in London because my little sister was there, my little sister and my brother’s girlfriend, so I got to hang out with them and I haven’t seen them in a while. And Mexico. Mexico was the craziest event that we’ve had. There were literally thousands, several thousands of people there. The reception was incredible.

Am I allowed to drop this? Oh, yes, that is what this [interview] is for. I’m wearing a Louis Vuitton suit—custom, custom—that Jason [Bolden] and I have worked together on, and I’m a big fan of the boots. The boots are pretty dope.

I feel a lot more comfortable in these clothes nowadays, and it’s actually become a lot more enjoyable to put them on. And it feels like more of an armor and less of a scary thing, and it feels like I build a lot of confidence being able to do this.

My red carpet style, I think... I don’t know. Just whatever Jason puts me in for the night.

Yeah, I think just doing it so often and finding different looks and just being able to wear all the different brands and find what I’m comfortable in.

I pride myself on my ability to have vulnerability. I think as a young man, that’s what I find interesting in these performances of these young men coming of age, and I think that was really what I was just looking for in my early career. I modeled my career on people like Timothée Chalamet and Lucas Hedges, and I love the way that they kept their heart on their sleeve and how they feel like an open nerve. I love being able to portray that in my performances.

I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes and really, really felt like I was there every single day and just had the most incredible support in terms of my cast mates and my directors and my producers. And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.

I guess everything just kind of changed just like that. Everything just changed in one quick second, and it feels like... I guess I haven’t really thought about what it was like before. I’ve just kind of been trying to ride the wave. I’m sure being able to go back home for Christmas, I’ll have some time to reflect, but right now it’s just—what’s the day ahead of me? And just making sure I’m ready for all of that.

I’m just excited to be at home every single day and watch movies with my mom and my siblings and see all my friends. That’s what I’m really excited for. I’m just excited to also just turn off my phone for a little bit, maybe go on a little road trip down to South Australia and get a little beach house and not bring my phone and have six days where I’m just off the grid.

That’s a great question. I’ve got Apocalypse Now on 4K Ultra HD on my projector that I bought at home, and I cannot wait. I feel like people ask me what was the best part of my year, and I just start naming all the movies that I’ve watched. And genuinely the happiest that I ever am is when I’m watching a film, which is kind of sad but also kind of cool.

I think... I don’t know. I loved Wild Horse Nine. That’s a favorite I’ve watched in cinemas. I loved Primetime too, because I love Rob Pattinson. I love Skyler Gisondo.

I did just see the Bond casting news! I am chuffed. That is so exciting. That is beyond exciting. He is just the most phenomenal actor, and he really just makes the most interesting choices. And I think him in that role, the stoicism that he’ll bring along with those really interesting choices, it’s going to make that character so interesting. He’s a really special actor. It feels like every young male actor that I speak to feels like that is a person to look to right now and a person’s career to emulate in terms of the risks and the commitment to his craft and all these roles that he’s churning out.

I don’t know. It’s so ridiculously helpful to have a book with you because it’s just so much information, and I love preparing for roles and having a book because it’s just an internal monologue, which is what you should be doing for every character. You read a scene, and you should be writing what is going through your character’s head. And when you have a book, it’s all done for you, or at least you have a good foundation.

I hope I get to do as many book adaptations as possible, but I think what I’m really looking for is just a great director and a great script. I’m not sure what’s [next]. I’ve got a fresh slate right now, but there’s a couple of things floating around.

#6675. Inside Well Beyond Breast Cancer’s Fundraiser to Give Survivors Access to Rehabilitation

Many don’t realize that breast cancer care doesn’t end with treatment.

Under violet lights, hanging florals, and rattan lanterns, guests at Well Beyond Breast Cancer’s third annual fundraising event mingled, cried happy tears, and came together in New York City to support survivors. Well Beyond Breast Cancer is a nonprofit organization that helps survivors access rehabilitation services after breast cancer treatment. Founder Amanda Grilli, an oncology physical therapist, decided to start the organization just three years ago after moving to the United States from Canada and recognizing a major gap in care.

“I was shocked by the differences in the health care system between the two countries,” Grilli told ELLE. “I quickly realized that the majority of individuals who are affected by breast cancer don’t have access to a therapist like myself because they’re experiencing so many barriers, whether that’s financial toxicity, insurance gaps, or a fragmented health care system. [Many] people aren’t able to access this care on their own.”

For breast cancer survivors, care continues even after surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation end. But rehabilitation is a major piece of breast cancer recovery that often isn’t considered. Grilli says, “So many people experience lingering pain, or they have difficulty lifting their arms. What these therapists are doing is helping people overcome these side effects so that they can get back to living well.”

Guests had the opportunity to hear from one of the organization’s beneficiaries, Allison Berg, an independent documentary filmmaker who was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2025. Even after treatment, her recovery continued. Berg described shooting pain through her arms and fingertips, tightness every time she reached for anything, and tender scars. “My body is part of my equipment,” she shared. “I was having trouble just sitting at a laptop and typing. How was I ever going to carry gear and hold a camera again?” Well Beyond Breast Cancer covered 12 one-hour rehabilitation sessions for Berg, and in September, she was able to shoot for a new film.

Prior to the event yesterday, Well Beyond Breast Cancer had funded 250 breast cancer rehab appointments and allocated more than $50,000 to direct patient care. Last night, at ILA Penthouse in Manhattan, guests were able to participate in a live auction, which is still ongoing and has already raised thousands of dollars. Before they left, guests were also invited to share a wish with the “Keeper of Wishes,” a figurehead with “hopes” pinned to her dress, creating a growing display and fountain of hope that continued throughout the night.

Katie Berohn is ELLE’s beauty editor. Previously, she held the same title at Who What Wear, where she was promoted from associate beauty editor. She’s written for publications like The Cut, Cosmopolitan, Good Housekeeping, and Mashable. Her interests include fragrance, vintage shopping, hot yoga, food, travel, music, books, and attempting to make every NYT Cooking recipe. She’s on the endless hunt to find the perfect shade of red lipstick.

#6674. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6673. The 40 Best Wedding Dresses for Every Ceremony Style and Venue

You can plan out the perfect menu and spend hours curating playlists; but when it comes down to it, there’s really just one item that’s front and center on the big day, and that’s your wedding dress. From picking out the right style to managing alterations to juggling multiple options (do you really want a different dress for the ceremony and the reception? For the after-party? How many gowns does one person need?), it’s a lot—even if you’re planning a courthouse affair. We’re here to streamline the process, with our edit of the best wedding dresses you can buy online.

If you don’t have a dream design in mind and are feeling stuck on where to start, you may want to consider your venue. Are you hosting a beach ceremony? If so, opt for breezy, looser styles in airy fabrics that err on the laid-back side to be in line with the seaside setting. (Think: off-the-shoulder styles in shell white or an asymmetrical dress, loosely knit with pearlescent beadwork.) Are you headed to City Hall? Go sleek, modern, and maybe even short—without the confines of a strict dress code, this is your chance to experiment. If you’re planning a more formal fête, you may want to lean into tradition with a bridal look that stars full-skirted organza and floor-sweeping styles. Not all white dresses are created equal.

It starts with getting a sense of what’s out there; so to help kick off your search, we pulled together a range of wedding dresses that’ll suit every setting, dress code, and personal style.

Looking to go traditional? There’s no beating a classic, fairytale-inspired dress. These designs are built to be showstoppers, whether you opt for a bubble-skirt gown from Danielle Frankel or a style with subtle drama by Self-Portrait, Emilia Wickstead, or The OWN Studio.

Sleek, minimalist, and effortlessly elegant, a column wedding dress works for an array of dress codes. Sculptural, contoured versions by Marmar Halim and Safiyaa are perfectly polished for traditional venues, while Simkhai’s sleeveless number seems just right for a city ceremony.

Strapless dresses are an especially lovely option if you’re getting married in a warmer climate, though the silhouette is appropriate year-round. Rachel Gilbert’s corseted gown is great for more formal dress codes, and gives the illusion of a fuller skirt with a hand-draped sash. You can also lean into unexpected shapes with Magda Butrym’s architectural neckline or Balenciaga’s draped design.

For civil ceremonies and backyard weddings that take a more casual approach, why not choose a short-sleeve style? Rixo leans romantic with a v-neckline, ruffles, and floral detailing; Heirlome and Khaite offer modern takes with open backs, while Jacquemus goes asymmetric with a single sleeve.

One-shoulder, off-the-shoulder, fringe trim… the more irregular, the better with this kind of wedding dress, which places emphasis on the neckline and is great if you’re going with a simple updo. Naturally, Vivienne Westwood excels at draping with a sweetheart neckline; for a touch of drama and movement, go with Taller Marmo. Or if you need a courthouse look, Altuzarra’s shift dress has you covered.

For brides who consider sleeves a non-negotiable (or are hosting a wedding in a colder climate), a long-sleeved wedding dress should read as elegant and assured, never frumpy. Brandon Maxwell makes the case for demure sensuality with a body-skimming crepe gown, while Bernadette keeps things slightly casual with a midi silhouette.

Whether you’re exchanging vows at City Hall or simply not convinced you want a full-length gown, a tea-length dress is worth considering. Look to Prada and St. Agni for easygoing options suited to warm-weather nuptials, or Leo Lin for a more formal take that works in any season. (This is the occasion to pay particular attention to your bridal shoes; they’ll be on full display!)

Torn between a ball gown wedding dress and something a little more on-trend? Consider a drop waist, one of bridal’s most popular silhouettes. Markarian offers a classic look with a fitted bodice and an off-the-shoulder neckline; Ilkyaz Ozel suits the bride who wants to make an entrance; Danielle Frankel brings a whimsical touch in flowy organza; Amsale turns heads with its double-tiered skirt.

A halter neckline channels the pared-back ease of ’90s minimalism. In liquid satin or fluid silk, styles from Givenchy, Reformation, Ralph Lauren, and Halfpenny London feel aisle-ready—and they’re just as fitting for the dance floor, so consider this your ceremony and reception look in one.

If all you want from your wedding dress is a little something special, look to designs that stand out from the crowd with some element of the unconventional. Whether it’s a lace Dior gown embroidered with bows, Clio Peppiatt’s crystal-studded maxi with a draped scarf neckline, or Christopher John Rogers’s sequin paillette-embellished, mermaid-like gown, the appeal is in the details.

What should brides look for in a wedding dress?

Start by getting to know the many (many) wedding dress silhouettes, from ball gowns and A-lines to mermaid styles and beyond; your ceremony setting will likely help narrow things down. From there, look to fabrics. Silk and satin are classics that, depending on the style, can be both structured and soft (though beware wearing them in hotter climates, as they’re more prone to showing sweat stains), while airy materials like chiffon, organza, and tulle offer a delicate look.

It’s also a good idea to have a few wedding dress designer names in your back pocket to reference in your research. Oscar de la Renta, Danielle Frankel, Vivienne Westwood, and more are Vogue favorites, and you can find many of them online at trusted retailers like Net-a-Porter, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman. One last thing: If you’re shopping online for your special day, don’t forget to double- and triple-check the shipping and returns policy to avoid surprise fees.

Making such a consequential purchase from the comfort of your couch can feel like a risk—and if you can, it doesn’t hurt to try on your dream look in a store before you buy—but there are benefits to wedding dress shopping online. For one, you’ll have a clearer idea of the cost upfront and can filter by price; it’s also easier to browse by style, material, and even length. Not to mention, if you’re shopping with time constraints, it’s more convenient to see products that are in stock and ready to ship, taking out the guesswork and minimizing delays.

When should brides order wedding dresses (and when should alterations begin)?

While the general rule of thumb is to buy your gown eight to nine months before the wedding day, online shopping offers a little more flexibility when it comes to speedier delivery. Getting the purchase done early also allows more wiggle room for alterations; experts say to book those well ahead of the 10-week pre-wedding mark.

Should brides buy two wedding dresses for the ceremony and reception?

This one’s completely up to you—every bride and every ceremony is different. If you’re on the fence, why not consider a bridal gown rental? The practice is rising in popularity and is a smart solution for anyone who wants multiple looks but doesn’t want to be stuck with multiple gowns (or, at the very least, shoulder the cost of multiple gowns).

What are the most popular wedding dress styles and silhouettes?

The classics are classics for a reason: A-line silhouettes and ball gowns, mermaid silhouettes and fit-and-flares, and sophisticated column silhouettes remain bridal dress mainstays. But lately, drop waists, corseted bodices, and bias-cut styles, along with shorter hemlines for civil ceremonies and receptions, are seeing a surge in popularity. The best shape ultimately depends on your venue, dress code, and how you feel in your chosen piece, so be sure to try on a few shapes before committing to the final look.

#6672. Robert Pattinson, I’m Begging You For a Quirked-Up James Bond

Our long international nightmare is finally over: two-time Meme of the Year nominee Robert Pattinson has been chosen as Daniel Craig’s James Bond successor, bringing an end to an exhausting series of “reports” and “leaks” about Amazon’s search for a new 007. Finally we can stop the debates and fan-casting and let Patts and Denis Villeneuve cook until they’re ready to present their new vision. But that would require a level of restraint that the internet doesn’t typically exercise. Immediately after the protracted process of casting Bond concluded, the internet moved on to naming its dream picks for Bond Girls and Bond Villains (sometimes, to brilliant effect.) I can’t say I have a dog in either fight, at least not right now. My Bond WishList is of a different magnitude altogether: can we make James Bond silly again? Just a little, even, 15 percent goofball?

In the hands of another (read: more limited) actor, I’d never suggest such a risky swerve. But the best thing about Pattinson is his range. Sure, if Villeneuve and co. want to render Bond as the stoic and taciturn gentleman he’s generally been this century, Rob has proven he can do that, as every Tenet truther has been gleefully preaching for the last 24 hours. But more often than not, Pattinson is keen to get weird, whether that’s going Full Freak, as he does in Primetime, or approaching certain archetypal parts with a silly, goofy mood (like his conniving suitor in The Odyssey). He can do a “voice” (Mickey 17), he can do scumbag grime (Good Time), he can do hapless screwball (The Drama). Why not make what’ll be his biggest role to date a little cocktail of all his best elements? (Okay, he can leave the Mickey 17 voice behind.)

20 years ago, Casino Royale was a refreshing reset and a crucial corrective to the overflowing ridiculousness of the Piece Brosnan era. But in the past two decades, the pendulum has swung back—the gritty reboot has become studios' stock-in-trade. I feel the same way about Batman; the actual risky choice would be to make something less like Nolan’s series that, instead, hewed a little closer to, say, Batman Forever, or even the gothic camp of Tim Burton’s two films.

Of course, Robert Pattinson was at the center of a Batman reboot as well, and the result was a movie that felt more like a spiritual cousin to David Fincher’s Se7en; audiences ate it up so much that the hunger for a sequel persists even after endless delays. When it comes to franchises as high-stakes as Batman or Bond, you can’t trust these increasingly sauceless execs to make anything but the basic choice. There’s no reason to expect Jeff Bezos isn’t texting Denis screenshots from Skyfall for reference from his megayacht at this very moment.

But if there’s anybody capable of putting a little English on the handle while still giving the mainstream what it wants, it’s Big Bob Pattinson. He could easily make his James Bond a little off, or he could go full seductive cad who smiles like Neil Tenet, has a ki with Q, and charms women with some playful banter instead of simply brooding them into submission. I’m not looking for invisible cars and sharks with lasers, or a Lothario like Roger Moore who speaks in puns. All I’m asking is that we give camp a chance. Because ultimately, the most exciting thing Villeneuve and Pattinson can do to set their Bond apart would be to loosen him up a little.

#6671. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6670. The Press-On Nails That Made Me Quit Nail Salons

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As a chronic nail biter (gross, I know), I’ve tried just about every type of manicure out there in an attempt to heal my nails and kick my habit. From acrylics and tips to builder gel and dip powder, nothing has ever worked for me. But one simple option has never let me down: press-ons. They provide a natural-looking manicure without damaging your nails, take just minutes to apply, and can be done from the comfort of your own home. There’s no drying, intense filing, or pricey appointments required. What’s not to love?

Recently, I fell down a glue-filled rabbit hole in search of the best press-on nails out there. Every week, I’d apply a new set in the name of research, meticulously assessing each for quality, durability, and longevity. I have very small nail beds, so finding a size, shape, and length that fit my fingertips was essential. After about a year of testing (and an absurd amount of nail glue), there was a clear winner: Glamnetic.

We praised the product last year, and that praise still holds true. The application is not only simple, but I actually find it quite therapeutic. I start by pushing back my cuticles with the included wooden stick and filing the entire surface of the nails, not just the edges. Doing this helps the press-ons adhere better and last longer. Next, I match each of my fingers to the best-fitting press-on. Finally, I remove any oils from my nails using the alcohol pad, and glue on the set. I start with my pinkies and move toward my thumbs, placing a dot of glue at the base of each press-on and holding it down for about 30 to 45 seconds. Before I know it, I’m left with a perfect manicure that’s affordable, natural-looking, and long-lasting.

While it’s always fun to experiment with different shapes and lengths, my personal favorite is the brand’s “Short Oval” collection. For under $20, each set comes with 30 nails in varying sizes, and all of the above materials. They are incredibly durable without looking or feeling thick, and each set lasts about two weeks.

Whether you prefer a milky pink shade like Strawberry Icing or a more festive set like Snowfall, Glamnetic is known for its impressive designs. From magnetic cat-eye polish to 3-D chrome appliqués, there’s a set for every style, season, and mood. For a nail biter who has destroyed just about every expensive manicure imaginable, finding a budget-friendly option that can actually keep up with me feels like a small miracle.

#6669. ‘I’ll be reelected as majority leader,’ Schumer says

Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer speaks outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington on Wednesday about his party’s big night. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats look ahead to their new Senate majority for the next Congress, their current leader Charles E. Schumer made a prediction on Wednesday: “I’ll be reelected as majority leader.”

Schumer, a Democrat from New York, would be helming a larger caucus than most anticipated, ranging from 54 to 56 seats after the dust settles from Tuesday’s wins.

Not all the new incoming members say they will support the 75-year-old, and some have called for new blood. But so far, no formidable opponent has emerged.

“The issue is not me,” Schumer told reporters outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Wednesday morning when asked about working with those new senators. “The issue is focusing on the American people and what they want.”

The leadership election for Senate Democrats will likely take place in early December and include the senators-elect in a secret ballot race.

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who won a Senate election against Republican Michele Tafoya, told NBC’s Meet the Press NOW in August, “I think it is time for new leadership,” when asked if she’d support Schumer.

She reupped that sentiment on a Wednesday press call, saying, “Many of us were elected who refused corporate PAC money, who are beholden only to the people who elected us, and are ready to fight for bold change. And so I think it’s time for new leadership.”

Schumer has served in both the minority and majority as Democratic leader after landing the job in 2017 when then-leader Harry Reid retired. He faces reelection in 2028.

Former state Senate President Troy Jackson of Maine, the Democrat who defeated Republican Sen. Susan Collins in her bid for a sixth term, told reporters on Monday, “I’ve already said that I told Sen. Schumer that I’m gonna support somebody else. It’s no different now.”

He said he would push Schumer to deliver on health care changes like “Medicare for All.”

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, who bested John Sununu in his bid to return to the Senate, said in an interview last week that “it’s very clear voters are hungry for new voices at the table and for a new generation of leadership in the Senate.”

“I’ve heard that throughout this campaign. I think above all, people want folks who understand the challenges out there and are going to fight with the urgency that these challenges deserve,” he said. “Too often, we’ve seen leadership flat-footed.”

His campaign did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about whether that was indicative of his support for Schumer.

Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist church who unseated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, told CNN in September: “I’m not supporting Schumer for leader.”

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer, but we need new leadership. We need new, younger leadership, young blood. I don’t mean just age, but people who are bringing fresh ideas and fresh leadership,” he said. “We’ve got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together. Not just Democrats, but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems.”

“I think people are frustrated with the gridlock and the sense that people are not working together,” he added, pointing to Democrats blocking the farm bill in the Senate Agriculture Committee earlier this year.

Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, told MS NOW earlier this fall he would want to support Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen as leader.

“I would definitely support Sen. Chris Van Hollen and I would love to see him as Senate majority leader,” he said.

Van Hollen is seen as a presidential contender, and has been “kicking the tires” on 2028 instead of Senate leadership when he’s been asked.

El-Sayed told NBC’s Today Show on Wednesday, just hours after his race was called, “We need action. We need leadership toward that action. I’m interested to see, working with our caucus, to see what options we’ve got,” saying he hopes there is “two or more options” but not mentioning Van Hollen.

“I’m going to vote for the option that gives me the best chance at getting money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All,” he said.

Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton made it part of her Senate primary pitch earlier this year that she was the only Democrat in the race who didn’t support Schumer. “I’ve made it clear that I would not support Chuck Schumer as leader of the Democratic caucus because I think right now what I’m hearing from voters all across the state of Illinois is that they are fed up. They’re fed up with what’s happening in Washington,” she told political YouTube commentator Jack Cocchiarella in March.

A spokesperson for Stratton’s campaign reiterated Wednesday her position hasn’t changed. The campaigns of El-Sayed, Hamilton and Jackson did not immediately respond to questions Wednesday about their stances.

Even if some candidates were eager to distance themselves from establishment Democrats on the campaign trail before facing voters, it’s hard to deny that Schumer helped bring home a resounding victory for Democrats on Tuesday night.

So far, among Democratic incumbents, it’s not clear anyone would have the appetite to challenge Schumer, who flexed his political prowess and recruited several of the key flips last night, like former and incoming Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio to recapture the state for Democrats.

Having prevailed in a special election, Brown is expected to be seated before the end of the year.

A Democratic staffer familiar with the current mood of the caucus predicted: “Nope. Schumer will be the leader,” when asked if there was any serious challenger.

Former Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota had a similar prediction. “Given the big night Senate Democrats had, I doubt anyone will challenge him. But some new members may withhold their vote, in keeping with their campaign comments,” Daschle said.

Schumer on Wednesday said Democrats will be united in addressing costs for the American people with what he described as “an amazing crop of new senators” and a “generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America not only now, but on into the future.”

“These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want. They entrusted us with the majority to do what they, the American people, want,” he said. “Republicans received that opportunity two years ago and completely squandered it. The GOP misread Americans’ demand for change as a mandate to do Trump’s self-serving bidding, and Trump spent half his time talking about things that were irrelevant to their lives.”

#6668. Upgrade Your Basics: Best Undershirts for Men in 2026

Just because you don't see a building's foundation doesn't mean it isn't holding everything up. In much the same way, the best undershirts for men are the humble base layer of countless great outfits. Many GQ staffers, in fact, wear-test theirs daily, and yet they're often overlooked, even though they've long-perfected their role: to be the protective layer between your gross body and your steezy, attention-hungry shirts and polos.

And while they're certainly good for some added warmth in the winter, there's a common misconception that they can make the wearer too hot. In fact, lightweight, moisture-wicking undershirts made from fabrics like modal, or cotton blends can actually transfer the sweat away from your body, speeding up your cooling down. All that's to say: Undershirts are more than just men’s underwear. They’re the cornerstone of a hall-of-fame fit.

An undershirt is an undershirt is an undershirt. If you want the most straightforward version, the kind that you’re picturing in your head is most likely from Calvin Klein. It’s a classic crewneck undershirt that’s made of a lightweight jersey that’s 100% cotton which has a smooth, very slightly brushed hand that feels worn-in in the best way possible. The slim fit won’t cause any weird bunching or bulging and it’s got enough length to stay tucked even when you’re out on the town cutting rugs.

My colleague, GQ senior commerce editor Avidan Grossman, has been wearing CK's genre-defining undershirts since his high school years. (He could do without the logo at the hem, but has made his peace with it, given that you never see it once it's tucked.) Otherwise, he prizes Calvin Klein's riff for its simple, pared-down design and blessed lack of modern-day frills. After all, not every shirt needs to moisture wick or odor block. If you just want an undershirt that gets the job done, don't overthink it.

Sometimes, sleeves are just too much undershirt. That’s where tanks come in. Also known as A-shirts, the humble, sleeveless tank has been rocked by every heartthrob and neighborhood grandpa as far back as anyone can remember. And while the low neck and lack of sleeves means you’ll practically never see them underneath a button-up, the irony is that they look great shown off with an unbuttoned camp shirt or on their own.

For the money, we think Hanes takes the cake with their multipack of undershirts. The stretchy ribbed jersey is made of 100% cotton and fits snug with a low neck that’s slightly squared off compared to most tanks. They may cost just under twenty bucks for a pack of six, but they look like a million bucks. “I’ve had buyer's remorse over many a menswear garment over the years,” explains GQ editor Jordan Bowman, "but the one thing that has never let me down is the humble tank top from Hanes. They nailed the fit and the material, and the great thing is, you can buy a pack just about anywhere."

If every part of your wardrobe has to be fit for a king, down to the most basics of basics, then CDLP is what we’d recommend, my liege. The reality is that most luxury tees don’t offer much more than the regular stuff. It’s diminishing returns after a certain price point, but CDLP is the notable exception. My colleague, our contributing editor Louis Cheslaw, has put his same CDLP cottons through the ringer year after year, and says they still haven't lost their luster.

It’s a pricey undershirt, for sure, but the high-quality fabric has a silky hand and lightweight feel that’s unparalleled. (It really feels like you’re almost wearing nothing.) Thanks to a wider neckline, you’re a lot less likely to see the tee poking out, too. And if you feel like such a nice T-shirt is wasted as underwear, don’t worry—the cut and shorter length means it looks great untucked, and can double as your regular T-shirt too.

Mack Weldon’s silver series of garments is what happens when you get nerdy about chemistry and fashion (in the best possible way). The Ionic+ technology embeds silver charged silver ions which are naturally antimicrobial into the fabric itself. Essentially, that means bacteria and odor is neutralized, which means you can take it easy on the deodorant. Beyond that, the tees are made of super long staple Supima cotton and a smidge of lycra for an extra silky fee, comfortable stretch, and long-lasting wear.

The main bummer is that they’ll cost you more than most tees, so stocking up for the week can get pricey. Still, it’s one of those undershirts that makes you realize you’ve been settling for squalor—plus, you can bundle up and get 10% off to help offset the sticker shock.

Not everything at Uniqlo is a great value. But when it comes to upgraded basics at an affordable price, you’d be hard-pressed to find brand that does it better. When you need an airy, breathable undershirt that's truly lightweight, the Japanese mega-retailer’s AIRism tees are legendary. They’re crafted from a smooth and breathable cotton-polyester-spandex blend that dries quickly, feels cool to the touch, and fights odors—a triple threat that’ll have sweaty days in a headlock. I personally wear these—they're a failsafe way to save my expensive dress shirts from dreaded pit stains, but they’re also perfect for wearing as a gym shirt. And at just $15 per tee, there’s no other undershirt that can do as much for the price.

GQ contributor Evan Malachosky was always a little skeptical of Skims, but the brand's tees won him over. He found that Skims’s proprietary fabrics are silky on the skin, and are neither too thin (and therefore exposing), nor too thick (and therefore too hot). Pleasingly, the brand has applied just as much care to its undershirt, even though—or perhaps because—it's designed to look invisible under your clothes. (The design team even thought about cleaning up the seam lines, so nothing would show through.) Made from 100% cotton, and available in an incredibly wide range of sizes, our favorite detail is that it's a little bit longer than the brand's standard tees, so that there's no risk of any unsightly seams being visible at the hemline, either.

If the purpose of an undershirt is to fly under the radar, then it stands to reason that a V-neck one—which remains invisible even when you unbutton your shirt collar—might be the most efficient of all the styles here. You'll still want to trust the classic makers here, which is why our favorite comes from Calvin Klein. Like the Calvin Klein crewneck option above, the fabric is smooth, slightly brushed, and 100% cotton. It's also affordable, and available in not just white, black, and gray, but also a multipack comprising all three. Lastly, CK's trademark slimmer fit means no bunching or bulging risk.

Are these “undershirts” far heavier than the usual ones? Yes. But they never lose their shape, and if you live in a bitterly cold climate, you'll want even your undershirt to max out its warming properties.

The luxury car of undershirts, Falke's premium undershirts go on just as smoothly (and last just as long) as the beloved German brand's famous socks.

You heard it here first: Ralph Lauren's Pony has become the coolest label in menswear again.

When James Bond—well, Daniel Craig as James Bond—needs an undershirt, he wears Sunspel's.

Kirkland Signature is somewhat of a fashion industry secret. These are made of soft, long-staple Egyptian cotton, and they're tube knit, meaning you don't have to worry about any uncomfortable side seams.

Made from rayon and polyester, Hanes’ moisture-wicking undershirts are fast-drying, cool to the touch, and silky smooth, all for just $5 a pop.

If you wanna let your clavicles shine uninhibited by any undershirt peek-age, a V-neck is the best way (short of a tank) to do it.

Cut from a premium cotton, this lightweight undershirt is going to feel a little thicker and warmer than others on this list, purely because Reigning Champ's premium cotton fabrics tend to lean towards the beefier end of the spectrum.

Though Mack Weldon’s 18-Hour Rib Tank doesn’t come with the microbe-smashing odor technology as their Silver crew neck undershirt, it does have an even silkier fabric and plenty of stretch.

The first thing I noticed when I met Wythe's founder was not his jeans, or amazing western shirt. It was actually this ribbed tank.

Undershirts are meant to be that intermediate layer between your outermost layers and your body, a protective guard that keeps your star garments fresh and free of sweat. Therefore, it's materials, construction, and fit that are the main components that determine how good an undershirt (and, well, every garment) actually is.

Above all else, your undershirt's fabric should be breathable, soft, comfortable, and, ideally, sweat-wicking. We primarily love undershirts and tanks that are made from high-quality 100% cotton, which has many of those characteristics naturally, but we also feel like there’s a time and place for synthetics, which are often used for their ability to wick away moisture and dry easily—especially for those who run particularly hot. And note: Stretchy materials like Spandex are helpful for comfort, but their elasticity will eventually degrade over time.

Undershirts should almost always fit closer to the body than your regular T-shirts. This is because they’ll be layered underneath another shirt or sweater, and can bunch in odd ways if too baggy. They don’t need to be skin-tight, but they should be slim enough to layer comfortably and long enough to tuck into your shirt. In fact, Peter Middleton, founder of Wythe, even told us that they should fit slim to start, since they are cotton and are knit, and will therefore stretch a little over time. If they are loose to start with, they are only going to become looser and saggier, which is really not the point.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6667. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6666. Kate Middleton Shopped From Brentwood to Belgravia for Her Royal Tour

Last night, the Prince and Princess of Wales took to the red carpet for this year’s Earthshot Prize Awards, the centerpiece of their three-day tour of Mumbai and New Delhi. The ceremony awarded five environmental projects—tackling everything from forever chemicals in France to the protection of marine life in the Pacific Islands—over $1 million each to further their work. Making her first appearance at the event since she travelled to Boston in 2022, Catherine wore a hand-embroidered anarkali by Mahima Mahajan, which she is believed to have purchased for a modest—at least by royal standards—$892 from Lilly’s Boutique in Essex. (Perhaps during her visit to The Forward Trust in nearby Southend-on-Sea back in September?)

But this morning, on the final day of their trip, the Kate Middleton we know was back on more rarefied ground, stepping out in a tailored, fit-and-flare dress of cherry-red wool crepe by Sloane Street-based designer Emilia Wickstead, priced at $2,461. From Brentwood to Belgravia, then; two very different sides of the British retail landscape, both represented in the same suitcase. Alongside her trusty suede Manolo Blahniks and coordinating DeMellier Small Hudson bag were the additions of a hand-embroidered shawl and beaded bracelet, presented to her during a visit to the Chanakya School of Craft in Mumbai, which trains women from underserved communities in traditional Indian techniques and has paired up its graduates with the likes of Dior, Fendi, and Valentino. The Princess then traveled to the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital, known for offering affordable care to women from all walks of life.

Whether Catherine has another outfit change in her suitcase—she and William are due to attend a bilateral meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi before returning to Windsor—remains to be seen. What this trip has made clear, though, is that the future Queen Kate Middleton is as intentional with her wardrobe as ever. Consider the rewears—sustainable choices, yes, but also ones that avoid headlines about new purchases that might distract from the work at hand—or the range of price points, from relatively accessible DeMellier handbags to priceless jewels from the royal collection. Above all, though, is her continued ambassadorship of British fashion—a concept as ever-changing and expansive as the country’s identity itself—as demonstrated by an Indian-designed dress bought on an English shopping street.

#6664. Grand Theft Auto VI Review: Better Than The Hype

There are moments in GTA 6 that’ll have you levitating off your sofa. Unprecedented in its scope and production, it was created by a team of almost 5,000 developers over nearly 10 years. Its budget is rumored to rival the construction of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper; its first trailer set records with 93 million views in a day. Every social media brand account, from the White House to BMW, has jumped on the hype, while economists predict a national sick day as millions play hooky to game. When you do, you see the time, talent and flair on the screen. But, at its heart, Grand Theft Auto VI follows in series tradition: an epic American crime story, set in a stunning parody of the US that riffs on film, music, politics, style and satire.

Fronting the first franchise entry in more than 13 years are Jason and Lucia. Developer Rockstar attempted a multi-character arc in Grand Theft Auto V, but those three leads learned to loathe one another. Instead, VI tackles love, a game design challenge most developers have sworn off with good reason. Not a parent/child relationship like The Last of Us or God of War, but a mature, romantic, adult one. You can call or text each other at pretty much any point—to do missions together, commit robberies, explore, meditate, work out, fly, or just to coexist under the Vice City sunshine.

This isn’t some kind of ChatGPT fantasy to indulge in. Neither Jason or Lucia exists at your beck and call as some kind of hyper-realistic plaything. You have a role in their relationship, both in the way they speak to each other and where the story takes them. You can cruise down the Vice City waterfront together in your souped-up ’70s muscle wagon with one of you driving, the other scrolling through your Snapmatic feed (the in-game social media channel), before grabbing a drink and carving up the sidewalk with an assault rifle five minutes later. You just don’t get these detours in Call of Duty.

More than a car: in GTA VI, your vehicle is a mobile base of operations to stash your guns, fits, money, and drugs.

It’s a different pace from previous Grand Theft Autos too. Rockstar changed its dynamics with 2018’s Red Dead Redemption 2—a more thoughtful take on the outlaw tale that added friction to the action and a conscience to the narrative. For a developer that once experienced the spotlight of US Congress during 2005’s infamous “Hot Coffee" controversy (when a sexually explicit mini-game meant as an inside joke between developers was figured out by savvy users), this kind of nuance was revelatory. With VI, Rockstar takes Red Dead 2’s ethos and applies it to a modern city with 1,000 x the population. The result is staggering, but still an absolute blast to play. That is to say, the greatest hits of GTA—driving cars, shooting guns, and stealing money, drugs and more (all to spend on a better Beretta, G-Wagon replica, and impeccably modeled Air Jordan dupes)—but with added depth to how you play. Weapon slots are finite; you can no longer run amok with an entire arsenal stashed in your jacket pocket. Money is vulnerable; get killed or caught with cash in your possession, and you’ll lose it. And if you jack a car that’s fitted with a tracker, the police will find you quickly.

Should you get into a bust-up with the law after a jewelry store smash-and-grab gone wrong, the game’s action is frenetic. Roads are much narrower, traffic is denser, and you can’t see police on your minimap. That $40,000 in cash sitting on the back seat had better be worth the hassle. As such, the game supports your decision to play chaotically, but truly immerses you in playing methodically. Jason and Lucia each have a “criminal profile”—be unnecessarily violent and you’ll get a “psycho” rating—that adds replayability and roleplay. Still, I had the most fun when planning missions: using a silenced pistol, shooting to maim not kill, and wiping security footage to leave no trace. It’s the closest GTA has honed in on the art of crime. The feds will surround the store you’re robbing. “Come out right now with your hands above your head!” Do things right, and you’ll have prepped your partner with a getaway car out back. You’ll leave the scene anonymously as backup blares past you on the other side of the road.

Every club, pub and dingy dive bar in GTA 6’s Leonida has a distinct vibe—from the music to the decor to the sweaty Floridians inside.

The game kicks off with an electrifying setup accompanied by an original song from composers Justice. It perfectly sets the tone: VI has the ’80s flamboyance of Vice City made new and fresh. It takes its opening hours steadily, sending you on odd jobs to make a little money here and there. Gradually—then suddenly—you’re thrust into the most high-octane campaign in Grand Theft Auto history. Tense hospital escapes, daring bank heists, cross-country chases, and more. Its set pieces are balls-to-the-wall bravado, rivaling what you’d see in Nolan’s The Odyssey or Villeneuve’s Dune, upping in intensity through its chapters. Tonally, it’s the most “of the now” Grand Theft Auto game yet, as your two in-love criminals race to find a better life in an unfair world. No previous GTA has given you a savings account—it’s like playing the millennial curse. The only dings are some pacing in the game’s second chapter as the game wrestles with its story while still introducing mechanics. Think of it as VI’s version of RDR2’s Guarma, albeit with bargain bin stores and grimy strip malls instead of exotic Caribbean fauna.

And then to Leonida, with which Rockstar has created the most technically and artistically impressive game world ever made. The pre-release trailers promised beaches bustling with vacationers and nightclubs packed with dancers. That is the reality. From sea to sand to sky, the world is alive. Vice City alone could be an entire game in its own right, complete with distinct districts, an explorable international airport, and more. Yet, Rockstar spoils us with a massive expanse of varied towns, high-class beach resorts, lush green national parks, murky swamplands and sun-kissed island keys. All packed with people that range from useful, to funny, to completely unsavory (shout-out to the old woman who took one look at my Jason and said “I’mma take my teeth out and suck the skin off that dick”). The density and fidelity of it all often stretches the limits of even Sony’s PlayStation 5 Pro. Frame rate dips don’t spoil gameplay, but the slowdown is noticeable when you’ve punted a couple of grenades into passing cars to set off multiple explosions at once.

NPCs don’t just feel like backdrop mannequins anymore, but real people with an incredible range of faces, body types and outfits.

Every frame a photograph. Stop anywhere in GTA 6, and you’ll likely find something enticing to see, hear or interact with.

As with Red Dead Redemption 2, the most impressive of the game’s many achievements is how everything seems to live on without you. All it took to make this world was Rockstar founding an entire studio to work solely on Leonida’s population. I’ve seen a woman throw herself out of a cop car window as I scooted along Ocean Beach, and car thieves burst through the glass windows of a car dealership while the alarms howl. I saw a furry taken down by armed police, staged perfectly with a helicopter spotlight. During one 3 a.m. wander through the rough neighborhood of Crosstown, a man approached me to warn me of the local gang and tells me they have a nearby base. I accidentally tapped the button that brings up your in-game phone. “Ohhhh! You don’t just believe what I say” the man says, responding to my actions. “You do your own research!” In more than 70 hours of play, I have seen only one moment of repetition.

There is so much more besides. A cast of interesting, funny and believable characters; off-the-beaten-path secrets that can lead to side quests both big and small; perhaps the best radio track list of any GTA spanning from Travis Scott to Lana Del Rey; podcast episodes; golf to play; gators to hunt; dozens of supercars to steal and customize; weapons that feel punchy and satisfying; multiple racing series; a litany of actually interesting shops and bars and clubs to explore and buy things in. I’ve seen brilliant horror vignettes, startling science fiction, and laugh-out-loud comedy just by exploring. Rockstar has created a world that rewards you for spending time in it. Expect to spend 100 hours if you want to see everything.

As you’ll likely have seen and heard—in everything from Miami Heat takeovers, to Netflix launches, to Selfridges pop-ups—that this is the most-wanted entertainment property in the world. In a way, all it had to be was Grand Theft Auto V: The Second. But, on the largest and most scrutinized stage imaginable, Rockstar takes creative risks with its story, protagonists, and mechanics, and makes big leaps in what games can be. It’s unlikely other developers will catch up soon. In 2002, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City reshaped and refashioned pop culture to give us a playable version of a place and a time we already knew. A quarter of a century later, VI shows Rockstar at the peak of entertainment in its very own right.
